title: Scope functions overview
text: Walk me through let, run, with, apply and also. How do they differ? All five run a block on an object, and they differ on two axes. First, how the block sees the object: as this run, with, apply or as it let, also . Second, what the call returns: the lambda result let, run, with or the object itself apply, also . with is the only one that isn't an extension; you pass the object in as an argument. They're all inline , so they cost nothing at runtime. The choice is about readability and intent.

title: apply vs also
text: apply and also both return the object. When do you pick one over the other? I use apply to configure the object itself. Inside it, this is the object, so property assignments and setter calls read like a builder. I use also for an extra action that isn't part of building the object, like logging, validation, adding it to a list, or assigning it to a field. Because also names the object it , the outer this stays as it was, and that's exactly what you want when the side effect involves the enclosing class.

title: ?.let vs if-null check
text: When would you write x?.let { } instead of if x != null { } ? For a local val or a parameter, if x != null is clearer, and smart casts handle it. I reach for ?.let when x is a mutable var property or something the compiler can't smart-cast, such as an open property or a property from another module. ?.let reads the value once into it , which is a stable local, so there's no "smart cast impossible" error and no race between the check and the use. I don't use ?.let { } ?: run { } as an if/else, because the else branch also runs when the let block itself returns null.

title: run vs with vs T.run
text: There are two run functions plus with. What's the difference, and when is each one idiomatic? T.run { } is an extension. It makes T the receiver and returns the lambda result, which is good for computing something from an object, especially with ?.run . with obj { } does the same thing but takes the object as an argument, so it reads like "with this object, do these things". I use it for non-null objects where I'm calling many members, like a ViewBinding. Plain run { } isn't an extension at all. It's just a block that's also an expression. I use it to group statements where only an expression is allowed, most often after an elvis.

title: Scope functions under the hood
text: What do scope functions compile to, and what does that imply for return, performance and allocation? They're all inline with callsInPlace EXACTLY ONCE contracts. The compiler pastes the body in at the call site, so there's no lambda object, no virtual call, and no extra stack frame. The apply you see in source simply disappears in bytecode. That has three effects. A bare return inside one returns from the enclosing function. return@let exits only the block. And the compiler knows the block runs exactly once, so val initialization and smart casts after the block work.

title: takeIf / takeUnless
text: What do takeIf and takeUnless do, and where do they help or hurt? x.takeIf { pred it } returns x when the predicate is true and null otherwise. takeUnless is the inverse. They turn a condition into nullability, so you can chain ?. and ?: instead of writing if/else. They're good for things like file.takeIf { it.exists }?.readText . The catch is that the receiver is always evaluated first, even when the predicate fails, so expensive .takeIf { cheapCheck } still pays for expensive . And a long chain of takeIf, let and elvis is often worse than a plain if.

title: Choosing scope functions & readability
text: How do you decide which scope function to use, and when do you use none at all? I ask two questions: do I want the object back or a result, and do I need the outer this kept? That gives me apply or also versus let or run. Then I check whether a plain local val or an if would read better, and it often does. My team rules are: at most one scope function per expression, no nesting this -receiver functions apply inside with , always name it when nesting, and never use them just to avoid declaring a variable.

title: What extension functions are
text: What is an extension function, and what does it compile to on the JVM? An extension function lets you call receiver.foo on a type you don't own, without inheritance or wrappers. It doesn't modify the class at all. It compiles to a static method in a facade class named after the file, like StringExtKt , and the receiver becomes the first parameter. So "abc".isEmail compiles to StringExtKt.isEmail "abc" . That's why extensions can't touch private members, can't be overridden polymorphically, and why Java calls them as static utilities.

title: Static dispatch of extensions
text: If I declare fun Shape.name and fun Circle.name , then call name on a Shape variable holding a Circle , which one runs? The Shape one. Extensions are resolved statically at compile time from the declared static type of the expression, not the runtime type. The compiler sees Shape , picks Shape.name , and emits a static call. Overload resolution happens at compile time, and there's no vtable involved. If I need per-subtype behavior, I make it a member open or abstract , or I write one extension with a when over a sealed type.

title: Member wins over extension
text: What happens if a class already has a member function with the same name and signature as my extension? The member always wins. If the member's signature is applicable, the compiler never picks the extension, and the IDE warns "Extension is shadowed by a member". An extension with a different parameter list is just an overload, and overload resolution picks it normally. The danger is upgrades: if a library adds a member that matches my extension, my call sites silently switch to the library's implementation at the next compile, with no error.

title: Extensions on nullable receivers
text: How do extensions on nullable types work, and how does isNullOrEmpty let the compiler smart-cast afterward? Declare the receiver type as nullable, like fun String?.orDash . Then the call s.orDash doesn't need ?. , and inside the body this may be null, so you handle it yourself. That's how isNullOrEmpty , orEmpty and toString on Any? work. isNullOrEmpty also declares a contract, returns false implies this@isNullOrEmpty != null , so after if !s.isNullOrEmpty the compiler smart-casts s to non-null. Contracts are covered in the DSL chunk. The point here is that a nullable-receiver extension is null-safe by design, while s?.ext skips the call entirely on null.

title: Extension properties
text: Can extension properties have state? How would you attach data to a class you don't own, and what are the risks? No. Extension properties have no backing field, because they compile to static getter and setter methods and there's nowhere in the object to store state. So initializers aren't allowed, and each access recomputes in the getter. To attach data, you either use storage the type already provides, like View.setTag key, value , or an external map. An external map has to use weak keys, or it leaks every object you ever touched. Even then, an identity-based weak map on Android is easy to get wrong. Often the right answer is a wrapper class or a member on a type you do own.

title: Extension visibility & imports
text: How do visibility modifiers and imports work for extensions? How do you resolve two libraries defining the same extension? Extensions follow normal visibility. A private top-level extension is visible only in that file, internal only in the module, and public everywhere it's imported. An extension can only see what its scope can see. It can't touch the receiver's private or protected members, but a top-level extension can use private declarations in its own file. Callers in other packages must import it by name or with a star import. If two libraries clash, I import one with an alias, like import com.lib.a.toUiModel as toUiModelA , or call it in fully qualified form.

title: Extensions on companion objects
text: How do you write a "static-like" extension, like Intent.Companion.forDetail ... ? When does that work and when doesn't it? If a Kotlin class has a companion object, I can extend it with fun MyClass.Companion.create ... , and callers write MyClass.create ... as if it were static. Kotlin's companion is a real object instance, so the extension is just an extension on that object's type. The limit is that it only works when a companion exists. I can't add one to a Kotlin class I don't own that lacks one, and Java classes like Intent or String have no companion at all, so Intent.Companion doesn't exist. Then the options are a top-level factory function or an object holding factories.

title: Member extensions, dispatch vs extension receiver
text: What's a member extension? Explain dispatch receiver vs extension receiver, and which of them is virtual. A member extension is an extension declared inside a class, like class Formatter { fun Money.display = ... } . It has two implicit receivers: the extension receiver Money and the dispatch receiver the Formatter instance . It's only callable where a Formatter is in scope, inside the class or in with formatter { } . If you mark it open and override it, dispatch is virtual on the dispatch receiver, chosen by the runtime Formatter subclass. It's still static on the extension receiver, chosen by the declared type of Money . When names clash, the extension receiver's members win, and you reach the outer one with this@Formatter .

title: Designing extension APIs
text: When should something be an extension vs a member vs a plain top-level function? How do you design extensions for a large codebase? I make something a member when it's core to the type, needs private state, or needs polymorphism. I use an extension when I don't own the type, or when the function is a convenience that belongs to a specific layer, like Dto.toDomain in the data module, so the domain class stays clean of mapping concerns. I use a plain function when there's no natural "subject" object or there are two equal subjects. For a big codebase: scope extensions to the layer that needs them, keep them internal by default, avoid extending ultra-common types like String , Any and Context with domain logic, and make sure every extension is a pure function of its receiver plus its arguments, so it's trivially testable.

title: apply shadowing this
text: Find the bug, explain exactly why it happens, and fix it so it can't come back. A profile screen sends an update request. QA reports that after editing, the server receives the request but the user's displayed name never changes, and support sees about 1.2% of "profile update" tickets mentioning "my name reverts". There are no crashes, and the backend logs show requests arriving with name equal to the old name. The code passed review: class EditProfileViewModel private val api: ProfileApi : ViewModel { var name: String = "" // bound to the text field var bio: String = "" fun save current: Profile { val request = UpdateRequest current.id .apply { name = name // intent: copy VM's edited name bio = bio avatarUrl = current.avatarUrl } viewModelScope.launch { api.update request } } } class UpdateRequest val id: String { var name: String = ""; var bio: String = ""; var avatarUrl: String? = null } A red herring: the team recently upgraded Retrofit, and someone suspects serialization.

title: let returning null silently
text: What's going on, and how do you fix it and keep it from coming back? After release 4.12 rolled out to 50% of 2M DAU , product sees "login screen shown to already-logged-in users" rise from 0.1% to 3.4% of app opens. There are no crashes. The analytics funnel shows those users tap "login", and auto-login succeeds instantly. The change in 4.12 was a "cleanup" of the splash router: fun route session: Session? { session?.let { s - prefetcher.warmUp s.userId // new in 4.12: returns Job? null if prefetch disabled by flag } ?: navigator.toLogin session?.let { navigator.toHome it } } prefetcher.warmUp returns null when the remote flag prefetch enabled is off, and it's off for 70% of the rollout cohort. One more detail: the navigator ignores a second navigation within 300 ms on some devices , which is why only some users see it.

title: Static dispatch of extensions
text: Lead the review. What's the root cause, why did tests miss it, and what do we change? You're running a post-incident review. A feed with 6 item types FeedItem sealed interface: Post , Ad , Story , Poll , Video , Event shipped a "content descriptions for accessibility" change. A week later, TalkBack users report every item is announced as "Feed item" the generic text . Ad compliance also flags that ads aren't announced as "Sponsored", which is a legal requirement in some markets. The change: fun FeedItem.a11yLabel : String = "Feed item" fun Ad.a11yLabel : String = "Sponsored: $advertiser" fun Post.a11yLabel : String = "Post by $author" // ... one per subtype class FeedAdapter : ListAdapter<FeedItem, FeedVH Diff { override fun onBindViewHolder holder: FeedVH, position: Int { val item = getItem position // static type: FeedItem holder.itemView.contentDescription = item.a11yLabel holder.bind item } } Unit tests passed. They called Ad ... .a11yLabel directly. Screenshot tests passed because they don't check content descriptions. A red herring: the same release bumped RecyclerView, and one engineer believes view recycling reuses stale descriptions.

title: Over-chaining & readability
text: Review this. What's wrong functionally, what's wrong for maintainability, and what would you ask the author to write instead? You're reviewing a PR in a repository class that serves an offline-first article reader 800k MAU . The author is proud of "zero local variables": suspend fun article id: String : Article? = id.takeIf { it.isNotBlank } ?.let { dao.find it } ?.takeUnless { it.isStale clock.now } ?.also { analytics.cacheHit it.id } ?: id.takeIf { it.isNotBlank } ?.let { api.fetch it } ?.run { copy body = body.sanitize } ?.also { dao.upsert it } ?.also { analytics.cacheMiss it.id } Facts: api.fetch throws on network errors; dao.find returns Article? . Product reports that stale articles are shown offline about 0% of the time, and users see "Not found" when offline with a stale cache. That's a 2.1% complaint rate on the offline-reading NPS survey. Another reviewer approved it, saying "very idiomatic".

title: Extension properties hidden cost & leaks
text: Find the problems, quantify them, and fix them. A transactions list RecyclerView, typical 2,000 rows, fling-heavy on low-end devices 2 GB RAM, about 35% of users shows jank. Android vitals report slow frames at 18% on those devices vs 4% on high-end. A Perfetto trace shows onBindViewHolder at p95 = 6.8 ms budget about 16 ms per frame at 60 Hz, shared with layout and draw , with frequent GC pauses. LeakCanary separately reports TransactionsActivity retained after rotation. Relevant code: val Context.dateFmt: java.text.DateFormat get = java.text.SimpleDateFormat "dd MMM yyyy, HH:mm", resources.configuration.locales 0 val Long.asMoney: String get = java.text.NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance java.util.Locale "en", "IN" .format this / 100.0 private val rowColors = HashMap<Context, Int var Context.rowColor: Int get = rowColors.getOrPut this { ContextCompat.getColor this, R.color.row } set v { rowColors this = v } override fun onBindViewHolder h: VH, pos: Int { val t = getItem pos ; val ctx = h.itemView.context h.date.text = ctx.dateFmt.format java.util.Date t.timestamp h.amount.text = t.cents.asMoney h.itemView.setBackgroundColor ctx.rowColor } A red herring: the team's image loader was recently upgraded and someone wants to profile it first. There are no images in this list.

title: Member shadows extension after upgrade
text: What happened? How do you handle the live rollout, and how do you make this upgrade and future ones safe? Your app 3.5M DAU forwards analytics events to your own ingestion backend as well as to a vendor SDK. Years ago someone wrote: // EventExt.kt fun VendorEvent.toJson : String = buildJsonObject { put "name", name ; put "ts", timestampMs ; put "props", JsonObject props.mapValues { JsonPrimitive it.value } }.toString class EventForwarder private val backend: IngestApi { fun forward e: VendorEvent = backend.send e.toJson } You upgrade the vendor SDK from 4.x to 5.0 a Java library and ship to a 20% staged rollout. Within 2 hours your ingestion service's schema-rejection rate goes from 0.02% to 38% for the new app version. The rejected payloads look like {"event name":"checkout","time":"2026-10-30T10:12:01Z","attributes":{...}} . The build was green. CI shows about 1,200 compiler warnings, as usual. Red herring: the SDK release notes mention "new batching", and the backend team suspects batching changed payload sizes.

title: Extension sprawl & module design
text: How would you restructure this for a 10x larger team? Evaluate the tech lead's proposal. Your Android org is growing from 15 to about 150 engineers across 60 Gradle modules. Every feature module depends on :core:common , which holds 420 public extensions: 95 on Context , 70 on View , 60 on String , plus Fragment , Flow and others. Symptoms: changing any file in :core:common triggers rebuilds of 58 modules incremental build p50 goes from 40 s to 4.5 min after such a change . Three different fun Context.toast ... exist in different packages with different default durations. String.isValid means "valid email" in one package and "non-blank" in another. New hires complain that autocomplete on String shows 60 project suggestions. A tech lead proposes "one extensions module per type: :ext:context , :ext:view , :ext:string ".

title: ?.let then !! re-read
text: What's the bug, why does it only crash sometimes, and what's the correct fix? A file-upload screen shows progress. Crashlytics reports a new crash cluster of about 0.09% of upload sessions about 1,100 crashes per day , on all API levels, more on 8-core devices: Fatal Exception: java.lang.NullPointerException at com.app.upload.UploadManager.onProgress UploadManager.kt:41 at com.app.upload.ProgressRequestBody$writeTo$1.invoke ProgressRequestBody.kt:28 at okio.ForwardingSink.write ... ... OkHttp Dispatcher thread "OkHttp https://upload.app.com/..." class UploadManager { private var listener: ProgressListener? = null fun attach l: ProgressListener { listener = l } // main thread, Fragment onStart fun detach { listener = null } // main thread, Fragment onStop fun onProgress percent: Int { // called on OkHttp thread listener?.let { if percent % 5 == 0 listener!!.onProgress percent // line 41 } } } A teammate notes the crash "started after the Kotlin upgrade", because the exception type changed from KotlinNullPointerException in older builds.

title: Member extension receiver shadowing
text: Diagnose this. Why null for some events and binding objects for others? Fix it so the class of bug is designed out. The analytics team reports that for the last 3 weeks, 41% of button click events have screen = null and another 12% have values like com.app.databinding.ItemCartBinding@7f2a1c . Dashboards that rank screens by engagement are now useless. Nothing crashes. Three weeks ago a "tracking helper" was added to the shared base Fragment used by 80 screens: abstract class BaseFragment : Fragment { @Inject lateinit var analytics: Analytics protected fun View.onClickTracked event: String, action: - Unit { setOnClickListener { analytics.log event, mapOf "screen" to tag, "id" to id action } } } // usage in CartFragment binding.checkout.onClickTracked "button click" { viewModel.checkout } Fragments are added with replace R.id.container, CartFragment , "Cart" . Red herrings: the analytics SDK was also upgraded that month, and someone suspects ProGuard/R8 stripping fragment tags.

title: Invariance
text: String is a subtype of Any . Why can't I pass a MutableList<String to a function that takes a MutableList<Any ? Generic types in Kotlin are invariant by default. MutableList<String and MutableList<Any have no subtype relationship, even though String is a subtype of Any . If the compiler allowed it, the function could call add 42 on what it thinks is a list of Any . That would put an Int into a list the caller still holds as MutableList<String , and the caller would crash with a ClassCastException later, far from the bug. Invariance is the compiler refusing to let that happen. Java has the same rule: List<String is not a List<Object .

title: out/in variance (producer/consumer)
text: Explain out and in in Kotlin generics. When do you use each? out T makes a type covariant: if Dog is an Animal , then Producer<Dog is a Producer<Animal . The price is that T can only appear in output positions, like return types and val s. in T makes it contravariant: Consumer<Animal is a Consumer<Dog , and T can only appear in input positions, like parameters. The rule of thumb is "producer out, consumer in." Kotlin's List<out E is covariant and Comparable<in T is contravariant. The compiler checks every member against the declared variance.

title: List<out E> vs MutableList
text: Why is List<String assignable to List<Any but MutableList<String isn't assignable to MutableList<Any ? Because of how they're declared. kotlin.collections.List is List<out E , so it's covariant. Its API only hands E out: get , first , iteration. MutableList<E adds add E and set index, E , which take E in, so it has to be invariant. Both are the same java.util.List at runtime. The variance exists only in Kotlin's type system. That's a compile-time view of the object, not a property of the object itself.

title: Type erasure
text: What is type erasure, and what can't you do in Kotlin on the JVM because of it? On the JVM, generic type arguments exist only at compile time. After type checking, List<String and List<Int both compile down to plain java.util.List , and the compiler inserts casts where values come out. So at runtime I can't ask x is List<String , can't write T::class or is T in a normal generic function, and can't overload two functions that differ only in type arguments. What survives are declared signatures in class metadata, which is what reflection-based libraries like Gson and Retrofit read. The escape hatches are reified type parameters on inline functions, or passing a Class / KClass / KType explicitly.

title: Upper bounds & where
text: How do upper bounds work in Kotlin generics, and when do you need a where clause? <T : Number restricts T to Number or its subtypes, so inside the function I can call Number members on a T . With no bound, the implicit bound is Any? , so T may be nullable. When I need more than one bound, for example "a CharSequence that's also Comparable to itself," I use where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T . Only one bound can be a class. The rest must be interfaces. On the JVM, the parameter erases to the first bound, which matters for Java interop and reflection.

title: Declaration-site vs use-site variance
text: What's the difference between declaration-site and use-site variance in Kotlin? When do you need type projections? Declaration-site variance is when the class itself is declared out T or in T , like List<out E . Every use is covariant automatically. Use-site variance is for invariant classes like MutableList or Array that both read and write T . At a specific use I write MutableList<out Number or MutableList<in Int , which is called a type projection. A projection restricts what I can call through that reference. out lets me read but turns add into "takes Nothing," and in lets me write but reading gives me Any? . It's Java's ? extends / ? super , but Kotlin lets you declare variance once on the type, so you need projections less often.

title: Star projection
text: What does List< or MutableList< mean? How is it different from List<Any? and from Java raw types? means "some specific type argument I don't know." It's a safe way to refer to any instantiation. For an out parameter, Foo< is Foo<out Upper , so I can read values as the upper bound, usually Any? . For an in parameter it's Foo<in Nothing , so I can't pass anything in. For an invariant one like MutableList< , I can read as Any? but can't add anything. That's different from MutableList<Any? , which really accepts anything: a MutableList<String is a MutableList< but not a MutableList<Any? . Unlike Java raw types, star projections are type-safe, and the compiler won't let me write into one.

title: Array invariance vs Java covariant arrays
text: Java arrays are covariant and Kotlin's Array<T is invariant. Why did Kotlin change this, and what does it mean when you call Java APIs that take arrays? In Java, String is an Object , so you can store an Integer into it through the Object reference. The JVM catches that at runtime with an ArrayStoreException . That's a type hole patched with a runtime check. Kotlin makes Array<T invariant, so Array<String isn't an Array<Any , and I use Array<out Any when I only need to read. Arrays also keep their element class at runtime, unlike List , which is why creating an Array<T needs a reified T . And Array<Int is a boxed Integer , while IntArray is a primitive int .

title: Reified type parameters
text: How do reified type parameters work, why do they require inline , and what are their limits? A reified type parameter works because the function is inlined. The compiler copies the body into each call site and substitutes the actual type argument, so T::class.java becomes the literal User.class and x is T becomes instanceof User . Nothing survives erasure. The type is known at compile time at every call site. That's why it needs inline : a normal function has one body shared by all callers, so there's nothing to substitute. The limits: the caller must know the concrete type, so a non-reified T can't be forwarded; T::class loses nested arguments, so List<User becomes just List ; Java can't call it; and every call site gets a copy of the body.

title: T vs T : Any nullability
text: In fun <T foo value: T , can value be null? When should you write <T : Any , and what is T & Any ? Yes, it can be null. An unbounded T has the implicit bound Any? , so foo<String? null is legal. Inside, T is "possibly nullable." I can't call members without a safe call, except toString , hashCode , and equals , which have Any? extensions. I write <T : Any when null must be impossible, for example when the API uses null to mean "absent," or when I need KClass<T , whose parameter is bounded by Any . T & Any is the definitely non-nullable version of a possibly-nullable T . It's stable since Kotlin 1.7, and it mainly exists for overriding Java methods with @NotNull generic parameters.

title: Nothing as bottom type in generics
text: How does Nothing work in generics? Why can emptyList be shared for every element type, and why does UiState.Loading often extend UiState<Nothing ? Nothing is a subtype of every type, and it has no values. Combine that with covariance: if Foo is declared out T , then Foo<Nothing is a subtype of Foo<User , Foo<String , and every other Foo . So one singleton like the stdlib's internal EmptyList : List<Nothing can serve as an empty list of anything. The same trick lets object Loading : UiState<Nothing be a valid UiState<User without a type parameter on the object, because objects can't have type parameters. It only works with out . For an invariant type, Foo<Nothing is useless.

title: @UnsafeVariance and variance-check rules
text: What does @UnsafeVariance do, when is it legitimate, and which members are exempt from variance checks anyway? @UnsafeVariance suppresses the compiler's variance check for one position. The stdlib uses it on List<out E .contains element: @UnsafeVariance E and indexOf . Those take E as a parameter, which normally breaks out , but they only compare the element and never store it, so no bad value can leak out later. It's legitimate only when the value in the "wrong" position is never stored and never returned as T . Separately, the compiler doesn't check variance on constructor parameters or private members, because outsiders can't use those to inject a wrong value.

title: Generic type inference
text: How does Kotlin infer generic type arguments, when does inference fail, and what tools do you have when it does? Kotlin infers type arguments from the value arguments and from the expected type, for example the declared type of the variable or the parameter the result is passed into. When nothing constrains a type variable, as in val x = mutableListOf , it fails with "Not enough information to infer type variable." When arguments disagree, it picks a common supertype, sometimes an intersection like Comparable< & Serializable , which then leaks into my public types. My tools: an explicit type argument mutableListOf<User , a declared variable type, to infer just some arguments stable since Kotlin 1.7 , and builder inference for buildList { } -style lambdas. That runs automatically since 1.7, and the K2 compiler in Kotlin 2.0 handles more cases.

title: Variance of function types and position flipping
text: How does variance work for function types? Why can Flow<out T have a collect collector: FlowCollector<T method even though T appears in a parameter? A function type P - R is Function1<in P, out R . It's contravariant in its parameters and covariant in its return. So Animal - String can stand in for Dog - Any . Variance positions compose like signs: an in inside an in becomes an out . In Flow<out T , collect takes a FlowCollector<T , and FlowCollector is declared in T . A parameter is an in position, and in T inside it flips again, so T ends up in an out position. That's legal for out T without any annotation. Same reason fun forEach action: T - Unit is fine on a covariant type, while fun listener : T - Unit isn't.

title: Generic info that survives erasure (super type tokens, typeOf)
text: If generics are erased, how do Gson, Retrofit, Moshi, and kotlinx.serialization know that a field or return type is List<User ? What are super type tokens and typeOf<T ? Erasure removes type arguments from values and expressions , but the compiler still writes generic declaration signatures into the class file as Signature attributes. That covers fields, method parameters and returns, and superclasses. Reflection exposes them through Field.genericType , Method.genericReturnType , and Class.genericSuperclass . Retrofit reads the generic return type of your interface method, and that's how it knows List<User . A super type token exploits the superclass case: object : TypeToken<List<User {} creates an anonymous subclass whose superclass signature records List<User . In Kotlin, typeOf<T with a reified T gives a full KType , including nested arguments and nullability, computed at the call site. Strip the Signature attributes with R8, and every reflection-based approach breaks.

title: Recursive bounds and self-types
text: What does T : Comparable<T mean, and how do you write a fluent builder hierarchy in Kotlin, which has no self type? T : Comparable<T is a recursive bound. It means "a T that can be compared with other Ts," which is what sorted and maxOf need. For builders, Java uses Builder<B extends Builder<B so base-class setters return the subclass type. Kotlin has no Self type, so the same pattern needs an abstract self or an unchecked this as B . In Kotlin I usually skip it altogether: named and default arguments, copy on data classes, or apply {} on the concrete type give fluent construction. If I really need base methods that return the caller's type, a generic extension fun <T : Base T.withX : T = apply { ... } does it without recursive generics.

title: Unchecked cast `as T`
text: What's the bug, why does the "safe cast" not return null, and how do you fix it properly? A shared in-memory cache is used by 12 feature modules. Crashlytics shows a new crash on the Profile screen: 0.4% of sessions, starting with the release that added "prefetch profile on login" in a different module. Nobody touched the Profile screen. object MemoryCache { private val map = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, Any fun put key: String, value: Any { map key = value } @Suppress "UNCHECKED CAST" fun <T get key: String : T? = map key as? T // "safe cast, returns null if wrong type" } // Login module new : MemoryCache.put "profile", profileDtoFromLogin // ProfileDto // Profile module old : val user: User? = MemoryCache.get "profile" // ProfileViewModel.kt:42 user?.let { render it } ?: loadFromNetwork Fatal Exception: java.lang.ClassCastException: com.app.login.ProfileDto cannot be cast to com.app.profile.User at com.app.profile.ProfileViewModel.load ProfileViewModel.kt:42 The release also bumped Room and enabled a new R8 rule. Those are red herrings.

title: Generic arrays
text: Explain the crash, why the tests didn't catch it, and fix the class. A teammate wrote a fixed-size ring buffer for recent search queries. Unit tests with RingBuffer<Int pass. In the app, the search screen crashes on open for every user who has search history. That's 100% repro on the internal dogfood build. class RingBuffer<T private val capacity: Int { @Suppress "UNCHECKED CAST" private val items: Array<T? = arrayOfNulls<Any? capacity as Array<T? private var head = 0 private var size = 0 fun add item: T { items head + size % capacity = item; if size < capacity size++ else head = head + 1 % capacity } @Suppress "UNCHECKED CAST" fun snapshot : Array<T = Array<Any? size { items head + it % capacity } as Array<T } // SearchViewModel private val recent = RingBuffer<String 20 val chips: Array<String = recent.snapshot // SearchViewModel.kt:31 java.lang.ClassCastException: java.lang.Object cannot be cast to java.lang.String at com.app.search.SearchViewModel.<init SearchViewModel.kt:31 Red herrings: the crash started after the Compose BOM update, and the tests use RingBuffer<Int but only call add / size .

title: Use-site variance in API design
text: What would you change in the API and why? Explain the crash. You're reviewing a PR in a core-users module used by 9 feature modules. Since it landed, three teams have added copy-paste comparators and one added an unchecked cast. Code under review: open class User val id: String, val lastSeen: Long class Admin id: String, lastSeen: Long, val permissions: Set<String : User id, lastSeen class Guest id: String : User id, 0 val byLastSeen: Comparator<User = compareByDescending { it.lastSeen } fun <T MutableList<T .sortSafely cmp: Comparator<T { sortWith cmp } fun mergeInto target: MutableList<User , src: List<User { target.addAll src } fun countActive users: MutableList<User : Int = users.count { it.lastSeen 0 } // Feature module A: val admins: MutableList<Admin = loadAdmins admins.sortSafely byLastSeen // doesn't compile - they wrote byLastSeenAdmin @Suppress "UNCHECKED CAST" mergeInto admins as MutableList<User , listOf Guest "g1" // compiles admins.first .permissions // Crashlytics: Guest cannot be cast to Admin

title: Erasure with Gson and reified
text: Walk me through diagnosing and fixing this. E-commerce app, 2.1M DAU. A refactor "extracted a generic JSON helper" to replace 60 hand-written TypeToken s. After rollout to 50%, the crash-free sessions rate drops from 99.85% to 98.3%, all on the Orders and Wishlist screens. Product screens work fine. inline fun <reified T Gson.fromJsonTyped json: String : T = fromJson json, T::class.java // OrdersRepository val orders: List<Order = gson.fromJsonTyped body // ProductRepository val product: Product = gson.fromJsonTyped body Fatal Exception: java.lang.ClassCastException: com.google.gson.internal.LinkedTreeMap cannot be cast to com.app.orders.Order at com.app.orders.OrdersViewModel$uiState$1.invokeSuspend OrdersViewModel.kt:57 Same day, the backend changed the createdAt date format, and Gson was bumped by a minor version. Those are red herrings, but the on-call engineer suspects both.

title: Erasure, R8 and Signature attributes
text: What happened, and how do you get the upgrade out safely? You upgrade AGP from 7.4 to 8.x and Kotlin to 2.0 in one PR. Debug builds and all unit tests pass. The internal release build minified crashes on the first network call on all devices: java.lang.IllegalStateException: TypeToken must be created with a type argument: new TypeToken<... {}; When using code shrinkers ProGuard, R8, ... make sure that generic signatures are preserved. at com.google.gson.reflect.TypeToken.<init ... at com.app.data.CartRepository$special$$inlined$fromJsonTyped$1.<init ... java.lang.ClassCastException: java.lang.Class cannot be cast to java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType at retrofit2.HttpServiceMethod.parseAnnotations ... Gson is 2.10.1, and Retrofit is pinned to an older 2.x. The release goes to 8M users in 10 days. A teammate proposes reverting the Kotlin 2.0 upgrade, "because K2 changed how reified works."

title: Phantom types and generic type-state
text: What is a phantom type parameter, and how would you use one in Kotlin to make illegal states unrepresentable at compile time? A phantom type parameter is a type parameter that appears in the class declaration but is never used in any field or member. It exists only to tag the type. For example, Id<User and Id<Order both wrap a String , but they're different types, so I can't pass an order id to a user lookup. I can also encode state: Form<Unvalidated vs Form<Validated , where submit is only available as an extension on Form<Validated . The tag is erased at runtime, so it costs nothing beyond the wrapper object, and if the wrapper is a @JvmInline value class it can often be free.

title: Designing Result/UiState<out T>
text: Design the shared state type. Cover variance, mapping, what goes in the type vs outside, and how it behaves in a StateFlow. You're defining the shared UI state type for 40 screens in a 25-engineer app. Current state: each screen has its own sealed class OrdersState , ProfileState , ... , with duplicated loading/error handling, and a previous attempt at a shared type looked like this: sealed class UiState<T { class Loading<T : UiState<T data class Success<T val data: T : UiState<T data class Error<T val message: String : UiState<T } Reported issues: every Loading and Error allocates an object, MutableStateFlow<UiState<Orders can't be assigned a UiState<Nothing , mapping states needs unchecked casts state as UiState<B , and a screen needing "show cached data while refreshing" can't express it.

title: Retrofit CallAdapter and erasure

Your team added a custom Retrofit CallAdapter.Factory so suspend APIs can return a sealed ApiResponse<T instead of throwing. It works for ApiResponse<Unit endpoints. For endpoints returning data, QA reports blank screens, and in staging logs: E/ProfileVM: java.lang.ClassCastException: com.squareup.moshi.LinkedHashTreeMap... Red herring: the backend returns slightly different JSON casing in staging.

title: Variance and shared mutable generic state
text: Why does this compile and crash, and how would you redesign the bus? A typed event bus lets modules publish and listen to events. After a refactor to "make it more flexible with variance", QA reports intermittent ClassCastException in the checkout module only when a promo banner is shown. Review the code: open class AppEvent class CartUpdated val items: Int : AppEvent class PromoShown val code: String : AppEvent class Bus<out E : AppEvent { private val listeners = mutableListOf< E - Unit // private: not variance-checked fun listen l: @UnsafeVariance E - Unit { listeners += l } // "needed it to compile" fun publish e: @UnsafeVariance E { listeners.forEach { it e } } } val cartBus: Bus<CartUpdated = Bus cartBus.listen { println "cart has ${it.items} items" } val anyBus: Bus<AppEvent = cartBus // allowed because Bus is 'out' anyBus.publish PromoShown "SAVE10" // compiles java.lang.ClassCastException: com.app.PromoShown cannot be cast to com.app.CartUpdated at com.app.checkout.CheckoutKt$main$1.invoke Checkout.kt:12 Red herring: the stack mentions a lambda, and someone suspects R8 inlining.

title: Backing fields (`field`)
text: What is field in a Kotlin property accessor, when does the compiler actually generate a backing field, and what goes wrong if you write set value { name = value } ? A Kotlin property is a getter, and for a var also a setter. The JVM field behind it is optional. The compiler generates a backing field only when at least one accessor uses the default implementation, or when a custom accessor mentions field . Inside an accessor, field is the only way to reach that storage. Writing name = value inside the setter of name calls the setter again, so it recurses until you get a StackOverflowError .

title: Backing-property pattern
text: Why do Android codebases declare private val state = MutableStateFlow ... next to val state: StateFlow<... = state ? What does it actually protect, and is there a language-level replacement? It is the backing-property pattern. The class keeps the mutable type private and exposes only the read-only supertype, so only the owner can write state, which gives unidirectional data flow. It is a compile-time API boundary, not a runtime one: anyone can downcast state as MutableStateFlow and write to it. asStateFlow closes that hole by wrapping the flow in a read-only wrapper. Kotlin 2.3 added explicit backing fields as an Experimental feature behind -Xexplicit-backing-fields . They let you declare one property with a public read-only type and a private mutable field .

title: Custom getter vs initializer
text: What is the difference between val total = items.sumOf { it.price } , val total get = items.sumOf { it.price } and val total by lazy { items.sumOf { it.price } } ? The initializer runs once, during construction, and stores the result in a backing field. The custom getter has no field and recomputes on every access, so it is always fresh but costs O n per read. lazy computes on first access, caches the result forever, and adds a delegate object plus thread-safety overhead. Choose by asking two questions: can the inputs change after construction, and how often is the value read compared with how often it changes.

title: How delegated properties compile
text: What does val x: T by something compile to? What does the delegate object need to provide? The compiler creates a hidden field, x$delegate , that holds the result of the expression after by . It then generates a getter that calls x$delegate.getValue this, ::x , and for a var a setter that calls setValue this, ::x, value . The delegate needs operator fun getValue thisRef, property: KProperty< and, for var , setValue . These can be member or extension functions, and the delegate doesn't have to implement any interface. lazy works because the stdlib has an inline extension Lazy<T .getValue that returns value .

title: const val vs val vs @JvmField
text: When can you use const val , how does it differ from a plain val or a @JvmField val in bytecode, and why does that difference matter? const val is a compile-time constant. It's allowed only at top level or inside an object or companion, only for primitives and String , and only with a constant initializer and no custom getter. The compiler inlines the literal value into every call site , and it compiles to a public static final field, so it can also be used in annotations. A plain val is a private field behind a getter, read at runtime. @JvmField exposes the field directly, with no getter, but it is still read at runtime, not inlined. The trap: because const is copied into consumers, changing it in a library doesn't affect already-compiled consumers until they are recompiled.

title: Top-level properties
text: How do top-level properties compile on the JVM, when are they initialized, and what are the thread-safety and initialization-order consequences? A top-level property in Prefs.kt becomes a private static field of a facade class PrefsKt , with a static getter. Its initializer runs in PrefsKt 's static initializer when the class is first initialized, which happens on first access to any top-level member of that file. The JVM guarantees class initialization runs exactly once and safely publishes the values, so initialization is thread-safe. Mutation afterwards isn't. Across files, a circular initialization can expose default values null / 0 even for non-null types.

title: lazy thread-safety modes
text: Explain LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED , PUBLICATION and NONE : how each is implemented and when you would pick each on Android. SYNCHRONIZED is the default. It uses double-checked locking with a volatile field, so the initializer runs at most once and every thread sees the same value. PUBLICATION allows several threads to run the initializer concurrently, but a compare-and-set means only the first result wins and everyone sees it. NONE has no locking and no volatile, so it's only correct if the value is created and used on a single thread. After initialization the default mode costs just one volatile read, so I use NONE for main-thread-only objects as a micro-optimisation, and I keep SYNCHRONIZED whenever more than one thread can touch the value.

title: Delegates.observable / vetoable / notNull
text: What do Delegates.observable , Delegates.vetoable and Delegates.notNull do, when does each callback run, and when would you use them in an Android codebase? observable initial { prop, old, new - } stores the value and calls the handler after each assignment. It fires even if the new value equals the old one. vetoable initial { prop, old, new - Boolean } runs the handler before the assignment, and returning false rejects the new value. notNull is a var that throws IllegalStateException if you read it before assigning it. Unlike lateinit , it works with primitives. I use observable for local reactions such as an adapter that refreshes when items is set, vetoable for cheap validation, and I reach for StateFlow when anyone outside the class needs to observe.

title: Map delegation
text: How does val name: String by map work, what happens when the key is missing or the type is wrong, and where is map delegation a good or bad idea? The stdlib has getValue and setValue operator extensions on Map and MutableMap . They use property.name as the key, so val name by map is map "name" , cast to the property type. val needs a Map<String, and var needs a MutableMap . The map is read on every access, so it stays live, not copied. A missing key throws NoSuchElementException unless the map was wrapped with withDefault . A wrong value type fails with a ClassCastException at the point of access, not at construction. That makes it fine for loosely typed, already-validated data like remote config or test fixtures, and bad for core domain models.

title: Class delegation (`by`) for composition
text: What does class LoggingRepo private val inner: Repo : Repo by inner generate, and why is it the idiomatic way to build decorators in Kotlin? Class delegation implements an interface by forwarding every member you don't override to the object after by . The compiler generates the forwarding methods and keeps the delegate in a hidden field. You override only what you want to change, like logging, caching or metrics, and the rest passes through. It works only for interfaces, not classes, and it gives you the decorator pattern without writing 30 one-line forwarders or inheriting from a concrete class.

title: Custom ReadOnlyProperty / ReadWriteProperty
text: Write a custom property delegate, for example a Fragment-argument delegate, and explain the type parameters of ReadWriteProperty<T, V and the design choices you made. ReadOnlyProperty<in T, out V has getValue thisRef: T, property: KProperty< : V . ReadWriteProperty<in T, V adds setValue . T is the owner type: the delegate can only be used inside classes of that type, and it gets the instance through thisRef . V is the value type. For a Fragment argument delegate, T is Fragment , the key is property.name , and the value lives in arguments , not in the delegate. That matters because the Bundle is saved and restored across process death, while a field in the delegate would not be.

title: Android delegates: viewModels, activityViewModels, navGraphViewModels, navArgs
text: What do by viewModels , by activityViewModels , by navGraphViewModels and by navArgs actually return, when is it legal to access them, and how do you choose the ViewModel scope? All four are Lazy implementations. viewModels and activityViewModels return a ViewModelLazy that, on first access, asks a ViewModelProvider for the VM using an owner's ViewModelStore . That owner is the Fragment, the Activity requireActivity or a NavBackStackEntry for a nav graph. navArgs returns NavArgsLazy , which reads arguments and calls the generated Safe Args fromBundle . Declaring them is free, but the first access must happen while the Fragment is attached , normally from onCreate / onViewCreated onwards. Access too early or after detach and you get an IllegalStateException . Scope means lifetime: the Fragment for screen state, the nav graph for a multi-screen flow, the Activity only for state that truly spans the whole Activity.

title: lazy failure semantics & memory
text: What happens if a lazy initializer throws? What does a Lazy keep alive in memory before and after initialization, and how can by lazy cause a leak? If the initializer throws, nothing is cached. The exception propagates, and the next access runs the initializer again. That is good for transient failures but bad when the initializer is expensive or has side effects, because you get retry storms. Before initialization, the Lazy holds the initializer lambda and everything it captured. The stdlib sets the initializer to null after success, so captured objects are released. The value itself is held as long as the Lazy is, which means as long as its owner. So by lazy leaks when a long-lived owner a singleton or a top-level property caches something that holds an Activity, Fragment or View, or when it's never initialized and keeps the captured lambda forever.

title: Class delegation semantics & limits
text: With class delegation, if the delegate calls one of its own methods internally, does the wrapper's override run? What else does by not do that inheritance would? No. Delegation is forwarding, not inheritance. When inner.addAll internally calls this.add , this is the inner object, so your wrapper's add override never runs. Only callers that go through the wrapper see the overrides. Also, by forwards only interface members. It doesn't forward Any members equals / hashCode / toString , it can't reach protected or non-interface members of the delegate, and it binds the delegate once at construction. If your design depends on the inner object calling back into the wrapper, you need inheritance or an explicit callback, not by .

title: provideDelegate & PropertyDelegateProvider
text: What is provideDelegate , when is it called relative to getValue , and what real problem does it solve that a plain delegate can't? If the object after by has an operator fun provideDelegate thisRef, property , the compiler calls it once per property, when the owner is being constructed , and stores whatever it returns as the real delegate. getValue and setValue are then called on that returned object. This gives you a hook at declaration time with the property's name and type in hand, so you can validate duplicate keys, wrong types , register the property in a schema, or pick a delegate implementation. A plain delegate only finds out about the property on first access. The stdlib's PropertyDelegateProvider fun interface lets you write a provider as a lambda.

title: Delegating to another property, local delegates, delegation cost
text: Explain var old by this::new , local delegated properties such as val x by lazy {} inside a function, and the runtime cost of delegation objects, reflection, bytecode . Since Kotlin 1.4 a property can delegate to another property via a reference: by this::new , by ::topLevel or by other::prop . The compiler then calls the target's accessors directly, without a delegate object. This is the clean way to rename a public property: keep the old name @Deprecated and delegate it to the new one. Local delegated properties since 1.1 let you write val token by lazy { ... } inside a function, so it's computed only if a branch actually reads it. Costs: each ordinary delegated property means one delegate object per owner instance, plus a forwarding call per access. The class also gets static, lightweight KProperty objects. These don't need kotlin-reflect, but they are extra metadata and allocations at class init.

title: Custom getter allocating state
text: Find the bug, explain why the symptoms look exactly like this, and fix it. A new filter screen never updates. QA: "Tap a chip, nothing changes; rotate the device and it shows the default filter." No crashes, and logs show onFilterSelected being called. 5% of the team's screens use this ViewModel template. class FilterViewModel : ViewModel { private val filter get = MutableStateFlow Filter.ALL val filter: StateFlow<Filter get = filter fun onFilterSelected f: Filter { Log.d "Filter", "selected $f" filter.value = f } } // Fragment viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle Lifecycle.State.STARTED { vm.filter.collect { chips.check it.chipId } } } A reviewer suspects repeatOnLifecycle or a missing distinctUntilChanged .

title: `by lazy` on Fragment views
text: What's wrong, why does it show only after going back, and how do you fix it properly? Crash-free sessions dropped from 99.7% to 99.5% after a refactor that "removed findViewById boilerplate". The top crash is not a crash at all: users report the order list going blank after they return from the details screen. LeakCanary in debug shows OrdersFragment → ordersList$delegate → SynchronizedLazyImpl. value → RecyclerView detached . A crash in the same release is unrelated: NullPointerException in a third-party chat SDK. That's the red herring. class OrdersFragment : Fragment R.layout.fragment orders { private val ordersList by lazy { requireView .findViewById<RecyclerView R.id.orders } private val adapter = OrdersAdapter override fun onViewCreated view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle? { ordersList.adapter = adapter viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle Lifecycle.State.STARTED { vm.orders.collect { adapter.submitList it } } } } }

Crashlytics shows a new top crash, about 1,100 events per day, 0.04% of sessions, 70% on Android 10–12 low-end devices: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Can't access ViewModels from detached fragment at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.getViewModelStore Fragment.java:... at androidx.lifecycle.ViewModelLazy.getValue ViewModelProvider.kt:... at com.app.checkout.CouponFragment.getVm CouponFragment.kt:31 at com.app.checkout.CouponFragment.onCouponTimeout$lambda$3 CouponFragment.kt:88 at android.os.Handler.handleCallback Handler.java:... title: Preferences property delegate design
text: Evaluate the current delegate design, then decide how to migrate. Can you keep var x by ... on top of DataStore? The app has a Settings class with 45 properties like var darkMode by prefs.boolean "dark mode", false , built on a custom ReadWriteProperty over SharedPreferences. It is read from 120 call sites, including Compose code and Application.onCreate . Android vitals: ANR rate 0.41% the bad-behaviour threshold is 0.47% . The top ANR cluster is in QueuedWork.waitToFinish during Activity.onStop , and StrictMode in debug flags DiskReadViolation from Settings.getDarkMode . The team wants to "move to DataStore but keep the nice by syntax."

title: const val stale across modules
text: Explain how one source value yields two behaviours in the same release line, and fix both the immediate issue and the process. A feature module :payments reads PaymentConfig.MAX RETRIES from the :core-config module. Last Tuesday :core-config changed const val MAX RETRIES = 3 to 5 , and CI went green. Production telemetry still shows the checkout flow retrying exactly 3 times for 18% of sessions. Those sessions are all on build 8.12.0, shipped from the release branch. Sessions on 8.12.1 built on a different CI agent retry 5 times. Crashes are flat. The backend team claims "the server rate limiter changed that week" red herring .

title: Delegation in Compose: `by remember { mutableStateOf() }`
text: How does var count by remember { mutableStateOf 0 } work as a delegated property, and what goes wrong when you use it incorrectly, for example inside a lambda or when the state is created outside composition? mutableStateOf 0 creates a MutableState<Int . remember { } caches that object across recompositions in the composition's slot table. by is the property delegate: androidx.compose.runtime provides inline extension operators State<T .getValue and MutableState<T .setValue , which read and write .value . The read goes through the snapshot system, which records "this composition scope read this state". A later write invalidates that scope. So by is only syntax. The behaviour comes from .value access, and the delegation is resolved at compile time with no delegate object per property.

title: lazy initialization deadlock & ANR
text: Explain the deadlock, how you'd confirm it, and fix it without making startup slower. App on 4M DAU. ANR rate rose from 0.22% to 0.55% threshold 0.47% after release 9.3. Top ANR cluster about 60% : main thread blocked in SynchronizedLazyImpl.getValue inside CartProvider , while a DefaultDispatcher-worker-3 thread is blocked in SynchronizedLazyImpl.getValue inside PricingEngine . Thread dump excerpt: "main" prio=5 tid=1 Blocked at com.app.PricingEngine$Companion.getRules PricingEngine.kt:21 // waiting for monitor held by worker-3 at com.app.CartProvider.<init CartProvider.kt:14 "DefaultDispatcher-worker-3" Blocked at com.app.CartProvider.getInstance CartProvider.kt:30 // waiting for monitor held by main at com.app.PricingEngine$rules$2.invoke PricingEngine.kt:25 Only a few percent of cold starts hit it, mostly on 4-core devices. A reviewer suspects the new analytics SDK red herring .

title: Decorator via `by` and interface evolution
text: Run the post-incident review: causes, contributing factors, what you'd change in code and process. Post-incident review. An AuditedPaymentGateway decorates PaymentGateway using class AuditedPaymentGateway private val real: PaymentGateway, private val audit: AuditLog : PaymentGateway by real . It overrides charge to write an audit record. Release 7.2 added fun chargeWithToken token: String, cents: Long to the PaymentGateway interface for a new checkout. The new method went through the decorator via compiler-generated forwarding, so 41k payments about 6% of transactions over 9 days were charged with no audit record . No crash, no failed tests: the new method was covered by gateway tests but not by decorator tests. Finance noticed a reconciliation gap.

title: activityViewModels scope misuse
text: Critique the design and propose a scoping and state-persistence plan, with a migration path that doesn't stop feature work. An e-commerce app single Activity, 14 Fragments uses private val shared: AppStateViewModel by activityViewModels in 9 Fragments as a convenient shared store. It holds the cart, selected address, applied coupon, filters and the last search results about 1.8 MB of parsed product models . Symptoms: after completing checkout and starting a new one, the old coupon appears pre-applied QA: "ghost coupon" . Memory profiler shows the retained size of AppStateViewModel at 14 MB after a long session. TransactionTooLargeException appears in some onSaveInstanceState paths 0.02% sessions . Crash-free is 99.6%. Product wants a "guest checkout" flow that can open from three entry points, and for the cart to survive process death.

title: Read-only vs immutable collections
text: Kotlin has List and MutableList . Is a List immutable? What exactly does the type guarantee? No. List is a read-only interface : it only lacks mutator methods. It says "you can't mutate it through this reference", not "nobody can mutate it". At runtime both List and MutableList map to java.util.List , so the same object can be mutated through another reference, by a cast, or from Java. If I need a real guarantee I use a defensive copy or a truly immutable type like ImmutableList from kotlinx.collections.immutable.

title: List vs Array vs IntArray
text: What is the difference between List<Int , Array<Int and IntArray ? When do you choose each? IntArray compiles to a primitive int : no boxing, 4 bytes per element. Array<Int compiles to Integer , so every element is a boxed object. List<Int is usually an ArrayList backed by an Object of boxed Integer s, but it is resizable and has the full collection API. I default to List for app-level data. I switch to IntArray / LongArray / FloatArray for large numeric data or hot paths: pixel buffers, sensor samples, chart points, ID sets in the 100k range.

title: Default implementations & ordering
text: What concrete classes do listOf , mutableListOf , mapOf , setOf and their friends return, and what ordering guarantees do you get? mutableListOf gives an ArrayList . mapOf / mutableMapOf give a LinkedHashMap , and setOf / mutableSetOf a LinkedHashSet , so iteration follows insertion order, and the docs promise that. hashMapOf / hashSetOf give plain HashMap / HashSet with no ordering promise. sortedMapOf / sortedSetOf are TreeMap / TreeSet . Empty and single-element factories return special classes EmptyList , Collections.singletonList , and listOf a, b, c is an Arrays.asList wrapper on the JVM. That's why casting them to mutable fails in odd ways. I rely on the documented ordering , never on the concrete class.

title: Sequences basics
text: What is a Sequence in Kotlin and how does it differ from operating on a List ? Collection operators are eager and horizontal: filter runs over every element and builds a full list, then map runs over that list and builds another. A Sequence is lazy and vertical: intermediate operations only build a pipeline, nothing runs until a terminal operation like toList , first or sum , and then each element goes through the whole chain before the next one starts. That avoids intermediate lists and lets short-circuiting operators like take and first stop early.

title: groupBy / associateBy / associate / partition
text: Explain groupBy , associateBy , associate , associateWith , partition and groupingBy . What happens with duplicate keys? groupBy builds Map<K, List<T and keeps every element. associateBy builds Map<K, T , and on duplicate keys the last element wins silently. associate takes a lambda returning a Pair and also lets the last one win. associateWith uses the elements as keys and computes values. partition splits into a Pair of matching and non-matching lists. groupingBy returns a lazy Grouping so I can do eachCount or fold per key without building intermediate lists. All the map results preserve the order in which keys first appeared.

title: fold vs reduce
text: What's the difference between fold and reduce , and when does reduce crash? fold initial { acc, e - } starts from an explicit initial value, so it works on empty collections and the accumulator can be any type. reduce { acc, e - } uses the first element as the initial accumulator, so the accumulator must be a supertype of the element type, and on an empty collection it throws UnsupportedOperationException . I default to fold , or reduceOrNull Kotlin 1.4+ when "no value" is meaningful.

title: windowed / chunked / zip
text: Explain chunked , windowed , zip and zipWithNext . What are their defaults and costs? chunked n splits into non-overlapping blocks of n, and the last block can be smaller. It is exactly windowed n, step = n, partialWindows = true . windowed size, step = 1, partialWindows = false produces sliding windows that overlap by default, so each element shows up in up to size windows. zip pairs two collections element by element and stops at the shorter one. zipWithNext pairs each element with its successor. The transform overloads avoid allocating Pair s or window lists, but the window passed to the lambda is ephemeral and must not be stored.

title: Sorting, stability, comparators
text: Is Kotlin's sort stable? How do you sort by several keys, with nulls and descending order, and what does it cost? Yes. The stdlib documents sorted , sortedBy , sortedWith and in-place sort as stable: equal elements keep their relative order. On the JVM they delegate to java.util sorting, which is TimSort for objects. For multiple keys I build one comparator with compareBy { a }.thenByDescending { b } , and handle nulls with nullsLast . I don't chain two sortedBy calls. sorted returns a new list, while sort mutates a MutableList in place. A selector runs about n log n times, so expensive keys should be precomputed.

title: Chained-operator allocations
text: How many objects does list.filter { }.map { }.take 10 allocate? How do you write collection chains that are both readable and cheap? Each eager operator builds a new ArrayList . That chain allocates three lists filter, map, take plus their growing backing arrays, and map also creates whatever objects it returns. The lambdas themselves cost nothing because collection operators are inline . Elements aren't copied, only references. I cut allocations by using fused operators mapNotNull , filterIsInstance , firstOrNull { } , count { } , sumOf , any { } , ordering cheap filters before expensive maps, using ...To destination variants, or switching to a sequence when there's early termination over a large input.

title: ConcurrentModificationException
text: What causes ConcurrentModificationException , why can it happen on a single thread, and how do you remove elements safely while iterating? ArrayList , HashMap and the other java.util collections are fail-fast. They keep a modCount that increments on every structural change. An iterator records the count when it's created and checks it on next . If the collection changed by any route other than that iterator, it throws CME. So it happens on one thread when you remove inside a for / forEach . Across threads it's best-effort: you may get a CME, an IndexOutOfBounds , or silent corruption. To remove safely I use removeAll { } / retainAll { } , iterator.remove , or I build a new filtered list. For cross-thread use I publish immutable snapshots.

title: buildList / buildMap / buildSet
text: What are buildList , buildMap and buildSet , and why use them instead of mutableListOf plus returning it? buildList { add ... } gives me a MutableList receiver inside the lambda and returns a read-only List afterwards. The stdlib builder is frozen at the end, so the returned list isn't a mutable ArrayList in disguise, and no toList copy is needed. It keeps the mutable phase scoped, which helps for conditional construction. It has a capacity overload, and buildMap , buildSet and buildString work the same way.

title: When sequences are slower
text: When is a Sequence slower than a plain list chain, and what pitfalls come with sequences besides speed? Sequences are slower when the input is small or the chain is short. Each element goes through a chain of iterator objects with virtual hasNext / next calls and non-inlined lambda invocations, which costs more than the few lists they save. They give no benefit with stateful operators like sorted or distinct , or with a terminal like toList with no early exit, because everything is still processed and buffered. And they re-run the whole pipeline on every terminal operation, which repeats work and side effects. I use them for large inputs with early termination or long chains, and I benchmark the rest.

title: Casting read-only to mutable; API boundaries
text: What happens at runtime if someone does myList as MutableList .add x ? Walk me through the different results for different factories, and how you design APIs so this can't corrupt state. The cast always compiles, and it usually succeeds at runtime because both types are java.util.List . What happens next depends on the real class. A list from mutableListOf / toList size ≥ 2 / filter / map is a real ArrayList : the add succeeds and mutates whatever that object is shared with. listOf a, b is an Arrays.asList view: set works, add throws UnsupportedOperationException . emptyList , listOf x and buildList throw on any mutation. So "read-only" depends on runtime luck. At boundaries I expose snapshots, ImmutableList , or a builder-frozen list, and I never hand out my backing MutableList .

title: Sequence internals & the sequence builder
text: How are sequences implemented under the hood, and how does the sequence { yield ... } builder work? What are its limits? A Sequence<T is just an interface with operator fun iterator : Iterator<T . Each intermediate operator wraps the upstream in a small class, like FilteringSequence or TransformingSequence , that stores the lambda and returns a decorating iterator. A terminal operator pulls from the outermost iterator, which pulls through the chain. The lambdas are stored in fields, so they can't be inlined. The sequence { } builder is a restricted coroutine: yield suspends the builder's state machine and hands one value to the iterator's next . Because of @RestrictsSuspension , you can only call yield / yieldAll inside it, not delay or other suspend functions.

title: kotlinx.collections.immutable & persistent data structures
text: What does kotlinx.collections.immutable give you over List , how are persistent collections implemented, and what do they cost? kotlinx.collections.immutable is a JetBrains library with two layers. ImmutableList / ImmutableSet / ImmutableMap are read-only interfaces that promise the contents never change. PersistentList / PersistentMap add "modifying" operations that return a new collection and share most of their structure with the old one. Under the hood, the list is a wide trie, and the hash map is a compressed hash trie CHAMP-style . Updates are effectively O log₃₂ n instead of an O n copy. I use them for UI state models and frequently updated large collections. I don't use them for small, rarely changed lists, where a plain List copy is simpler and faster. The library is still 0.x 0.4.0 as of 2025, verify the current version , so the API may evolve.

title: Collections & Compose stability
text: Why does the Compose compiler treat List<T parameters as unstable, how did strong skipping change this, and what are your options? List is an interface, and the real object could be a MutableList mutated behind Compose's back, so the compiler can't prove it's stable. Before strong skipping, any composable taking a List param was non-skippable and recomposed whenever its parent did. Since Kotlin 2.0.20 where the Compose compiler lives in the Kotlin repo , strong skipping is on by default. Composables with unstable params can now skip, but unstable params are compared by instance identity === , while stable ones use equals . So the key in practice is don't create a new list instance on every recomposition . My options are stable references hoisted, remembered, produced in the ViewModel , ImmutableList from kotlinx.collections.immutable, which the compiler treats as stable, a stability configuration file listing kotlin.collections. , or an @Immutable wrapper.

title: ConcurrentModificationException
text: Find the root cause and fix it. Explain why "it's read-only" didn't protect anything. A food-delivery app 1.5M DAU shows a "recently viewed restaurants" carousel. Release 7.4 added prefetching: a background coroutine appends restaurants to an in-memory cache as the user scrolls the main feed. Crashlytics: java.util.ConcurrentModificationException at 0.35% of sessions, all on 7.4, 60% on 8-core devices. java.util.ConcurrentModificationException at java.util.ArrayList$Itr.checkForComodification ArrayList.java:1013 at java.util.ArrayList$Itr.next ArrayList.java:967 at com.app.home.RecentAdapter.submit RecentAdapter.kt:41 at com.app.home.HomeFragment$onViewCreated$1.invokeSuspend HomeFragment.kt:88 @Singleton class RecentCache @Inject constructor { private val items = mutableListOf<Restaurant val recent: List<Restaurant get = items // "read-only" fun add r: Restaurant { items.add 0, r ; if items.size 50 items.removeLast } } // Prefetcher Dispatchers.Default : cache.add r // HomeFragment Main : adapter.submit cache.recent.filter { it.isOpen } Also in 7.4: a Glide → Coil migration and an upgrade to kotlinx.coroutines 1.9.

title: Sorting & comparator contract
text: Find every bug, explain why it only crashes on some products, and rewrite it. A price-comparison screen ranks offers. Requirement: price ascending, unknown price last, ties broken by rating descending. After release, Crashlytics shows a new crash at 0.4% of offer-screen opens. It only happens on products with many sellers. QA can't reproduce on test products 3–10 offers each . The release also bumped Kotlin from 1.9.24 to 2.0.21, which someone suspects. java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract! at java.util.TimSort.mergeHi TimSort.java:903 at java.util.TimSort.mergeAt TimSort.java:520 at java.util.Arrays.sort Arrays.java:1424 at kotlin.collections.ArraysKt ArraysJvmKt.sortWith ... at kotlin.collections.CollectionsKt CollectionsKt.sortedWith ... at com.app.offers.OfferRanker.rank OfferRanker.kt:19 data class Offer val seller: String, val price: Long?, val rating: Float object OfferRanker { private val byPrice = Comparator<Offer { a, b - when { a.price == null - 1 b.price == null - -1 else - a.price - b.price .toInt } } fun rank offers: List<Offer : List<Offer = offers.sortedByDescending { it.rating }.sortedWith byPrice }

title: Large-list processing performance
text: Make it fast. Quantify where the time goes before you change anything. A personal-finance app keeps up to 100,000 transactions in memory loaded from Room at screen start for an instant-search screen. Users filter by up to 300 selected categories and a text query. Analytics: p50 filter time 220 ms, p95 1.8 s on low-end devices Helio G35 / 3 GB RAM, 35% of users . Typing feels laggy, and logcat shows frequent Background concurrent copying GC freed ... lines. The work runs on Dispatchers.Default per keystroke debounce is handled elsewhere and is out of scope . fun filter all: List<Txn , selectedCategoryIds: List<Long , query: String : List<TxnUi = all.filter { it.categoryId in selectedCategoryIds } .filter { it.note.lowercase .contains query.lowercase } .map { it.toUi } // formats currency + date, 15 µs each .sortedByDescending { it.date } .take 50

title: Collection ops in RecyclerView bind
text: Diagnose and fix. Explain how you'd prove the image-loader migration isn't the cause. A messaging app's inbox View system, RecyclerView with 30 visible rows got a redesign in v5.2: each row shows the last message preview, unread count and a reaction summary. Since the release: slow frames went from 6% to 31% and frozen frames from 0.1% to 0.9% Play Console vitals , concentrated on users with large inboxes. A Perfetto trace during fling shows RV OnBindView slices of 9–14 ms on a Snapdragon 680. The same release migrated image loading from Glide to Coil, which the team suspects. override fun onBindViewHolder holder: VH, position: Int { val thread = threads position val msgs = allMessages.filter { it.threadId == thread.id } // allMessages: 20k val last = msgs.maxByOrNull { it.sentAt } val unread = msgs.count { !it.read } val reactions = msgs.flatMap { it.reactions } .groupBy { it.emoji } .mapValues { it.value.size } .entries.sortedByDescending { it.value }.take 3 holder.bind thread, last, unread, reactions holder.avatar.load thread.avatarUrl }

title: Collection ops in composition
text: Why is it janky, why didn't ImmutableList help, and how would you restructure it? A Compose catalog screen LazyColumn of up to 4,000 products, 1.2M DAU, 40% on 3 GB devices has a filter chip row, a sort dropdown and a search field. After the v8.0 rewrite from Views, JankStats shows 38% janky frames while typing in search was 7% . Layout Inspector shows ProductList recomposing on every keystroke, and the Compose compiler report lists ProductList as restartable skippable . The app is on Kotlin 2.0.21 strong skipping on . @Composable fun CatalogScreen vm: CatalogViewModel { val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle // products: List<Product 4,000 var query by remember { mutableStateOf "" } Column { SearchField query { query = it } ProductList items = state.products .filter { it.name.contains query, ignoreCase = true } .sortedWith state.sort.comparator .map { it.toRowUi LocalContext.current }, // formats price, builds badges } } The team tried converting List to ImmutableList everywhere and saw no improvement.

title: associateBy / distinctBy duplicate semantics
text: Find the bugs, explain exactly which duplicate wins and when, and fix both functions. An e-commerce app syncs the user's wishlist from two sources: the local DB cache and a fresh API response. A support ticket says "items I removed price alerts from reappear with the old alert". Another says total wishlist value is occasionally wrong. Metrics: 1.1% of sync runs affected. No crash. The ticket analysis shows it happens when a product appears in both sources. data class WishItem val productId: Long, val priceAlert: Long?, val updatedAt: Long fun merge cache: List<WishItem , remote: List<WishItem : List<WishItem = cache + remote .associateBy { it.productId } // dedupe by product .values .toList fun totalAlertValue items: List<WishItem : Long = items.map { it.priceAlert }.reduce { a, b - a ?: 0 + b ?: 0 }!! // hmm Both lists come ordered by updatedAt ascending cache and by server ranking remote, unordered w.r.t. time .

title: Sequence re-evaluation & laziness hazards
text: Explain every symptom from the code, and fix it without making the screen slower. A travel app 900k DAU exposes search results from FlightRepository as a Sequence<Flight "to avoid allocating big lists" . After v3.9: backend request volume on the pricing-enrichment endpoint is up 4.6x, API bills up $18k/month, and a StrictMode build shows DiskReadViolation on the main thread. Users report prices flickering between two values. No crashes. class FlightRepository private val api: PricingApi, private val dao: FlightDao { fun results query: Query : Sequence<Flight = dao.loadAll query .asSequence // already in memory List .map { it.copy price = api.blockingPrice it.id } // HTTP call per item, blocking .filter { it.price != null } } // ViewModel main thread : val flights = repo.results q state.value = UiState count = flights.count , items = flights.take 20 .toList analytics.log "results", flights.sumOf { it.price!!.toLong }

title: Boxing & primitive collections at scale
text: Estimate memory at 10x, find what breaks, and design the data layer so it holds up. A fitness app records heart-rate, GPS speed and cadence at 25 Hz during workouts. The current model keeps three MutableList<Float per workout in memory for live charts. Sessions are ≤ 90 minutes. Product wants 10x: a "multi-sensor" mode with 10 streams, up to 4 hours, and a live full-resolution chart. Today's numbers: p99 session memory 55 MB heap, GC pause count 40 per workout, OutOfMemoryError in 0.08% of long sessions on 2 GB devices.
