It is meant for CPU-bound work: parsing, sorting, diffing, image transforms, crypto. Because there are only as many threads as cores, any blocking call on Default I/O, Thread.sleep , waiting on a lock, runBlocking takes a core-sized slot out of a very small pool. That causes starvation Q316 .

title: Dispatchers.IO
text: Why does Dispatchers.IO exist separately from Default, and what is its thread limit? IO exists for blocking calls: file and disk access, legacy synchronous DB drivers, blocking sockets, SDKs that block. A blocked thread uses no CPU, so you want many more of them than cores. By default IO allows up to 64 tasks in parallel, or the core count if that is larger. The limit is configurable with the kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism system property. Threads are created on demand and retired when idle, so it is elastic, and it shares its threads with Default.

title: IO and Default share a pool
text: The docs say IO and Default share threads. What does that mean in practice? Both dispatchers are front-ends of one CoroutineScheduler . Default limits CPU tasks to core-count parallelism. IO limits blocking tasks to 64. Threads move between roles. When a coroutine on Default does withContext Dispatchers.IO , the scheduler usually keeps running it on the same thread. It just marks the thread as "blocking" and releases its CPU permit so another thread can take a CPU task. Switching between Default and IO is therefore often a bookkeeping change, not a real context switch. Peak thread count is roughly 64 + cores, not 64 + cores of separate pools.

title: Dispatchers.Unconfined
text: What does Dispatchers.Unconfined do, when is it legitimately used, and why is it dangerous in app code? Unconfined never dispatches. The coroutine starts in the caller's thread and runs until its first suspension. After that, it resumes on whatever thread completed the suspending operation : an OkHttp thread, a timer thread, a Binder thread. That makes thread affinity unpredictable, so it is unsafe for UI and for thread-confined objects. It exists for cases where you truly don't care about the thread and want zero dispatch overhead, such as some operator internals or bridging an already-thread-safe callback. In app code I treat it as a red flag.

title: Main-safety convention
text: What does "main-safe" mean, and do I need withContext Dispatchers.IO around Room or Retrofit suspend calls? A suspend function is main-safe if you can call it from the main thread without blocking it. The function itself is responsible for moving any blocking or heavy work off the main thread. Room suspend DAO methods and Retrofit suspend interface methods are already main-safe. Room runs the query on its own executor, and Retrofit enqueues the call on OkHttp's dispatcher threads. So wrapping them in withContext Dispatchers.IO adds a hop and buys nothing. The convention is that the class that does the blocking work owns the dispatcher switch, and callers never have to think about it.

title: Where the dispatcher switch belongs
text: In a ViewModel → Repository → DataSource architecture, where should withContext live, and what does a redundant switch cost? The switch goes at the lowest layer that does the blocking or CPU-heavy work, usually the data source or a dedicated parser or mapper. The ViewModel launches on viewModelScope Main.immediate and calls main-safe suspend functions, and it never picks IO itself. A redundant switch is cheap but not free. If the target dispatcher equals the current one, withContext takes a fast path with no dispatch. If it differs, you pay a dispatch on entry and another on exit, which means queueing latency and possibly a thread hop. That only matters in hot loops.

title: limitedParallelism semantics
text: What does CoroutineDispatcher.limitedParallelism n do, and what does it not do? limitedParallelism n returns a view of an existing dispatcher that never runs more than n tasks at the same time. It uses the parent's threads and doesn't create a pool. It was added in kotlinx.coroutines 1.6.0 as experimental, became stable in 1.9.0, and 1.9.0 added an optional name parameter for debugging. What it does not do: it doesn't limit how many coroutines are in flight, because a coroutine suspended in a network call or a delay isn't running and doesn't hold a slot. It doesn't pin work to one thread, even with n = 1. And the limit is per view instance, so creating a new view per call gives you no limit at all.

title: limitedParallelism on IO vs Default
text: Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism 4 and Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism 4 look the same. How do they actually differ? A Default view is a slice of Default's core-count budget. All Default views together still compete for the same CPU permits, so a view can throttle work but cannot add capacity. An IO view is elastic. Per the docs, Dispatchers.IO and its views are all views of one conceptually unbounded blocking pool, and IO views are not counted against IO's 64 limit. So IO.limitedParallelism 100 really can run 100 blocking tasks, on top of IO's own 64. That is great for isolating one blocking resource so it can't be starved by others, but every IO view you create raises the worst-case thread count.

title: newSingleThreadContext, Executor dispatchers, closing
text: When would you use newSingleThreadContext or Executor.asCoroutineDispatcher , and why do they need to be closed? Both create dispatchers backed by threads you own. newSingleThreadContext "name" makes a dedicated thread. executor.asCoroutineDispatcher wraps any ExecutorService . I use them when I need true thread affinity, meaning the same OS thread every time some native SDKs, OpenGL-style contexts , or real isolation from the shared pool. Because they own threads, they must be closed. close shuts the executor down, and if you forget, the threads live for the life of the process. newSingleThreadContext is annotated @DelicateCoroutinesApi for exactly this reason. When I only need "one at a time" and not "same thread", Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism 1 is the better tool, because it has nothing to close.

title: Injecting dispatchers
text: Why should dispatchers be injected rather than hard-coded, and how do you do it with Hilt? Hard-coding Dispatchers.IO inside a class means tests can't control when that work runs. It escapes the test scheduler, so tests either race or need real sleeps. Injecting a CoroutineDispatcher lets tests pass a test dispatcher so virtual time controls everything. It also lets production code swap in a limited view or a custom executor without touching call sites. With Hilt I provide each dispatcher behind a qualifier annotation @IoDispatcher , @DefaultDispatcher from a SingletonComponent module, and constructor-inject them. Dispatchers.Main is the exception: the test library replaces it globally with Dispatchers.setMain .

title: Starvation from blocking on Default
text: Explain mechanically how blocking calls on Dispatchers.Default cause starvation, and when it becomes a deadlock. Default has as many CPU permits as cores. A blocking call on Default holds its thread and its permit while doing nothing, and the scheduler doesn't compensate the way it does for IO tasks. With N cores and N blocked tasks, every other Default coroutine parsing, diffing, combine logic, flow operators just waits, while the CPU sits nearly idle. That is starvation: high latency at low CPU. It turns into a deadlock when the blocked tasks are waiting on something that itself needs a Default thread. The typical case is runBlocking or future.get on a Default worker, waiting for a coroutine that was dispatched to Default.

title: CoroutineScheduler internals
text: Walk me through how the scheduler behind Default and IO works internally: queues, work stealing, and thread lifecycle. Default and IO both run on one CoroutineScheduler , a work-stealing pool. Each worker thread has a small local queue, and there are global queues for CPU tasks and blocking tasks. A task is tagged CPU or blocking depending on which dispatcher submitted it. A worker must hold a CPU permit there are core-count permits to run CPU tasks, while blocking tasks run without one. Idle workers steal from other workers' local queues, and they park, then terminate after a keep-alive period with no work. That design gives good locality and throughput, cheap Default↔IO switches, and elastic thread counts.

title: Classifying work to dispatchers
text: For each of these, which dispatcher and why: JSON parsing, bitmap decode, reading a file, a Room query, AES encryption, SharedPreferences.commit , DiffUtil.calculateDiff ? I ask one question: is the thread computing or waiting? If it is computing, it goes on Default. If it is blocked waiting on disk, network, or a lock, it goes on IO. If it is already a main-safe suspend API, I add no switch at all. So: JSON parsing goes on Default, unless the converter already runs it on OkHttp's thread. Bitmap decode is mostly CPU, so Default or a bounded view, with the file read on IO. File reads go on IO. Room suspend needs no switch. AES goes on Default. commit is blocking disk, so IO, or better, apply or DataStore. DiffUtil goes on Default, or use ListAdapter / AsyncListDiffer , which run it on their own background executor.

title: Dispatcher choice for background work
text: What does "never slow the app" mean concretely, and how would you design the threading for this? The PM writes: "Analytics batching must never slow the app down." Current state: about 1.2M DAU and roughly 300 events per session. Every event does scope.launch Dispatchers.IO { db.insertBlocking e ; if count 50 uploadBlocking } using a legacy blocking HTTP client. On 4-core Android 10 devices about 30% of users , Android vitals shows slow frames at 9.8% versus 4.1% on 8-core devices. A Perfetto trace during scroll shows 12–20 DefaultDispatcher-worker threads runnable, and the UI thread is runnable-but-not-running for 3–6 ms chunks. The backend team says upload payloads are gzip-compressed on the client CPU . A red herring: a recent Glide upgrade also landed in the same release.

title: runBlocking on Main
text: Explain both failure modes slow and forever and fix it without a theme flash. After release 6.4, the user-perceived ANR rate went from 0.21% to 0.62%, above Google Play's 0.47% bad-behaviour threshold, which risks reduced store visibility. 85% of the ANRs are in MainActivity.onCreate , and they are concentrated on devices with slow eMMC storage. The release added a "dynamic theme" feature: override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { val theme = runBlocking { settingsDataStore.data.first .theme } // added in 6.4 setTheme theme.resId super.onCreate savedInstanceState } ANR trace excerpt: "main" prio=5 tid=1 Waiting at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park Native method at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.parkNanos LockSupport.java:... at kotlinx.coroutines.BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking Builders.kt:... at kotlinx.coroutines.BuildersKt BuildersKt.runBlocking Builders.kt:... at com.app.MainActivity.onCreate MainActivity.kt:41 Also in 6.4: a Firebase SDK bump red herring . About 3% of the ANRs show the main thread parked forever , even after the disk read should have finished.

title: Starvation from blocking DB calls
text: Diagnose this and fix it. Explain why "just switch to IO" is only half the answer. An offline-first field-service app about 80k DAU, mostly 4-core rugged devices shipped a "sync all jobs" feature. After that, the job list takes 4–9 s to update after sync starts, and the search box a debounce + combine pipeline doing CPU filtering on Dispatchers.Default freezes for several seconds. Battery and CPU look fine: CPU utilization is about 15–20% during the freeze. The sync code: suspend fun syncAll jobs: List<Job = coroutineScope { jobs.map { job - // typically 200 jobs launch Dispatchers.Default { val local = legacyDb.loadJobBlocking job.id // SQLCipher sync call, 30-120 ms val merged = merge local, api.fetchJob job.id // Retrofit suspend legacyDb.saveJobBlocking merged // 40-150 ms, takes the write lock } } } Thread dump during the freeze: all 4 DefaultDispatcher-worker- threads in SQLiteConnection.nativeExecuteForChangedRowCount or waiting on SQLiteConnectionPool.waitForConnection . Red herrings: a GC log showing frequent young-gen collections, and a backend p95 of 600 ms.

title: Bitmap decode on the wrong dispatcher
text: Identify each bug, its symptom, and the fix. A profile-photo editor. Crashlytics shows 0.4% of sessions with an ANR on the editor screen and some OutOfMemoryError s on 2–3 GB RAM devices. Find all the dispatcher bugs. class EditorViewModel private val repo: PhotoRepo : ViewModel { val preview = MutableStateFlow<Bitmap? null fun open uri: Uri = viewModelScope.launch { preview.value = repo.decode uri // 1 } fun applyFilters filters: List<Filter = viewModelScope.launch Dispatchers.IO { filters.map { f - async { f.apply preview.value!! } } // 2 .awaitAll .last .let { preview.value = it } } fun save out: File = viewModelScope.launch { withContext Dispatchers.IO { / open stream / } FileOutputStream out .use { preview.value!!.compress JPEG, 90, it } // 3 } } class PhotoRepo private val resolver: ContentResolver { suspend fun decode uri: Uri : Bitmap = // 4 resolver.openInputStream uri !!.use { BitmapFactory.decodeStream it } } Photos are 12 MP 4000×3000 . The preview view is 1080 px wide.

title: Sizing parallelism by the scarcest resource
text: The business wants 10x the batch size. How do you size the concurrency, and what do you change? A document-scanning app processes pages: read the camera JPEG about 3 MB, 12 MP , decode, de-skew and sharpen CPU , then encode to a 300 KB PDF page. Today users scan about 5 pages at a time. A B2B launch will have clerks scanning batches of 200 pages from a queue, on a fleet of 3 GB RAM, 8-core 4 big + 4 little devices. The current code is pages.map { async Dispatchers.Default { process it } }.awaitAll . Beta with 60-page batches: 11% of sessions end with OutOfMemoryError in BitmapFactory.nativeDecodeStream , and average page time is 2.4 s even though a single page takes 0.7 s in isolation. The Java heap limit is 256 MB largeHeap not set . Red herring: the PDF encoder library was updated last sprint.

title: Leaked dispatcher threads
text: Find the cause, fix it, and design it so ordering still holds. A messaging app about 2M DAU sees a slow-growing crash: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread create 1040KB stack failed: Try again , 0.7% of sessions, clustered on power users after 3+ hours of use, and on 2–3 GB devices. Crashlytics breadcrumbs show nothing special. A heap dump is clean Java heap is 40% used . A thread dump from a QA device after a long session shows 380 threads, of which about 300 are named room-ordering-1 , room-ordering-2 , and so on, all parked idle. The relevant code was added 3 weeks ago: class ChatRoomSession private val roomId: String, private val scope: CoroutineScope { // "Guarantees message order per room" private val orderingDispatcher = newSingleThreadContext "room-ordering-$roomId" fun onMessage m: Message = scope.launch orderingDispatcher { apply m } fun leave { / unsubscribes sockets, clears UI state / } } Red herrings: a Glide version bump, and an existing known 1% leak in an analytics SDK.

title: Thread affinity vs serialization
text: A vendor SDK must always be called from the same thread. Is Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism 1 enough? What are the options? No. limitedParallelism 1 guarantees that only one task runs at a time and that memory effects are visible between tasks, so it gives serialization. It does not guarantee the same thread, because it borrows whichever worker of the parent pool is free, so successive tasks can run on different threads. If the SDK uses thread-local state or checks Thread.currentThread , I need a real dedicated thread: a HandlerThread wrapped with Handler.asCoroutineDispatcher , or a single-thread Executor wrapped with asCoroutineDispatcher . Both own a thread, so I must create it once and close or quit it when the SDK shuts down. If the SDK needs the main thread, then Main is already the answer.

title: Migrating to injected dispatchers
text: How do you plan and execute this migration, and how do you measure that it worked? A 600k-line, 40-module app has about 1,100 hard-coded Dispatchers.IO / Default / Main references, 70 withContext Dispatchers.IO { retrofitCall } wrappers, and 25 GlobalScope.launch Dispatchers.IO calls. The unit-test suite has a 6% flake rate on CI and 18% of tests use Thread.sleep or delay with real time CI time 38 min . Product wants no regression in crash/ANR rates, and releases go out every 2 weeks with a 5% staged rollout. The tech lead asks you to "inject dispatchers everywhere" in one quarter. Constraints: teams own modules independently, and a big-bang change would conflict constantly.

title: Unconfined resume thread
text: Explain the crash precisely, why QA missed it, and what the postmortem's corrective actions should be. Postmortem draft for last Tuesday's incident. Release 8.2 crashed for 0.8% of sessions about 14,000 crashes in 36 hours with: android.view.ViewRootImpl$CalledFromWrongThreadException: Only the original thread that created a view hierarchy can touch its views. at android.widget.TextView.setText TextView.java at com.app.profile.ProfileFragment$observe$1.invokeSuspend ProfileFragment.kt:58 at kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.BaseContinuationImpl.resumeWith ContinuationImpl.kt:33 at okhttp3.internal.connection.RealCall$AsyncCall.run RealCall.kt:... The change in 8.2 reviewed by two people, passed QA was meant to "avoid an unnecessary thread hop and speed up first paint": viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch Dispatchers.Unconfined { viewModel.profile.collect { binding.name.text = it.name } } viewModel.profile is a StateFlow fed by repo.profile , which is flow { emit cache.get ?: api.fetch }.stateIn ... in viewModelScope . QA tested on Wi-Fi with a warm cache. The crash is higher on 3G users and on first launch.

title: Structured concurrency guarantees
text: What is structured concurrency, and what does it actually guarantee you in kotlinx.coroutines? Structured concurrency means every coroutine starts inside a scope and becomes a child of that scope's Job, so coroutines form a tree. That tree gives three guarantees. A parent doesn't complete until all its children complete. Cancelling a parent cancels every descendant. A child that fails with a real exception cancels its parent, and therefore its siblings, so errors can't be silently lost. Put simply, the lifetime of concurrent work is bound to a lexical block or an owning object, the same way a local variable's lifetime is bound to its block.

title: CoroutineContext basics
text: What is a CoroutineContext? What elements does it typically hold, and how do you read one? A CoroutineContext is an immutable, indexed set of elements, keyed by type. Each element has a unique Key . The usual ones are a Job lifecycle , a ContinuationInterceptor , which in practice means a CoroutineDispatcher where code runs , a CoroutineName debug label , and a CoroutineExceptionHandler . You read an element with the index operator, coroutineContext Job or coroutineContext CoroutineName , and combine contexts with + . Every coroutine carries one, and children derive theirs from the parent's.

title: Job lifecycle states
text: Walk me through the states of a Job. What do isActive , isCompleted and isCancelled return in each one? A Job starts as New only with CoroutineStart.LAZY or Active the default . When its body finishes it moves to Completing and waits for its children, then becomes Completed . If it fails or is cancelled, it moves to Cancelling while children and finally blocks wind down, then becomes Cancelled . Observers see Completing as still active. isCompleted is true for both final states, and isCancelled is true from Cancelling onward, including when the job failed with a real exception.

title: CoroutineScope interface vs scope builders
text: What's the difference between the CoroutineScope interface, the CoroutineScope ... factory function, and the coroutineScope { } builder? CoroutineScope is just an interface with one property, coroutineContext . It's the receiver that launch and async need. CoroutineScope context is a factory that builds a standalone scope object and adds a Job if you didn't pass one. You use it for a component that owns work, and that component must cancel it. coroutineScope { } is a suspending builder: it creates a child scope of the current coroutine, runs the block, waits for every child, and rethrows failures. It's how a suspend function does parallel work without leaking it.

title: CoroutineName
text: What is CoroutineName for, and how do you actually see it at runtime on Android? CoroutineName is a context element that labels a coroutine for debugging. Children inherit it unless they override it. It doesn't change behaviour. You see it in the coroutine's toString , in DebugProbes dumps and in the IDE coroutine debugger, and with debug mode on system property kotlinx.coroutines.debug , the thread name gets suffixed with @name id while the coroutine runs. On Android, debug mode isn't on by default, so you enable it explicitly in debug builds.

title: Context plus, minusKey, Key
text: Explain exactly how + works on CoroutineContext. What happens on key collisions, what does minusKey do, and how are keys defined? a + b produces a context with all elements of both. When the same key appears on both sides, the element from b , the right-hand side, wins. minusKey k returns the context without that key. Keys are usually companion objects implementing CoroutineContext.Key<E , so ctx Job reads naturally. Dispatchers use a polymorphic key, AbstractCoroutineContextKey , so both ctx ContinuationInterceptor and ctx CoroutineDispatcher find the same element. The implementation is a small immutable linked structure, and the interceptor is deliberately kept at the end so dispatch lookups are fast.

title: Context inheritance rules
text: When I call scope.launch ctx { } , how exactly is the new coroutine's context computed? Which elements are inherited and which are always new? The parent context is the scope's context plus whatever I pass, with my argument winning on clashes. If the result has no dispatcher, Dispatchers.Default is added. In debug mode, a coroutine ID is added too. Then the new coroutine creates its own Job, a child of whatever Job is in that parent context, and its final context is the parent context plus its own Job. So the dispatcher, name and handler are inherited or overridden, but the Job is never inherited as-is. It's always a fresh child Job whose parent is the Job found in the combined context.

title: Parent-child relationship, join, children
text: Describe the parent-child contract between Jobs: what a parent waits for, what flows in which direction, and how join and children fit in. The contract has three rules. Downward: cancelling a parent cancels all its children, recursively. Upward: a child that fails with a non-CancellationException cancels its parent, which then cancels the other children, unless the parent is a SupervisorJob. A child that's merely cancelled doesn't affect the parent. Waiting: a parent only reaches a final state after all its children have. join suspends until a job is final, whatever the outcome, and doesn't throw on the child's failure. children gives me the current direct children as a Sequence, which is mainly useful for debugging or targeted waits.

title: SupervisorJob and supervisorScope semantics
text: What exactly does a SupervisorJob change, and what does it not change? How is supervisorScope different from coroutineScope ? A SupervisorJob changes one rule: a failing child doesn't cancel the supervisor or its siblings. Everything else stays the same. Cancelling the supervisor still cancels all children, it still waits for children, and the failed child's exception still has to go somewhere. For a launch child, that's a CoroutineExceptionHandler in its context or the thread's uncaught handler, which crashes an Android app. Supervision only applies to direct children; grandchildren under a regular Job still fail their parent normally. supervisorScope {} is the suspending builder with those semantics: children are isolated, but if the block's own code throws, the scope fails and rethrows like coroutineScope .

title: launch(Job()) / launch(SupervisorJob()) breaks structure
text: Why is scope.launch SupervisorJob { ... } or launch Job a bug? What does it actually do? The Job you pass becomes the new coroutine's parent, replacing the scope's Job. So the coroutine is no longer a child of the scope. Cancelling the scope, say viewModelScope in onCleared , doesn't cancel it. The scope doesn't wait for it. And the "supervision" people wanted is pointless, because the new SupervisorJob has exactly one child and nothing else to protect. Worse, that fresh Job is never completed, so it stays Active forever. The kotlinx.coroutines KDoc for launch now explicitly calls passing a Job an unsupported pattern that breaks structured concurrency. The fix is supervisorScope {} , or handling the exception inside the child.

title: scope.cancel() vs cancelChildren()
text: What's the difference between scope.cancel , scope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren , and cancelling an individual Job? When do you use each? scope.cancel cancels the scope's own Job, which cancels every child and puts the scope into a terminal state. Any later launch on it creates a coroutine that's cancelled immediately and never runs. coroutineContext.cancelChildren cancels the current children but leaves the scope's Job active, so the scope can be reused. Cancelling an individual Job stops just that subtree. I use cancel when the owner is being destroyed for good, cancelChildren for a reset like logout or "restart all work", and per-job cancel for replacing one operation, such as a new search query.

title: Creating and owning custom scopes
text: When should you create your own CoroutineScope, and what rules must a class that owns a scope follow? I create a custom scope only when some object has a real lifecycle that framework scopes don't model, such as a media session, a socket connection, or an SDK client with close . The rules: the scope is private, created once, with an explicit Job usually a SupervisorJob so independent tasks don't kill each other , an injected dispatcher, and ideally a CoroutineExceptionHandler for logging. The owner cancels it exactly when its lifecycle ends. If its lifetime is part of something bigger, the Job is parented to that bigger scope so cancellation cascades. Never create a scope per call, and never expose a scope for others to cancel.

title: Job() factory, CompletableJob, complete()
text: What does the Job factory return, and what are complete and completeExceptionally for? Why might job.join on such a Job never return? Job and SupervisorJob return a CompletableJob , a Job with no code of its own. A coroutine's Job completes when its body and children finish. A CompletableJob only moves toward completion when someone calls complete or completeExceptionally , and then it still waits for its children. If nobody calls complete , it stays Active forever, even with zero children, so join on it never returns. CoroutineScope ... creates one of these, which is why a scope's Job is ended by cancel , not by work finishing.

title: coroutineContext ambiguity & the CoroutineScope receiver convention
text: Inside suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo , which coroutineContext do you get? Why is a suspend function with a CoroutineScope receiver considered a smell, and what is the right convention? There are two coroutineContext s. One is the CoroutineScope.coroutineContext property on the receiver. The other is the top-level suspend property from kotlin.coroutines , which is the context of the coroutine actually running this code. In suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo , the receiver's property wins resolution, so you may read the scope's Job instead of the current coroutine's. When those differ, isActive checks and launch calls bind to the wrong lifetime. currentCoroutineContext always gives the running coroutine. The convention: suspend functions do their work and return, and use coroutineScope {} if they need concurrency. Functions that start background work and return immediately are non-suspend extensions on CoroutineScope . Never both.

title: Custom CoroutineContext elements
text: How do you design a custom CoroutineContext element, for example a request/trace ID that follows work across coroutines? What are the pitfalls? I'd write an immutable class extending AbstractCoroutineContextElement with a companion object as its Key , add it at the entry point with launch TraceId id or withContext TraceId id , and read it anywhere downstream with currentCoroutineContext TraceId . It propagates automatically to every child, because children inherit all non-Job elements. The pitfalls: it's shared by reference, so it must be immutable. It doesn't cross into other scopes, so work launched into an app scope loses it. Code that reads ThreadLocals MDC-style loggers, OpenTelemetry won't see it unless the element is also a ThreadContextElement see the ThreadLocal discussion in the suspend edge-cases section . Equality affects withContext fast paths, so a data class is a good choice.

title: Job internals (how parent and child are linked)
text: Under the hood, how does a child Job attach to its parent, how does cancellation reach children, and how does a child's failure reach the parent? How does SupervisorJob change that? Every Job is a JobSupport object whose state lives in one atomic field: a small state machine of Empty/NodeList/Finishing/final values plus a list of completion handlers. When a child coroutine starts, it calls parent.attachChild this , which registers a child-handle node in the parent's handler list. When the parent is cancelled, it walks that list and calls parentCancelled on each child. When a child fails, it calls childCancelled cause on its parent handle. A regular Job returns true, cancels itself and takes responsibility for the exception. SupervisorJob overrides childCancelled to return false, so the child must handle its own exception: a CoroutineExceptionHandler, or else the uncaught handler. Completion waiting works by registering handlers on each remaining child before the parent finalizes.

title: Scope ownership in layered APIs
text: Review this design. What would you change, and when, if ever, should a data-layer API take a scope? A PR in a 1.2M-MAU news app refactors the data layer. Every repository now takes a scope: class ArticleRepository private val api: Api, private val dao: ArticleDao { fun refresh scope: CoroutineScope { scope.launch Dispatchers.IO { val fresh = api.latest dao.upsert fresh } } } // caller fun onPullToRefresh { repo.refresh viewModelScope ; state.update { it.copy refreshing = false } } The author's justification: "the repository shouldn't decide lifetimes; callers pass their scope". QA reports the pull-to-refresh spinner stops instantly, and errors from api.latest show up as crashes in Crashlytics IOException via the uncaught handler, about 0.12% of sessions on flaky networks instead of an error banner. A reviewer suggests making the repository a CoroutineScope itself as an alternative.

title: Breaking the parent link
text: Find the bug s , explain the stale results and the leak mechanically, and fix it. A search screen p95 query latency 450 ms, 85k daily searches shows stale results: typing "kotl" then quickly "kotlin flow" sometimes leaves the "kotl" results on screen. Also, LeakCanary in internal builds occasionally reports SearchViewModel retained after leaving the screen about 1 in 40 sessions in QA runs . class SearchUseCase private val api: SearchApi { suspend operator fun invoke q: String : List<Hit { val scope = CoroutineScope currentCoroutineContext + SupervisorJob return scope.async Dispatchers.IO { api.search q }.await } } class SearchViewModel private val search: SearchUseCase : ViewModel { private var job: Job? = null val results = MutableStateFlow<List<Hit emptyList fun onQuery q: String { job?.cancel job = viewModelScope.launch { val hits = search q results.value = hits } } } A teammate suspects MutableStateFlow conflation and wants to switch to SharedFlow.

title: Job vs SupervisorJob in an owned scope
text: What happened, and how do you fix it? An analytics uploader in a fitness app 400k DAU batches events every 30 s: @Singleton class EventUploader @Inject constructor private val api: EventsApi, private val store: EventStore { private val scope = CoroutineScope Dispatchers.IO fun schedule { scope.launch { while isActive { val batch = store.next 500 if batch.isNotEmpty { api.send batch ; store.ack batch } delay 30 000 } } } fun flushNow { scope.launch { api.send store.all } } } After a release, the data team sees event volume drop 18% day over day. The drop is concentrated on users on flaky networks rural, subway . Crashlytics shows nothing. On-device event backlog store.size for affected users grows to 50k+. A teammate suspects a server-side rate limit a few 429s show in backend logs .

title: Failure policy per operation (coroutineScope vs supervisorScope)
text: Explain the logs, decide the correct failure policy, and implement it. A photo-backup feature uploads selected photos in parallel batch of up to 50, 4 concurrent via a Semaphore . After a release that added server-side size validation, support tickets rise: "I backed up 50 photos and only 3 uploaded". Logs per batch: 12:01:03.120 upload start x50 12:01:04.870 HTTP 413 Payload Too Large photo=IMG 2231.HEIC 48 MB 12:01:04.874 kotlinx.coroutines.JobCancellationException: Parent job is Cancelling x46 12:01:04.880 BackupViewModel: backup failed: HttpException 413 The code: suspend fun backup photos: List<Photo = coroutineScope { photos.map { p - async { limiter.withPermit { api.upload p } } }.awaitAll } OkHttp timeouts were also raised from 10 s to 60 s in the same release, and a teammate suspects they're involved.

title: Replacing GlobalScope
text: How do you migrate safely? A ride-hailing app 2M MAU, Android 8-14, 35% low-RAM devices has 140 call sites of GlobalScope.launch , added over six years. Crashlytics shows OutOfMemoryError at 0.4% of sessions, and heap dumps show many StandaloneCoroutine objects holding Activity references via lambdas. The team wants to remove GlobalScope in one 3-week push, without changing user-visible behaviour. Rough categories from a grep: about 90 are "do this for the screen" load, submit , about 30 are "must finish even if the user leaves" send receipt, upload trip rating , about 20 are periodic or app-lifetime loops location ping, token refresh timer . A manager proposes a regex replace of GlobalScope with a single shared appScope everywhere.

title: Many children in one scope
text: What is going on, and how do you design this to scale? A messaging app indexes attachments for offline search. An IndexingManager has one private scope SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.Default and does scope.launch { index file } for every incoming file. With 5k files per user this worked. A new bulk-import feature produces up to 400k files per import. Observed on mid-range devices 4 GB RAM : heap grows by roughly 90 MB during import, GC pauses of 40-60 ms show up as jank, and tapping "Cancel import" scope.cancel freezes the UI for about 700 ms. Log excerpt: Choreographer: Skipped 42 frames! . Someone suggests simply moving to Dispatchers.IO for more threads.

title: Work escaping the tree
text: Explain why cancelChildren did not stop the work, and fix it, including the logout design. A banking app's logout flow calls sessionScope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren and clears the token store. After a release, security QA finds that after logout, a "transactions" screen's prefetch still fires authenticated requests for up to 20 s, and 0.3% of logouts end with a crash: NullPointerException: token from an OkHttp interceptor reading the cleared store. The prefetch code: class TxRepository private val api: TxApi, private val appScope: CoroutineScope { suspend fun prefetchAccounts ids: List<String { ids.forEach { id - appScope.launch { cache.put id, api.transactions id } } } } It's called from sessionScope.launch { repo.prefetchAccounts ids } . sessionScope is a child scope of appScope created per login. Backend sees about 11 authenticated calls per logout after the token is revoked, returning 401.

title: App / session scope design
text: Design the scope hierarchy and rules. You're designing the lifetimes layer for a fintech app with 300 screens-equivalents, Hilt, and a multi-account feature user can switch accounts without restarting the app . Requirements: a work started by a screen should stop when the screen goes away, unless it is explicitly "must finish"; b must-finish work submit payment confirmation, upload KYC photo should survive screen exit; c everything account-specific must stop on account switch or logout; d one failed background task must not take down the others; e all of it must be testable. A colleague proposes one @Singleton CoroutineScope injected everywhere.

title: Post-incident review of a scope leak
text: Run the review: causes, contributing factors, fixes, and what process changes you'd make. Post-incident review. Three weeks after a release, a video-chat app 800k DAU saw: median memory at 6 minutes of use up 38%, "Out of memory" crash rate up from 0.15% to 0.9%, and battery complaints background CPU wake-ups . A bisect landed on a "resilience" PR whose description said: "wrap network work so one failing call can't kill the screen". Merged code: abstract class BaseViewModel : ViewModel { protected fun safeLaunch block: suspend CoroutineScope. - Unit : Job = viewModelScope.launch SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.IO + handler { block } protected suspend fun <T safeIo block: suspend - T : T = withContext Job + Dispatchers.IO { block } private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { , e - Log.e "VM", "failed", e } } It is used by 120 ViewModels. Memory leak traces show ChatViewModel retained with SupervisorJob nodes and a while true { delay 5000 ; refreshPresence } loop still running after the chat screen was closed.

title: Cooperative cancellation
text: What does it mean that coroutine cancellation is "cooperative"? What actually happens when I call job.cancel ? job.cancel doesn't stop any code. It flips the Job into a cancelling state and records a CancellationException as the cause. The coroutine only reacts the next time it reaches a cancellation point: a cancellable suspending call like delay , withContext , await or Channel.receive , or an explicit check like ensureActive . At that point it throws CancellationException , which unwinds the stack through finally blocks. Code that never suspends and never checks keeps running to the end. That is what "cooperative" means.

title: isActive / ensureActive / yield
text: What is the difference between isActive , ensureActive and yield ? When would you pick each? All three check the Job. isActive is a boolean read with no side effects, so I use it as a loop condition when I want to exit gracefully and maybe return a partial result. ensureActive throws CancellationException if the Job isn't active, so it behaves like any other cancellation point and unwinds through finally . yield is a real suspension point: it checks for cancellation, and on a dispatcher that needs dispatching it also gives the thread to other coroutines waiting on it. I use it when a long CPU task must stay fair on a shared, limited pool.

title: CancellationException semantics
text: What is CancellationException in coroutines, and why doesn't an uncaught one crash the app the way other exceptions do? Cancellation is delivered as a CancellationException thrown at a cancellation point, so finally blocks and use {} run as the stack unwinds. On the JVM it's a typealias for java.util.concurrent.CancellationException . The coroutine machinery treats it as normal completion of a cancelled coroutine, not as a failure. It doesn't cancel the parent, it isn't passed to a CoroutineExceptionHandler , and it doesn't reach the thread's uncaught exception handler, which is why it never crashes the app. Any other exception means failure: it cancels the parent and, at the root, crashes.

title: withTimeout vs withTimeoutOrNull
text: What's the difference between withTimeout and withTimeoutOrNull , and how does each signal a timeout? Both run a suspending block and cancel it if it exceeds the time limit. withTimeout then throws TimeoutCancellationException , which is a subclass of CancellationException . withTimeoutOrNull catches its own timeout and returns null . Since a timeout is just cancellation, the block only stops at cancellation points, so withTimeout around blocking code does nothing. I prefer withTimeoutOrNull when a timeout is an expected outcome, because a thrown TCE inside a launch silently ends the coroutine instead of failing it.

title: cancel vs cancelAndJoin, Job states
text: What's the difference between job.cancel and job.cancelAndJoin ? Walk me through isActive , isCancelled and isCompleted during cancellation. cancel only requests cancellation and returns immediately. cancelAndJoin requests it and then suspends until the Job has actually completed, meaning its finally blocks and children are finished. While the Job is cancelling, isActive is false and isCancelled is true, but isCompleted is still false. isCompleted only becomes true once everything has unwound. If I'm about to restart the same work, for example writing the same file, I use cancelAndJoin so the old and new runs never overlap.

title: CPU loop that never cancels
text: What's wrong, and how would you fix it? A photo editor applies filters to a 12 MP image 4000x3000 = 12M pixels on Dispatchers.Default . When users drag a slider, each change cancels the previous job and starts a new one. On a Pixel 6 8 cores it's fine. On low-end 4-core devices, about 30% of the user base, sliders feel frozen for 2–3 s and the "Save" button also on Default doesn't respond. Profiling shows all 4 Default workers busy running applyFilter . A teammate suspects GC pressure from bitmap allocation. class FilterViewModel : ViewModel { private var filterJob: Job? = null fun onSliderChanged value: Float { filterJob?.cancel filterJob = viewModelScope.launch Dispatchers.Default { val pixels = sourcePixels.copyOf // IntArray 12 000 000 for i in pixels.indices { pixels i = adjust pixels i , value // pure math } withContext Dispatchers.Main { preview.setPixels pixels } } } }

title: Cancellation points
text: Is every suspend function a cancellation point? Which calls are cancellable and which are not? No. suspend only means the function may suspend. A function is a cancellation point only if it suspends through a cancellable primitive like suspendCancellableCoroutine , or explicitly checks the Job. All the kotlinx.coroutines suspending functions are cancellable: delay , yield , withContext , await , join , channel ops, Mutex.lock . Retrofit and Room suspend calls are too. But a suspend function that just runs blocking code, or one built on plain suspendCoroutine , ignores cancellation until it returns.

title: Swallowing cancellation
text: Why are catch e: Exception and runCatching dangerous inside coroutines? What's the correct pattern? CancellationException is an Exception it's IllegalStateException → RuntimeException on the JVM , so a catch-all or runCatching , which catches Throwable , catches the cancellation signal too. If you don't rethrow it, the coroutine thinks it recovered. It keeps running past the point where it should have stopped, often looping or writing state for a screen that no longer exists. The fix is to rethrow CE before handling anything else, or to call ensureActive in the catch block. For Result -style code I use a runSuspendCatching helper that rethrows CE.

title: finally & NonCancellable
text: What happens if I call a suspend function in a finally block of a cancelled coroutine? How and when should I use NonCancellable ? The finally block runs, but the coroutine is already cancelled, so the first cancellable suspension inside it throws CancellationException and the rest of the cleanup is skipped. Plain non-suspending cleanup like close is fine. If cleanup has to suspend, for example telling the server or writing a "failed" row through a suspend DAO, I wrap just that part in withContext NonCancellable { } . NonCancellable is only for short cleanup and only with withContext . It's not for launch , and not for making a whole operation unkillable.

title: TimeoutCancellationException semantics
text: TimeoutCancellationException extends CancellationException . What consequences does that have, and how do nested timeouts behave? Since a TCE is a CE, it inherits cancellation semantics. Uncaught inside a launch , it ends that coroutine as cancelled, silently, without failing the parent or reaching a handler. Inside coroutineScope / runBlocking it propagates to the caller like any exception. With nesting, each timeout only handles its own TCE. withTimeoutOrNull returns null only if the TCE came from its timer. If an inner withTimeout fires, the inner TCE passes through the outer withTimeoutOrNull unchanged. And catching CancellationException to handle timeouts also swallows real cancellation, so I catch TimeoutCancellationException specifically.

title: Swallowed cancellation
text: Walk me through the investigation and the fix. A fitness app 1.2M DAU shows a live leaderboard. The ViewModel polls every 10 s while the screen is visible. After the 5.4 release, backend RPS on /leaderboard rose from about 9k to 31k with no DAU change. Battery complaints went up and Android vitals shows "excessive wake-ups" on a subset of devices. Crashlytics non-fatals now show about 2M/day of: Non-fatal: kotlinx.coroutines.JobCancellationException: Job was cancelled; job=SupervisorJobImpl{Cancelling}@4f1a2c at LeaderboardRepository.fetch LeaderboardRepository.kt:41 The 5.4 diff included a new safeApiCall helper, an OkHttp upgrade 4.11 → 4.12 , and a refactor of the screen to a new Fragment. suspend fun <T safeApiCall block: suspend - T : ApiResult<T = runCatching { block } .fold { ApiResult.Ok it }, { crashlytics.recordException it ; ApiResult.Err it } // ViewModel init { viewModelScope.launch { while true { when val r = safeApiCall { api.leaderboard } { is ApiResult.Ok - state.value = Ui.Data r.value is ApiResult.Err - state.value = Ui.Error r.error } pollDelay } } } private suspend fun pollDelay = runCatching { delay 10 000 }

title: runInterruptible
text: What is runInterruptible , how does it work, and when does it actually help? runInterruptible context { blockingCall } runs a non-suspending block, by default on the current dispatcher or the context I pass usually Dispatchers.IO . If the coroutine is cancelled while the block runs, it calls Thread.interrupt on that thread. APIs that respond to interruption, like Thread.sleep , Object.wait , BlockingQueue.take , Future.get and NIO interruptible channels, then throw, and runInterruptible rethrows that as a CancellationException . It only helps with interruptible APIs. Classic socket InputStream.read and most JNI calls ignore interrupts, so for those I need the API's own cancel or close method.

title: Retrofit/OkHttp cancellation
text: When a coroutine running a Retrofit suspend call is cancelled, what happens to the HTTP request, on the client and on the server? Since Retrofit 2.6, suspend functions are implemented with suspendCancellableCoroutine around call.enqueue , plus invokeOnCancellation { call.cancel } . When the coroutine is cancelled, the continuation resumes immediately with a CE and OkHttp's call.cancel runs. OkHttp then tears down the stream or connection, and its callback reports IOException "Canceled" , which is ignored because the continuation is already done. On the server, a cancel is just the client hanging up. If the request was already sent, the server may fully process it. So cancellation saves client resources and bandwidth, but it's not a rollback. Non-idempotent calls need idempotency keys.

title: Asynchronous timeout & resources
text: The kotlinx.coroutines docs describe a resource leak with withTimeout even when the code "looks" correct. Explain the race and the fix. The timeout fires asynchronously relative to the block. The block can finish and produce a value, say a freshly opened resource, and the timeout can still fire before control returns to the caller. withTimeout then throws a TCE and the value is discarded, so the resource you returned is never closed. The documented fix is to never let a resource be owned only by the return value. Store it in a variable declared outside the timeout block, assigned the moment it's acquired, and close it in a finally outside the timeout.

title: Foreign CancellationException
text: What happens if a coroutine that is not cancelled receives a CancellationException , for example from await on a cancelled Deferred ? Why is that dangerous? The coroutine machinery can't tell "I was cancelled" from "some code threw a CE at me". If a CE escapes the body of an active launch , that coroutine completes as cancelled. Its parent isn't notified of a failure, no handler runs, and nothing is logged, so the work just stops. A common source is await on a Deferred that was cancelled, for instance one cached in a shared map and cancelled by another caller's scope. The defense is to treat a CE as cancellation only when ensureActive confirms my Job is cancelled. Otherwise convert it into a real error.

title: Prompt cancellation guarantee
text: What is the "prompt cancellation guarantee" in kotlinx.coroutines, and what does it imply for code like withContext Dispatchers.IO { db.insert x } ? Since kotlinx.coroutines 1.4, withContext and suspendCancellableCoroutine guarantee that if the Job is cancelled while the coroutine is suspended, it won't resume normally, even when the result has already arrived and is waiting to be dispatched back. For withContext IO { db.insert x } , that means the insert can commit on IO, then the caller is cancelled before Main runs the continuation, and the caller gets a CancellationException instead of the inserted ID. So "my suspend call threw CE" does not mean "it didn't happen". Writes must be idempotent or confirmed separately.

title: Cancellation in Room transactions
text: What happens if a coroutine is cancelled while it's inside a Room withTransaction { } block, or during a suspend DAO call? Is partial data written? Room's withTransaction follows "commit only if the block completes normally". If the coroutine is cancelled at a suspension point inside the block, the CE propagates out, the transaction is ended without being marked successful, and SQLite rolls back. So you don't get half of the block's writes. Two caveats. First, if cancellation arrives after the commit, the caller may still see a CE prompt cancellation , so the data is saved but the caller thinks it failed. Second, a long-running SQL statement is only interrupted where Room can cancel it. Cancellability of an individual query has varied by Room version, so I'd treat a single statement as running to completion.

title: Cancellation propagation & cancelled scopes
text: How does cancellation propagate between parent and child? And what happens if I launch into a scope that has already been cancelled? Cancellation flows down. Cancelling a Job cancels all its children recursively, and the parent then waits in the Cancelling state until they finish. Cancelling a child, or a child completing with a CE, does not cancel the parent or its siblings. Only a real failure, a non-CE exception, propagates up C6 . If you launch into a scope whose Job is already cancelled, launch still returns a Job, but that Job is born cancelled. With default start, the body never runs: no code, no finally , no error. It silently does nothing.

title: Suspend calls in finally
text: Find the bug, explain the metrics, and fix it so the event is reliably recorded. A video app tracks playback session end with watch time, which product uses for content payouts. Analytics shows about 4% of sessions have a start event but no end , and on Android only iOS is 0.3% . It's worst when users swipe the player Fragment away 12% and nearly 0% when the video plays to the end. Engineers suspect the analytics SDK batching it flushes every 30 s and Doze on Samsung devices. // PlayerViewModel fun startSession videoId: String { viewModelScope.launch { val start = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime analytics.track "playback session start", videoId // suspend fun try { player.awaitCompletion // suspends until playback ends } finally { val watched = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime - start analytics.track "playback session end", videoId, watched // suspend fun - writes to Room queue } } }

title: Timeout on blocking code
text: Why doesn't the timeout work, and how do you actually enforce the 2 s budget? A banking app's home screen calls a third-party fraud-check SDK before showing balances. The SDK only exposes a blocking riskScore : Int . The team wrapped it in a 2 s timeout so a slow SDK can't block the screen: suspend fun riskScoreOrDefault : Int = withTimeoutOrNull 2 000 { withContext Dispatchers.IO { fraudSdk.riskScore } // blocking, sometimes 8–15 s on poor networks } ?: DEFAULT SCORE Field metrics: home-screen p50 is 900 ms, but p95 is 9.4 s and p99 is 15.2 s. That's the SDK's latency, not 2 s. 1.8M DAU, 40% on 3G/poor networks in some regions. Product insists on "never wait more than 2 s". A teammate says the IO dispatcher is saturated because a Perfetto trace shows 40+ IO threads busy.

title: Timeout & resource leaks
text: Lead the review: root cause, why it got worse two weeks ago, the fix, and the action items. Post-incident review. A QR-scanner feature opens Camera2 through a callback wrapper under a 3 s timeout. Over two weeks, the "camera unavailable" rate rose from 0.2% to 3.1% of scanner opens. It's concentrated on low-end devices and recovers only after the app process restarts. Logcat from an affected device: E CameraService: Camera "0" is already open by client com.example.app pid 8812 W CameraDevice-JV-0: ... ERROR CAMERA IN USE The code unchanged for months , plus a change two weeks ago that cut the timeout from 5 s to 3 s: suspend fun openCamera id: String : CameraDevice = withTimeout 3 000 { suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont - manager.openCamera id, object : CameraDevice.StateCallback { override fun onOpened device: CameraDevice { cont.resume device } override fun onDisconnected device: CameraDevice { device.close } override fun onError device: CameraDevice, error: Int { device.close if cont.isActive cont.resumeWithException CameraOpenException error } }, handler } } // caller val device = openCamera "0" try { startPreview device } finally { device.close } Red herrings in the timeline: a CameraX version bump in an unrelated feature, and an Android 14 security patch rollout on two OEMs.

title: Cancellation and side effects
text: A user cancels a coroutine that is mid-way through a non-idempotent operation, such as submitting an order. What guarantees does cancellation give you about the side effect, and how do you design for it? Cancellation guarantees only that my coroutine stops waiting and unwinds. It guarantees nothing about the side effect. The HTTP request may be fully processed by the server, a Room write may have committed just before the CE prompt cancellation , and a half-sent upload may or may not have been applied. So non-idempotent operations get an idempotency key generated once per user intent. Retries and re-submissions reuse the key, and the server or a local unique constraint dedupes. On cancel, I treat the outcome as unknown, and I reconcile by querying state by key instead of showing "failed".

title: Cost of cancellation checks
text: How do you balance cancellation latency with throughput here? An offline-first notes app imports a 300k-row CSV on Dispatchers.Default 4 cores on the target low-end device . A code review added "responsiveness" by calling yield after every row. QA now reports the import takes 41 s versus 12 s before. Users cancel the import often, and before the change, cancellation took up to 12 s to take effect the loop had no check . Profiler: 70% of time in DispatchedContinuation.resumeCancellableWith and queue operations, with the parse and insert itself well under 30%. A teammate wants to remove yield entirely. Another suggests delay 1 per row to "let the UI breathe". suspend fun import rows: Sequence<String = withContext Dispatchers.Default { for line in rows { yield dao.insertBlocking parse line // 35 µs per row } }

title: Cancellation in Flow collection
text: How does cancellation work when collecting a Flow ? What happens to the producer when the collector is cancelled or stops early with first or take ? A flow is collected in the collector's coroutine, so cancelling that coroutine cancels the flow. The producer's emit is a suspension point and throws CE, unwinding the flow {} body through its finally . Operators like first and take n stop early by throwing an internal CancellationException subclass that aborts the upstream; they are cancelling this collection , not your coroutine. Flow builders check the Job on emit, so a flow that emits regularly is cancellable. A flow {} that never emits or suspends is not. And since a Flow's CE is a CE, catch blocks inside it can swallow it, and emit inside a catch-all can mask it.

title: NonCancellable misuse
text: What's wrong, why does it leak and ANR, and what's the right way to make "mark read" reliable? A news app's article screen saves a "read" marker and prefetches the next 5 articles. After a refactor to "make saving reliable", crash reports and memory graphs changed: ANR rate rose from 0.15% to 0.45%, and heap dumps from OOM crashes 0.6% of sessions show ArticleFragment instances retained after onDestroy . Leak path in LeakCanary: ┬ GC Root: Thread DefaultDispatcher-worker-2 ├─ kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedContinuation ├─ ArticleViewModel$onLeave$1 anonymous Function2, captures this ├─ ArticleViewModel └─ ArticleFragment.binding → retained, leaking The code: class ArticleViewModel private val repo: ArticleRepo : ViewModel { fun onLeave article: Article { viewModelScope.launch NonCancellable { // "so it always finishes" repo.markRead article.id // 20 ms repo.prefetch article.nextIds // 5 network calls, 2 s each on slow links events.value = Event.Saved // StateFlow<Event? collected by the Fragment } } } Red herring: the team also upgraded Coil in the same release.

title: Propagation launch vs async
text: How does an exception thrown inside launch behave differently from one thrown inside async ? launch is fire-and-forget, so nobody is waiting to receive its exception. It propagates up the Job tree straight away. If it reaches the root unhandled, it goes to a CoroutineExceptionHandler or else to the thread's uncaught-exception handler, which on Android crashes the app. async returns a Deferred that can carry a result or an exception. As a root coroutine it stores the exception and rethrows it when someone calls await . As a child it does both: it still cancels its parent right away, and await also rethrows.

title: try/catch around launch
text: Why doesn't wrapping scope.launch { ... } in try/catch catch the exception thrown inside it? launch doesn't execute the body in my call stack. It schedules a new coroutine and returns a Job at once, so the try block has already exited by the time the body runs. The exception is then thrown on a different call stack, inside the dispatcher's task, and it propagates through the Job hierarchy, not through my stack frames. The try/catch has to go inside the coroutine, or around a suspending call that waits for the work, such as coroutineScope , withContext or await .

title: Uncaught exceptions crash Android
text: What exactly happens on Android when a coroutine throws and nothing handles the exception? Does it matter which dispatcher it ran on? The coroutine fails and propagates up. If no coroutine above it takes the exception and there's no CoroutineExceptionHandler in its context, kotlinx.coroutines calls the current thread's uncaught-exception handler. On Android that's normally Crashlytics wrapping the platform's default handler, which kills the process. The dispatcher doesn't matter: an uncaught exception on an IO worker thread crashes the app the same way as one on main.

title: CoroutineExceptionHandler basics
text: What is a CoroutineExceptionHandler , what is it good for, and what can it not do? CEH is a context element that's called only for uncaught exceptions, meaning exceptions no parent took and no await consumed. By the time it runs, the coroutine has already completed with that exception, so I can't resume, retry in place, or return a value. I use it for logging, crash reporting, and maybe a generic UI signal. Recovery belongs in try/catch inside the coroutine, or in Result types.

title: coroutineScope / withContext rethrow
text: If I start several children inside coroutineScope { } and one fails, what happens, and where can I catch it? coroutineScope is a regular, non-supervisor scope. If any child fails, it cancels its remaining children, waits for them to finish, and then rethrows the original exception from the coroutineScope call itself. It doesn't go to a handler. So the try/catch goes around coroutineScope , not around individual awaits inside it. withContext behaves the same way for its block.

title: Where CoroutineExceptionHandler works
text: Where does a CoroutineExceptionHandler have to be installed to actually be invoked? Why is a handler on a child coroutine ignored? A handler is consulted only by the coroutine that ends up being responsible for the exception: the one whose parent refuses it. In practice that's a coroutine launched directly in a scope the scope's Job takes no responsibility , a coroutine directly under a SupervisorJob or supervisorScope , or a true root launched with no parent. A handler on a nested launch under a regular parent is ignored because the parent accepts the failure. A handler on async is always ignored, because async puts its exception in the Deferred.

title: Root vs child async
text: Compare a root async with a child async . When does each one's exception surface, and can it ever be lost silently? A child async under a regular parent fails the parent immediately, whether or not anyone awaits it, and await also rethrows. A root async holds the exception in its Deferred and rethrows only on await . Here's the subtle part: async launched directly in a SupervisorJob scope such as viewModelScope acts like a root. The supervisor refuses the failure and async doesn't report it as uncaught, so if nobody awaits it, the exception disappears without a log.

title: supervisorScope and handlers
text: How do exceptions behave inside supervisorScope ? Which handler is used, and what happens if the supervisorScope body itself throws? supervisorScope changes one thing: a failing child no longer cancels the scope or its siblings. Each direct child is responsible for its own exception. A child launch looks up a CoroutineExceptionHandler in its own context, which includes whatever the outer coroutine had, and with no handler it goes to the thread's uncaught handler, which still crashes. A child async keeps its exception for await . If the supervisorScope body throws, the scope fails like a normal scope: it cancels all children and rethrows to the caller.

title: CancellationException is special
text: Why are CancellationException s ignored by exception handlers and not propagated to the parent as a failure? How can that bite you? The machinery treats CancellationException as normal termination, not as an error. A child that ends with it doesn't cancel its parent, and no CoroutineExceptionHandler or uncaught handler is ever called. That's what allows job.cancel to work without crashing anything. The problem: any CancellationException gets this treatment, including one you didn't intend. A business exception that extends it, a TimeoutCancellationException escaping an inner withTimeout , or await on a Deferred that was cancelled will all end your coroutine silently.

title: Aggregated / suppressed exceptions
text: If several children of the same parent fail at almost the same time, which exception does the handler or caller receive, and what happens to the others? The first exception wins. The parent completes with the first non-cancellation exception it was notified of. Exceptions that arrive later while the parent is already cancelling, from other children or from children's finally blocks, are attached as suppressed exceptions on the first one through Throwable.addSuppressed . CancellationExceptions caused by the cascade aren't added. On the JVM you see them as Suppressed: entries in the stack trace. The kotlinlang docs say aggregation works on Java 1.7+ and is limited on JS/Native.

title: Misplaced CoroutineExceptionHandler
text: Does this fix the crash? Walk me through what happens on a 503 from repo.orders , and rewrite it. A teammate adds error handling to a ViewModel after Crashlytics shows HttpException: HTTP 503 as the 2 fatal 0.6% of sessions, 1.2M DAU . The PR description says "added CoroutineExceptionHandler, crash fixed." QA can't reproduce because staging never returns 503. The code: class OrdersViewModel private val repo: OrdersRepository : ViewModel { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { , e - state.value = OrdersState.Error e.message ?: "unknown" } private val state = MutableStateFlow<OrdersState OrdersState.Loading val state: StateFlow<OrdersState = state fun load { viewModelScope.launch { val orders = async handler { repo.orders } val badges = async handler { repo.badges } launch handler { repo.markSeen } state.value = OrdersState.Content orders.await , badges.await } } }

title: Observing failure from outside
text: I have a Job from launch and a Deferred from async . How do I find out from outside whether each one failed, was cancelled, or succeeded? For a Deferred, await returns the value or rethrows the failure. For a Job, join does not rethrow the job's failure; it only waits, and it throws only if the coroutine calling join is itself cancelled. To tell outcomes apart I use invokeOnCompletion { cause - } : null means success, a CancellationException means it was cancelled, anything else means it failed. Properties like isCancelled are true for both failed and cancelled, so they can't separate the two.

title: What to catch: Exception vs Throwable vs specific types
text: Inside coroutines, should I catch Throwable , Exception , or specific types like IOException ? What changes compared with normal Kotlin code? I catch the specific, expected types: IOException for network, HttpException for HTTP errors, my own domain exceptions. In coroutines a broad catch e: Exception also catches CancellationException , because on the JVM it extends IllegalStateException . So any broad catch has to rethrow cancellation first. I almost never catch Throwable mid-stack, since that swallows OutOfMemoryError , StackOverflowError and initialization errors that the process can't recover from. Only top-level reporting boundaries see everything, and they report and rethrow.

title: ViewModel error-handling strategies
text: What are the options for handling errors from coroutines in a ViewModel, and which do you use by default? viewModelScope is SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.Main.immediate with no exception handler. So a failing launch doesn't affect its sibling launches, but an uncaught failure crashes the app. My default: repositories and use cases throw only for unexpected bugs and return typed results for expected failures. The ViewModel maps those results to UI state inside the launch, and a small report-only CoroutineExceptionHandler on fire-and-forget launches records anything unexpected as non-fatal. I don't use one global catch-all that turns every failure into a generic error screen.

title: Exceptions vs Result types
text: Should suspend functions in your data layer throw exceptions or return Result /sealed types? What's wrong with using kotlin.Result and runCatching everywhere? I use exceptions for things the caller can't reasonably handle programmer errors, broken invariants and typed results for expected outcomes the caller has to handle: offline, not found, validation, unauthorized. A sealed type with domain-specific cases beats kotlin.Result<T , because Result erases the error to Throwable , so callers can't exhaustively when on it. And runCatching catches Throwable , including CancellationException , so used around suspend calls it breaks cancellation and also wraps genuine bugs as "failures."

title: Silent swallowing in parallel loads
text: What's going on, and how would you fix it so it neither crashes nor fails silently? A home dashboard loads 4 sections in parallel. Last sprint, to "fix crashes" an HttpException fatal at 0.3% , a developer rewrote it as below. Crashes dropped to 0. Two weeks later product reports that 7% of home loads show at least one blank section, recommendation click-through fell 11%, and support tickets say "home is empty after I come back to the app." No new crashes, no error logs. Backend dashboards show /recs p95 rising from 400 ms to 2.8 s at peak, with 4% 5xx. A red herring: an OkHttp upgrade went out in the same release. fun loadHome = viewModelScope.launch { supervisorScope { val header = async { repo.header } val recs = async { repo.recommendations } val promos = async { repo.promos } val recent = async { repo.recent } state.value = HomeState header = runCatching { header.await }.getOrNull , recs = runCatching { recs.await }.getOrNull , promos = runCatching { promos.await }.getOrNull , recent = runCatching { recent.await }.getOrNull , } }

title: Awaiting a Deferred cancelled elsewhere
text: Explain the endless spinner and fix the dedup. A ConfigRepository Hilt @Singleton deduplicates concurrent config fetches so 3 screens opening at once don't fire 3 requests. Since this shipped, 1.5% of sessions see an endless spinner on the Settings screen. No crash, no ANR, no error log. It happens mostly when users open Settings right after backing out of Home. Retrying reopening Settings fixes it. A red herring: the config endpoint had a 30-minute outage on the same day the bug was first reported. @Singleton class ConfigRepository @Inject constructor private val api: ConfigApi { private var inFlight: Deferred<Config ? = null suspend fun config : Config = coroutineScope { val existing = inFlight if existing != null && existing.isActive return@coroutineScope existing.await val d = async { api.fetchConfig } inFlight = d d.await } } class SettingsViewModel repo: ConfigRepository : ViewModel { init { viewModelScope.launch { state.value = Loading state.value = Ready repo.config // spinner forever for some users } } }

title: Exceptions thrown while handling exceptions
text: What happens when an exception is thrown during exception handling: inside a finally block, inside an invokeOnCompletion handler, or inside a CoroutineExceptionHandler itself? There are three different behaviors. A finally that throws replaces the original exception under normal Kotlin/JVM rules; it isn't automatically suppressed onto it. However, if the coroutine is already failing and a child's cleanup throws, the Job collects it as a suppressed exception. A throwing invokeOnCompletion handler is wrapped in CompletionHandlerException and sent to the coroutine exception-handling path. A CoroutineExceptionHandler that throws gets wrapped together with the original into a RuntimeException that goes to the thread's uncaught handler, so you crash after all.

title: Internals of exception routing in the Job tree
text: Walk me through how kotlinx.coroutines decides, internally, who handles a failed coroutine's exception. What are childCancelled , handlesException , and scoped coroutines? When a coroutine finishes with an exception, JobSupport picks a root cause from the collected exceptions, then asks two questions. First, cancelParent cause : scoped coroutines return true straight away they'll rethrow to the caller , cancellation exceptions count as handled, and otherwise it calls parent.childCancelled cause , which a supervisor answers with false and a regular coroutine answers with true. Second, if the parent didn't take it, handleJobException cause runs. launch overrides it to call the CEH or the uncaught handler, async doesn't override it, so the exception stays in its state. A root Job cancels itself but reports "not handled," because its handlesException is false when it has no handling parent.

title: Scope with Job() dies after first failure
text: You build CoroutineScope Dispatchers.IO + handler for a long-lived manager and one launch throws. The handler logs it, but later launch calls do nothing. What happened, and how do you build a scope that survives child failures? CoroutineScope context adds a plain Job if the context has no Job. A plain Job is a regular parent: a child's failure cancels it and therefore every sibling. The handler fires because that child was the top of the chain, but the scope's Job is now Cancelled, and launch on a cancelled scope returns a Job that's already cancelled and never runs the body, with no error. The fix is SupervisorJob in the scope's context, plus a handler or try/catch for the children, since supervision stops propagation but doesn't make failures disappear.

title: launchSafe wrapper
text: You're leading the post-incident review. What went wrong, what do you change, and how do you prevent this class of failure? Eight months ago a platform team added BaseViewModel.launchSafe to "end coroutine crashes." Adoption: 140 call sites. Today's incident: for 36 hours, 9% of checkout attempts silently failed spinner, then the screen returned to the cart with a generic "Something went wrong" . Crash-free sessions stayed at 99.96% the whole time, so no alert fired. Root cause was found by support: a backend change returned a new JSON field type, and a SerializationException in the checkout response was caught by launchSafe . Another symptom found in the review: the app sometimes continued to show "Order placed" after the user had navigated away. A red herring: the payment gateway had a short latency blip the same week. abstract class BaseViewModel : ViewModel { protected val error = MutableSharedFlow<String extraBufferCapacity = 1 val error = error.asSharedFlow protected fun launchSafe block: suspend CoroutineScope. - Unit = viewModelScope.launch { try { block } catch e: Throwable { error.tryEmit "Something went wrong" } } }

title: Retry inside a handler
text: Explain the traffic pattern and rewrite the retry so it's safe. A messaging app 2M DAU syncs unsent messages with a SyncScope . After a release, backend SRE reports request spikes to /messages/send : 6x normal volume during a 20-minute regional degradation, then the API's rate limiter starts returning 429 and the spike continues for 40 more minutes. Devices on bad networks show battery drain in vitals. Crashlytics shows nothing. The release note: "automatic retry for failed syncs." A red herring: a CDN change shipped the same day. object SyncScope { private val handler: CoroutineExceptionHandler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { ctx, e - Reporter.nonFatal e scope.launch { sync } // "retry" } val scope = CoroutineScope SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.IO + handler fun sync = scope.launch { outbox.pending .forEach { api.send it } // throws IOException on bad network } }

title: Domain exceptions and layering
text: How do you design the exception types that flow through repository, domain and ViewModel layers in a coroutine-based app? What rules do you set? The data layer converts library exceptions HttpException , SQLiteException , SerializationException into a small set of domain types at the boundary, keeping the original as cause . Expected failures are modelled as sealed result types or a sealed exception hierarchy under Exception . Unexpected ones aren't converted. Rules: never extend CancellationException , always pass cause , don't leak transport types upward, and map to user-facing text only in the UI layer.

title: Partial failure in fan-out
text: Design the fan-out so partial failure is first-class, and explain how exceptions and cancellation behave. A photo-sharing app lets users upload up to 30 photos at once. Product requirements, as written: "Upload all photos in parallel for speed. If some fail, tell the user which ones failed and let them retry just those. Don't fail the batch because one photo is bad. Cancelling the screen should stop the uploads." Current code uses coroutineScope { photos.map { async { upload it } }.awaitAll } . Data from the last month: 12% of batches have at least one failure mostly 10 MB files hitting a 413, and flaky networks ; in those cases users see "Upload failed" and all 30 photos restart. The server enforces 6 concurrent connections per client, and 429s appear when the app opens 30 at once. A red herring: an engineer proposes switching to WorkManager as the fix.

title: Multi-bug review
text: List every bug, say what each one does at runtime, and give the fix. You're reviewing a ViewModel before release. It handles a profile edit screen for an app with 800k DAU. QA reports "sometimes the screen shows Saved but the server has no change," "after a failed save, the Save button stays disabled forever," and Crashlytics has a growing non-fatal JobCancellationException count. Find the bugs. class EditProfileViewModel private val repo: ProfileRepository : ViewModel { private val ui = MutableStateFlow EditUi val ui = ui.asStateFlow private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { , e - ui.value = ui.value.copy error = e.message // 1 } init { viewModelScope.async handler { ui.value = ui.value.copy profile = repo.load } // 2 } fun save name: String { ui.value = ui.value.copy saving = true try { viewModelScope.launch { // 3 repo.save name ui.value = ui.value.copy saved = true } } catch e: Exception { ui.value = ui.value.copy error = e.message } ui.value = ui.value.copy saving = false // 4 } fun autosave draft: String { viewModelScope.launch Job { // 5 try { repo.saveDraft draft } catch e: Exception { // 6 Reporter.nonFatal e } finally { repo.markDraftSynced // 7 suspend fun } } } }

title: viewModelScope basics
text: What is viewModelScope , when is it cancelled, and why should most ViewModel coroutines run in it? viewModelScope is a CoroutineScope extension property on ViewModel . It's created lazily the first time you touch it, and it's cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared, right before onCleared runs. A ViewModel is cleared when its ViewModelStoreOwner goes away for good: the Activity finishes, the Fragment is removed, or the navigation back-stack entry is popped. It is not cleared on rotation. So anything launched there survives configuration changes and dies when the user leaves the screen. That's exactly the lifetime of "load data for this screen", so I don't have to cancel anything by hand.

title: lifecycleScope basics
text: What is lifecycleScope , when does it get cancelled, and how is it different in an Activity versus a Fragment? lifecycleScope is lifecycle.coroutineScope on any LifecycleOwner .
