It uses SupervisorJob plus Dispatchers.Main.immediate , and it's cancelled when the lifecycle reaches DESTROYED . It does nothing on STOPPED : coroutines keep running in the background. In an Activity, DESTROYED also happens on every rotation, so lifecycleScope work restarts on config change. In a Fragment, lifecycleScope follows the Fragment instance, which outlives its view when the fragment goes onto the back stack. For anything touching views I use viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope .

title: GlobalScope pitfalls
text: Why is GlobalScope discouraged on Android, and what does the @DelicateCoroutinesApi annotation tell you? GlobalScope has no Job . Coroutines launched there have no parent, so nothing cancels them, nothing waits for them, and failures don't propagate to anyone who cares. That breaks structured concurrency: leaks are invisible, tests can't control them, and a coroutine capturing an Activity lives as long as it runs. Since kotlinx.coroutines 1.5 it's marked @DelicateCoroutinesApi , so you get a warning unless you opt in. If I really need app-lifetime work, I inject an application CoroutineScope with a SupervisorJob , so it's at least owned, injectable and replaceable in tests.

title: viewModelScope internals
text: How is viewModelScope actually implemented? Walk me through its context, how it's created, and how it gets cancelled. It's a CloseableCoroutineScope whose context is SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.Main.immediate . It's created lazily on first access and stored in the ViewModel under a fixed key as an AutoCloseable . When the ViewModel is cleared, its closeables are closed, and closing the scope calls coroutineContext.cancel . That runs before onCleared . Since lifecycle 2.8 you can pass your own scope to the ViewModel viewModelScope constructor, which is how I inject a test scope. On KMP targets with no Main dispatcher, the library falls back to EmptyCoroutineContext .

title: Main.immediate in Android scopes
text: Both viewModelScope and lifecycleScope use Dispatchers.Main.immediate . What does immediate change in practice, and when does it surprise people? Dispatchers.Main always posts the coroutine to the main Looper's queue, even if you're already on the main thread. Main.immediate skips the post when you're already on main: isDispatchNeeded returns false, so the coroutine body runs synchronously inside launch up to its first suspension. In Android scopes, a launch from onCreate or a click handler starts right away, and a StateFlow update is visible before the next frame. The surprise is ordering. Code after launch {} runs after the coroutine's first segment, not before it. Re-entrancy can also bite, because nested immediate dispatches use an event loop to avoid stack overflow.

title: ViewModel clearing & closeables
text: What exactly happens when a ViewModel is cleared? Explain onCleared , addCloseable , and the ordering guarantees across lifecycle versions. ViewModelStore.clear calls an internal clear on each ViewModel. That marks the ViewModel cleared, closes every registered AutoCloseable , and then calls onCleared . viewModelScope is one of those closeables, so by the time onCleared runs, the scope is already cancelled. Since lifecycle 2.5 I register resources with addCloseable instead of overriding onCleared . 2.7 made addCloseable after clearing close immediately. 2.8 added keyed closeables addCloseable key, ... , getCloseable key and switched to AutoCloseable . The order in 2.8 is keyed closeables, then un-keyed ones, then onCleared .

title: launchWhenX deprecation
text: launchWhenStarted and the other launchWhenX helpers were deprecated. How did they work, why were they deprecated, and what replaces them? launchWhenStarted launched in lifecycleScope with a pausing dispatcher. When the lifecycle dropped below STARTED , it didn't cancel the coroutine. It just stopped dispatching it, so the coroutine sat suspended until the lifecycle came back. That's fine for a one-shot delay , but terrible for flows. A callbackFlow producer such as a location listener stays registered, and buffered upstream work keeps running in the background while nobody consumes it. It was deprecated in lifecycle 2.6.0. The replacement is repeatOnLifecycle , which cancels the block when you drop below the state and re-runs it when you return. That's what releases the upstream.

title: repeatOnLifecycle overview
text: What does repeatOnLifecycle do, why is it a suspend function, and where should you call it? Lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle state { ... } launches the block in a new coroutine each time the lifecycle reaches state . It cancels that coroutine when the lifecycle drops below state , and returns only when the lifecycle is DESTROYED . Because it suspends until destruction, nothing after it in the same coroutine runs while the UI is alive. So I put each independent collector in its own launch inside the block. I call it once from onCreate Activity or onViewCreated with viewLifecycleOwner Fragment , never from onStart / onResume , which would stack a new repeater on every start. It's been stable since lifecycle 2.4.0.

title: Fragment viewLifecycleOwner
text: Fragments have two lifecycles. When must you use viewLifecycleOwner instead of the fragment itself, and what breaks if you don't? The Fragment's own lifecycle runs from onCreate to onDestroy . Its view lifecycle runs from onCreateView to onDestroyView . When you navigate forward with a replace-and-add-to-back-stack, the view is destroyed but the Fragment isn't. If I collect in lifecycleScope from onViewCreated , the old collector keeps running against a dead view. When the user comes back, onViewCreated runs again and adds a second collector. You get duplicate work, leaked bindings, and crashes from touching a null view. Anything that touches views, or is started in onViewCreated , uses viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope and viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle . It's cancelled in onDestroyView and recreated with the next view.

title: Choosing scope for work outliving a screen
text: A user taps "Send" and immediately leaves the screen. Which scopes or mechanisms could run that send, and how do you pick? I ask how long the work must live and what happens if the process dies. If it's fine to cancel when the user leaves a screen load , use viewModelScope . If it should finish even if the user leaves but can be lost on process death a short cache write or an analytics flush , launch it in an injected application scope. If it must eventually happen even across process death and reboots sending a message, an upload , enqueue WorkManager unique work and persist the payload first. If it's user-visible, long-running and must run now playback, navigation, an ongoing call , use a foreground service with a declared type. The mistake is using one tool for all four.

title: Application scope via Hilt
text: Design an application-level CoroutineScope with Hilt. What goes in its context, how is it injected, and how do you keep it from becoming GlobalScope in disguise? I provide a @Singleton scope with a qualifier, @ApplicationScope , in SingletonComponent . Its context is SupervisorJob so one failure doesn't cancel all app work, an injected default dispatcher usually Default ; callers hop to IO with withContext , a CoroutineExceptionHandler that logs to crash reporting instead of crashing for known non-fatal paths, and a CoroutineName . Classes depend on the qualified CoroutineScope , never create their own, and tests replace it with TestScope / backgroundScope through a test module. The rule for using it: short, idempotent work that should outlive a screen but is fine to lose on process death. Anything that must happen goes to WorkManager.

title: CoroutineWorker basics
text: What is CoroutineWorker , how does it differ from Worker , and what does a correct doWork look like? CoroutineWorker is the Kotlin flavor of WorkManager's worker. doWork is a suspend function, so I can call suspend APIs directly. It runs on Dispatchers.Default by default, not on WorkManager's configured Executor like Worker . For blocking IO I wrap the code in withContext Dispatchers.IO , or rely on main-safe suspend APIs. I return Result.success output , Result.retry rescheduled with the request's backoff policy , or Result.failure . When WorkManager stops the work, the coroutine is cancelled automatically, and cooperative code just unwinds.

title: CoroutineWorker stop & cancellation semantics
text: When does WorkManager stop a running CoroutineWorker , what happens to the coroutine, and how do you write workers that behave correctly when stopped? A running worker can be stopped because its constraints stopped being met, because the app cancelled it or replaced it with REPLACE , because the system's execution limit hit JobScheduler gives roughly 10 minutes per run , or because of other system reasons like app standby quotas. CoroutineWorker cancels the doWork coroutine, so the next suspension point throws CancellationException . Any Result you return after being stopped is ignored, and unless the work was cancelled by you, WorkManager reschedules it. So workers must be idempotent and resumable: checkpoint progress, use server idempotency keys, clean up in finally , and never assume one run equals one completion. For runs over about 10 minutes, use setForeground long-running worker or split the work.

title: LifecycleService & coroutines in services
text: How do you use coroutines inside an Android Service ? What does LifecycleService give you, and what are its pitfalls? A plain Service has no coroutine scope. You either create CoroutineScope SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.Main.immediate and cancel it in onDestroy , or extend LifecycleService from androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-service , which makes the service a LifecycleOwner . Then lifecycleScope is cancelled at onDestroy and repeatOnLifecycle works. Pitfalls: you must call super in the overridden callbacks or lifecycle events don't fire, lifecycleScope runs on Main so heavy work needs withContext , and a running coroutine doesn't keep the process or service alive. On Android 8+ a background service is stopped within minutes, so real long work means a foreground service with a declared type, or WorkManager.

title: Process death implications
text: What happens to your coroutines, ViewModels and flows on process death, and how do you design so the user doesn't notice? On process death, the OS kills the process without any callback. No onCleared , no onDestroy , no finally blocks, no cancellation. Every coroutine, scope, StateFlow and singleton simply vanishes. When the user returns, Android recreates the task's Activity and Fragment stack from saved instance state, and new ViewModels are created empty. What survives is only what was persisted: the saved-state Bundle SavedStateHandle , rememberSaveable , navigation arguments , disk Room, DataStore, files , and WorkManager's persisted work. So I keep small UI-identifying state IDs, query text, scroll anchor in SavedStateHandle , re-derive everything else from the database, and route anything that must complete through WorkManager.

title: Save-on-leave patterns
text: A note-editing screen must never lose the user's text: not on back, home, app switch or process death. Where and how do you save, given how Android scopes get cancelled? I don't rely on a single "on leave" moment, because no callback is guaranteed to run before the process dies. First, autosave continuously: each edit updates a StateFlow , and a debounced collector in viewModelScope writes to Room roughly every 500 ms. Second, the current unsaved text goes in SavedStateHandle so process death can restore it. Third, there's a final flush when the user leaves. I trigger it from onStop or ViewModel onCleared as a synchronous hand-off , and the actual write runs in an injected application scope, so viewModelScope cancellation can't kill it mid-write. onStop is the last callback reliably delivered before the app can be killed in the background, so that's my flush point, not onDestroy .

title: viewLifecycleOwner
text: Find the bug s , explain the mechanism, and fix it. A list Fragment in a Navigation-based app. QA reports that after opening a detail screen and pressing back three times, each new item update triggers 4 network "mark seen" calls, and Crashlytics shows NullPointerException at binding.recycler in about 0.2% of sessions, all after back navigation. The RecyclerView adapter is fine. Nothing changed in the ViewModel, which a reviewer blamed first. class InboxFragment : Fragment R.layout.fragment inbox { private var binding: FragmentInboxBinding? = null private val binding get = binding!! private val vm: InboxViewModel by viewModels override fun onViewCreated view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle? { binding = FragmentInboxBinding.bind view lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle Lifecycle.State.STARTED { vm.items.collect { items - binding.recycler.adapter.let { it as InboxAdapter .submitList items } vm.markSeen items.firstOrNull ?.id } } } } override fun onDestroyView { binding = null; super.onDestroyView } }

title: launchWhenX migration
text: What went wrong, and how would you run this migration safely? You own a 400k-DAU app with about 180 launchWhenStarted / launchWhenResumed call sites. After bumping lifecycle to 2.8.x the deprecation warnings fail the build allWarningsAsErrors . A teammate opened a PR that mechanically replaces every lifecycleScope.launchWhenStarted { X } with lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle STARTED { X } } . In the beta channel 5% rollout , three things appeared: an onboarding tooltip shows every time the user returns from Settings, an analytics "screen view" event count rose 2.4x, and a payment screen started a second startActivityForResult -style launch when returning from the bank app. Crash rate is unchanged at 0.11%, a red herring for "nothing broke".

title: Work outliving a screen
text: Diagnose this and redesign the posting flow. A marketplace app 1.2M DAU, 60% Android, 35% of devices with 3 GB of RAM or less lets sellers upload 3–8 photos and then a listing. Since a redesign that added a "Post and keep browsing" button which immediately pops the screen, support tickets about "listing never appeared" jumped from about 20/day to 900/day. Server logs show photo uploads starting but about 18% never completing, with client connections closed mid-body. No crash spike. Crashlytics non-fatal logs show JobCancellationException: Job was cancelled in ListingViewModel.post . One engineer blames a new CDN timeout config deployed the same week. fun post draft: Draft = viewModelScope.launch { val urls = draft.photos.map { async Dispatchers.IO { api.uploadPhoto it } }.awaitAll api.createListing draft.copy photoUrls = urls }

title: Application scope leaks
text: Explain the leak, fix it, and say how you'd prevent this class of bug. After a release that introduced an injected @ApplicationScope for "background prefetch", the OOM rate on Android rose from 0.04% to 0.21% of sessions, concentrated on 2–3 GB devices and long sessions over 40 min . LeakCanary in internal builds reports: ┬─── │ GC Root: Thread DefaultDispatcher-worker-3 ├─ kotlinx.coroutines.internal.DispatchedContinuation │ ↓ continuation ├─ ProductPrefetcher$prefetch$1 suspend lambda │ ↓ this$0 / L$0 ├─ ProductDetailFragment │ ↓ mView ╰→ androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout destroyed view, 2.1 MB retained The prefetch code is called from ProductDetailFragment.onViewCreated . It retries fetchRelated with delay 30 000 backoff up to 10 times. Image cache size was also raised that release, which a reviewer suspects.

title: onCleared & cleared scopes
text: Why does the event never arrive, and how do you fix it? A "session end" feature: when the user leaves the checkout flow, the app must send a checkout abandoned event and release a payment SDK session. QA sees the SDK session released, but the server receives the abandonment event for 0% of users. No crash, no log. Analytics dashboard simply shows "no data" for the event since release 7.4. @HiltViewModel class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor private val analytics: AnalyticsRepo, private val paymentSdk: PaymentSdk, : ViewModel { override fun onCleared { viewModelScope.launch { analytics.send "checkout abandoned" // suspend, network } paymentSdk.release // plain function super.onCleared } }

title: Scope placement for polling
text: Where should the polling live, who owns its lifecycle, and how do you stop wasting battery? A ride-tracking app 900k DAU polls the driver's location every 5 s while a trip is active. Today a LifecycleService runs the poll in lifecycleScope and the UI binds to it. Product wants the same updates on three surfaces: the trip screen, a home-screen widget Glance , and the in-app mini banner on other screens. Battery tests show the service polls 100% of the time during a trip, even when the app is in the background with no visible surface, costing about 6% battery per hour. Pressure: ship in 2 weeks, no backend push available yet.

title: WorkManager vs scopes cost
text: What would you change, and how would you justify the numbers to the team? A news app 3M DAU schedules a "refresh feed" PeriodicWorkRequest every 15 minutes with CoroutineWorker , plus an additional appScope.launch { while true { refresh ; delay 60 000 } } started in Application.onCreate "to keep it fresh". Play Console vitals show the app in the "excessive wake-ups" bucket, and p90 background battery draw is 2.1x the category median. 41% of refreshes return identical content 304 or same ETag . The server team complains about 3M × 60 requests/hour peak. Another red herring: image prefetch is only 5% of the radio time.

title: lifecycleScope work across rotation
text: Clarify the requirement, then redesign it so the behavior is correct and testable. A PM asks: "When the user opens the Promo screen, show a 10-second countdown, then auto-navigate to the offer. If they rotate, it shouldn't restart or skip. If they leave and come back, it should restart." Current implementation, in an Activity: lifecycleScope.launch { for i in 10 downTo 1 { binding.timer.text = "$i"; delay 1 000 } startActivity Intent this@PromoActivity, OfferActivity::class.java } Observed: rotating restarts the countdown at 10 about 31% of sessions have a rotation, since the screen is used on tablets , backgrounding to answer a call then returning triggers a navigation while the app is in the background on some devices, and one tester saw the offer opened twice.

title: Process death & scope ownership
text: Lead the review: root cause, why detection was slow, what to fix and what process changes to make. Post-incident review for a 6-hour incident: after release 9.2, "lateinit property userSession has not been initialized" crashes hit 1.4% of sessions about 38k/day , concentrated on devices with 3 GB of RAM and less, and only for users returning from background after 10+ minutes. Crash stack: Fatal Exception: kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property userSession has not been initialized at com.app.account.AccountViewModel.loadProfile AccountViewModel.kt:41 at com.app.account.AccountFragment$onViewCreated$1.invokeSuspend AccountFragment.kt:58 userSession was set by LoginViewModel into an @Singleton SessionHolder after login. 9.2 added "Account" as a deep-link entry point. The timeline: crash started when 9.2 reached 20%, the on-call first suspected a bad coroutines-library bump in the same release it was exactly that, version 1.8 to 1.10 , and rolled it back at hour 3 with no effect. At hour 5 someone reproduced it using adb shell am kill .

title: Data races on multi-threaded dispatchers
text: I launch 100 coroutines on Dispatchers.Default , and each one does counter++ 1,000 times. Why is the final value usually less than 100,000? Why does the same code give exactly 100,000 inside a plain runBlocking ? counter++ isn't one operation. It's a read, an add and a write. Dispatchers.Default runs coroutines in parallel on a thread pool with one thread per CPU core minimum 2 . So two threads can read the same old value, both add one, and both write it back, and one increment is lost. Inside plain runBlocking , every coroutine runs on one thread through an event loop. counter++ has no suspension point, so no coroutine can get in the middle of it, and the result is exact. What matters is how many threads the dispatcher uses, not the fact that I'm using coroutines.

title: @Volatile is not enough
text: What does @Volatile do in Kotlin, and why doesn't it fix the counter race? @Volatile kotlin.concurrent.Volatile, or kotlin.jvm.Volatile on older versions marks the JVM field as volatile . Every read then sees the latest write from any thread, and writes can't be reordered past it. That fixes visibility only. counter++ is still read, add, write, so two threads can read the same fresh value and both write the same result. Volatile is the right tool for one writer and many readers, like a stop flag or publishing an immutable snapshot. For read-modify-write I need an atomic, a lock, or confinement.

title: AtomicInteger / AtomicReference and CAS
text: How do AtomicInteger and AtomicReference work, and when are they the right tool in coroutine code? Atomics are built on a CPU compare-and-set instruction: "if the value is still X, replace it with Y, otherwise fail". incrementAndGet loops on CAS until it wins, so no update is lost and no thread ever blocks. AtomicReference does the same for a reference. That's ideal for swapping a whole immutable snapshot updateAndGet { it.copy ... } . They work from any thread, never suspend, and are fine in coroutines. The limit is that they protect exactly one variable. As soon as an invariant spans two variables, or the update has to call a suspend function, I need a Mutex or confinement.

title: Mutex basics
text: What is kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex , how do you use it, and how is it different from a Java lock? Mutex is a coroutine lock with two states, locked and unlocked. lock is a suspend function. If the mutex is taken, the coroutine suspends and frees its thread, instead of blocking the thread like synchronized does. I nearly always use mutex.withLock { } , which does lock, try, and finally-unlock. Because it suspends, the critical section can contain suspend calls. That's the reason to choose it over synchronized . It's fair waiters get the lock in FIFO order and it is not reentrant.

title: Visibility when one coroutine hops threads
text: A coroutine writes a local var on one thread, then resumes on a different thread after withContext or delay . Do I need @Volatile or a lock for that variable? No. A single coroutine runs sequentially even when it hops threads. The library guarantees that everything before a suspension happens-before the code after resumption, because the hand-off goes through the dispatcher's queue and executor, and those include memory barriers. So locals and spilled state machine fields are always visible to the resumed code. What I do need to protect is state that two coroutines touch at the same time : a field on a class, a shared map, a global. The rule is about concurrent access, not about thread switches.

title: Mutex vs synchronized
text: When would you use Mutex and when synchronized or ReentrantLock in coroutine code? Why can't you just call suspend functions inside synchronized ? synchronized is tied to a thread. The monitor belongs to the thread that entered it, and the thread blocks while it waits. A suspension inside the block would let the coroutine resume on another thread while the original thread still owns the monitor, so Kotlin rejects a suspend call inside synchronized {} at compile time "suspension point is inside a critical section" . My rule: if the critical section is short, CPU-only and never suspends, synchronized or an atomic is cheaper and works from Java too. If the critical section must suspend, like a network call, a DB call or delay , I use Mutex , which suspends waiters instead of blocking threads.

title: Mutex is non-reentrant
text: Mutex isn't reentrant. What happens when a coroutine that holds the lock calls a function that tries to take the same lock, and how do you design around that? The second lock suspends forever. The mutex is held, and the only coroutine that could release it is the one now waiting. There's no exception and no ANR, because nothing is blocked; the coroutine just never resumes, and the screen spins forever. If I pass an owner token, the second lock with the same owner throws IllegalStateException instead, which at least fails fast. The real fix is structural: lock only at the public entry points, and have them call private Locked helpers that assume the lock is already held and never take it.

title: StateFlow.update and atomic state transitions
text: Why is state.value = state.value.copy ... unsafe from multiple coroutines, and how does MutableStateFlow.update {} fix it? state.value = state.value.copy x = 1 reads, computes and writes in three steps. If another coroutine on another thread does the same with a different field, one of the writes overwrites the other with a stale copy and an update is lost. update { it.copy x = 1 } runs a compare-and-set loop: read the current value, run my lambda, and compareAndSet old, new . If someone changed the value in between, it re-runs the lambda on the fresh value. So no update is lost. The lambda must be pure because it can run more than once. If the update needs a suspend call, I do that first and then apply only the cheap state change inside update .

title: Semaphore to limit concurrency
text: What does kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore do, how is it different from Mutex , and when do you use it? Semaphore permits allows at most N coroutines inside a section at once. acquire takes a permit or suspends, and release returns it. withPermit { } does both with try/finally. A Mutex is basically a semaphore with 1 permit, but Mutex is for protecting state exclusion , while a semaphore is for limiting throughput a resource cap, like 3 parallel uploads . It's fair and FIFO, it suspends instead of blocking, and over-releasing throws IllegalStateException . Important: it caps how many are in flight , but it does not cap how many coroutines I create. For 100k items I still shouldn't launch 100k coroutines.

title: Thread confinement with limitedParallelism(1)
text: Explain thread confinement as a way to avoid locks in coroutines. What's the difference between newSingleThreadContext , an executor dispatcher and Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism 1 , and is limitedParallelism 1 a mutex? Confinement means that all access to a piece of state happens on one thread or one at a time , so no lock is needed. I give the state an owner and run all access through a dispatcher with parallelism 1. The modern way is Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism 1 or Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism 1 if the code blocks . It's a view over the shared pool, needs no closing and doesn't permanently take a thread. newSingleThreadContext or Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor .asCoroutineDispatcher create a real dedicated thread that I must close . The key point: limitedParallelism 1 limits threads , not coroutines. Code is sequential between suspension points, but if a coroutine suspends in the middle, another coroutine on that view can start. So it protects counter++ , but not a "read, call suspend, write" sequence. For that sequence I need a Mutex.

title: Actor-style state ownership
text: What is the actor pattern for shared state in coroutines? Show how you'd build a safe counter or cache as an "actor", and why the old actor {} builder isn't the recommended way anymore. An actor is a coroutine that owns some state, plus a channel of messages. Everyone else sends messages. Only the actor's coroutine reads or writes the state, so there is no sharing and no lock. Because it processes one message at a time, operations are naturally serialized, and it can hold suspend calls in its handler. The actor {} builder is marked @ObsoleteCoroutinesApi ; the docs say it will be replaced by a more flexible design with more complex rules, so I build the same thing by hand: a Channel of a sealed interface Msg , a loop in a scope I own, and CompletableDeferred for replies. I accept the cost: serialization means one slow message delays everything behind it.

title: ConcurrentHashMap and thread-safe collections
text: When is ConcurrentHashMap enough in coroutine code, and where does it still allow races? What about Collections.synchronizedList and CopyOnWriteArrayList ? ConcurrentHashMap makes each single operation atomic and visible get , put , putIfAbsent , compute , merge . It's enough when my logic is one operation per entry, like counting with merge or compute . It breaks the moment I compose operations: if !map.containsKey k map k = v is check-then-act, and two threads can both pass the check. I use the atomic compound methods computeIfAbsent , putIfAbsent , compute , merge instead. Also, iteration is weakly consistent: it won't throw ConcurrentModificationException but may or may not show concurrent changes. And it can't hold a suspend call: computeIfAbsent 's lambda must be short, non-suspending and must not modify the map.

title: Races at suspension points on a single thread
text: Is code on Dispatchers.Main immune to races? Give an example of a data race-like bug in a single-threaded coroutine and explain how you'd fix it. Main has no parallel data races on plain fields, because only one coroutine runs at a time. But coroutines interleave at every suspension point, so logical races check-then-act with a suspend call in between are fully possible. Example: if !loading { loading = true; val d = api.load ; ... loading = false } is safe, since the check and the set happen with no suspension between them. But if cache == null { cache = api.load } lets 10 callers all see null before the first load finishes, so there are 10 network calls and the last write wins. Fix: remove the gap between check and claim set a flag or store a Deferred before suspending , or serialize with a Mutex.

title: Token refresh race
text: Find the cause, fix it in a way that holds up under N parallel 401s, and describe what you'd do about the users already logged out. A fintech app has 1.2M DAU. Access tokens live for 15 minutes. After a release that moved from Retrofit callbacks to coroutines, the support team reports random logouts: about 0.8% of sessions per day end with "Session expired, please log in again". Backend logs show that for those users, within 300 ms, there were 4 to 9 calls to POST /auth/refresh using the same refresh token. The first returned 200, and the rest returned 401 refresh token reused , which the server treats as theft and revokes the whole token family. The app code: class AuthInterceptor private val tokens: TokenStore, private val authApi: AuthApi : Authenticator { override fun authenticate route: Route?, response: Response : Request? { val refreshed = runBlocking { val r = authApi.refresh tokens.refreshToken tokens.save r.access, r.refresh r.access } return response.request.newBuilder .header "Authorization", "Bearer $refreshed" .build } } A home screen load fires 7 parallel requests. The token expires just before it loads. Red herrings: clocks on devices are off by a few seconds, and "this only started after the coroutines migration".

title: Double-tap duplicate submissions
text: Explain how two requests happen, fix it so it can't happen, and say what else you'd do beyond the client. A food-delivery app 400k orders per day has a "Place order" button. Support finds 0.3% of orders about 1,200 per day are duplicated, and customers are charged twice. Server logs show pairs of POST /orders 40 to 150 ms apart with different request ids. The handler: fun onPlaceOrderClicked { viewModelScope.launch { ui.value = ui.value.copy submitting = true val result = orderRepo.placeOrder cart // 600 ms to 3 s on poor networks ui.value = ui.value.copy submitting = false, done = result.isSuccess } } The button is disabled in the UI when submitting == true , which is collected with collectAsStateWithLifecycle . Red herrings: "Compose recomposes slowly", and a backend retry layer that is blamed first. The duplicates are mostly on low-end devices.

title: Per-key de-duplication cache
text: List every bug in this code, explain each mechanically, and rewrite it so each id is fetched at most once concurrently. A news app caches article details. After a refactor, the backend team reports that opening a feed with 30 visible cards triggers up to 90 requests for the same 30 article ids at once, and sometimes the UI shows the wrong article body in a card. Code: class ArticleCache private val api: ArticleApi { private val cache = HashMap<String, Article private val confined = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism 1 suspend fun get id: String : Article = withContext confined { cache id ?: api.fetch id .also { cache id = it } } suspend fun getIO id: String : Article = withContext Dispatchers.IO { cache.getOrPut id { runBlocking { api.fetch id } } } } Cards call get id , a prefetcher calls getIO id . Crash logs sometimes show ConcurrentModificationException in HashMap.resize . Red herring: "Retrofit is not thread-safe" it is .

title: Bounded parallel uploads
text: Why didn't the colleague's change work? Design the bounded upload with correct failure and cancellation behavior. A photo backup feature uploads up to 2,000 photos. First version: photos.forEach { launch { api.upload it } } inside a coroutineScope . On mid-range devices 3 GB RAM the app crashes with OOM at about 300 photos in flight, the server returns 429 for 35% of calls, and battery drain complaints rise. Each photo is read as a 4 MB byte array before upload. A colleague suggests Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism 3 . After that change the OOM is still there and 429 s drop only slightly. A trace shows 2,000 coroutines created and 300 uploads active at once.

title: Choosing a synchronization strategy
text: Pick a mechanism for each of the four, with reasons. Then say how you'd test the choices. You are designing the shared in-memory state for a messaging app's sync engine: 1 an unread counter updated by 3 sources socket, push, DB triggers at up to 200 updates/s in bursts, 2 a map of conversationId - draft mutated by UI and a background saver, 3 an "outbox" queue where order matters and each send includes a network call 200 ms to 5 s , 4 a "last sync token" read by many and written rarely. A teammate proposes "one global Mutex for everything". Another proposes "make everything @Volatile".

title: Mutex held across network I/O
text: Why is it slow, how do you prove it, and what is the right structure? A trading app's QuoteRepository protects its cache with one Mutex: class QuoteRepository private val api: QuoteApi, private val dao: QuoteDao { private val mutex = Mutex suspend fun quote symbol: String : Quote = mutex.withLock { dao.get symbol ?.takeIf { it.isFresh } ?: api.fetch symbol .also { dao.put it } } } At 50k DAU it was fine. After onboarding a partner 500k DAU and adding a watchlist of 40 symbols per screen, the watchlist takes 8 to 25 s to render p95 , though the API p95 is 180 ms. There are no crashes; ANR rate is unchanged. A thread dump shows nothing blocked. The product team suspects the API.

title: Legacy callback threads sharing state with coroutines
text: Design the safe boundary between the SDK callbacks and the coroutine world, and explain what went wrong in the runBlocking attempt. A video-conferencing app is migrating its call manager from Java to Kotlin coroutines, one class at a time. The vendor SDK Java, closed source delivers onParticipantJoined/Left callbacks on its own 2 internal threads. The new Kotlin CallViewModel keeps participants: MutableList<Participant , mutated by the SDK callbacks and read by a coroutine on Main that builds the UI state. Crash reports after the rollout to 10% of traffic: 0.6% of calls crash with ConcurrentModificationException , and 0.2% show a participant tile for someone who already left. A teammate wrapped the callback bodies in mutex.withLock via runBlocking , and ANR rate went from 0.1% to 0.9% on that cohort.

title: Channel basics
text: What is a Channel in Kotlin coroutines, how is it different from a Deferred or a plain BlockingQueue , and what are the main operations? A Channel is a hot, non-blocking queue between coroutines. send suspends when the channel cannot take the element, receive suspends when it is empty, so nothing blocks a thread. Unlike a Deferred , which carries exactly one value, a Channel carries a stream of values. Unlike a BlockingQueue , waiting costs a suspended continuation instead of a parked thread. It is split into SendChannel and ReceiveChannel so I can hand out only the half each side needs.

title: Channel capacities
text: Explain the Channel capacity options RENDEZVOUS, BUFFERED, CONFLATED, UNLIMITED and a custom number. What is the default and when would you pick each? Channel with no argument is RENDEZVOUS, capacity 0: sender and receiver must meet. BUFFERED is a fixed buffer, default 64 changeable by the kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer system property . CONFLATED keeps only the latest element and never suspends the sender. UNLIMITED never suspends the sender and grows without bound, so it can OOM. A positive number gives that exact buffer size. I pick based on whether I want backpressure RENDEZVOUS or sized , latest-wins CONFLATED , or never-block-and-I-accept-the-memory-risk UNLIMITED .

title: Suspension semantics of send/receive
text: Walk me through exactly when send and receive suspend for each capacity. What does "fair" mean and what happens when a suspended send is cancelled? receive suspends when the buffer is empty and no sender is waiting. send suspends when there is no room: on RENDEZVOUS that means no receiver is waiting; on a sized buffer it means the buffer is full. UNLIMITED and CONFLATED never suspend send . Waiting parties are queued FIFO, so channels are fair. If a suspended send is cancelled, that element is not delivered, and onUndeliveredElement fires if I configured it.

title: close vs cancel, iteration
text: What is the difference between close on a SendChannel and cancel on a ReceiveChannel? What exceptions do send and receive throw afterward, and how does for x in channel end? close is a graceful end-of-stream: no more sends, but receivers still drain what is buffered, then iteration ends. cancel is abandonment: it closes the channel and discards buffered elements. After close, send throws ClosedSendChannelException ; receive on a closed and drained channel throws ClosedReceiveChannelException unless the channel was closed with a cause, in which case that cause is thrown. A for loop ends normally on a plain close and throws the cause if closed with one.

title: produce, consumeEach, pipelines
text: What do the produce builder and consumeEach give you over manually creating a Channel, and how do you build a pipeline of stages with them? What are the lifecycle rules? produce launches a coroutine and returns a ReceiveChannel . The channel is closed automatically when the producer block finishes, and cancelled if it fails or its scope is cancelled. A pipeline is a chain where each stage is a produce that consumes the previous stage's channel. consumeEach iterates and then cancels the channel when done or on exception, which makes it the right terminal consumer for a single-consumer channel but a trap for fan-out.

title: Fan-out and fan-in
text: Explain fan-out and fan-in with channels. How is work distributed, how do you shut it down cleanly, and what are the pitfalls? Fan-out is several consumers receiving from one channel; each element goes to exactly one of them, so you get a worker pool. Fan-in is several producers sending into one channel. Distribution is FIFO-fair among waiting receivers, roughly round-robin but not guaranteed. For shutdown the producer closes the channel, workers use a plain for loop not consumeEach , and the scope waits for all workers. For fan-in someone must close the channel only after all producers finish.

title: onBufferOverflow and onUndeliveredElement
text: What do onBufferOverflow and onUndeliveredElement do on Channel ... , and when is each needed? onBufferOverflow decides what happens when the buffer is full: SUSPEND default, backpressure , DROP OLDEST , or DROP LATEST . onUndeliveredElement is a callback invoked for every element that was sent but never received: dropped by overflow, rejected because the channel was closed or cancelled, or taken by a receiver that was cancelled before it resumed. I use the callback whenever elements own a resource that needs releasing.

title: Channel lifecycle
text: What is wrong, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it? A junior's PR adds a batch importer. QA reports: "import finishes all 500 rows, but the progress dialog never dismisses and the screen's coroutine count grows by one per import." No crash, no log. Code: class ImportViewModel private val repo: Repo : ViewModel { val done = MutableStateFlow false fun import rows: List<Row { val ch = Channel<Row Channel.BUFFERED viewModelScope.launch { for row in rows ch.send row } viewModelScope.launch Dispatchers.IO { for row in ch repo.insert row done.value = true } } } Red herrings: the DB insert is already main-safe; the buffer size 64 being smaller than the list 500 is not the problem, because the producer just suspends and resumes.

title: trySend / trySendBlocking
text: What are trySend , trySendBlocking , and tryReceive ? Where would you use each, and what does ChannelResult tell you? trySend never suspends or blocks; it returns a ChannelResult telling me whether the element was accepted. It fails if the buffer is full and policy is SUSPEND or the channel is closed. trySendBlocking blocks the calling thread until sent, so it is only for background threads I control. tryReceive is the non-suspending receive. I use trySend inside callbacks and handle the failure case explicitly instead of ignoring it.

title: select expression
text: What is select in coroutines? Show how you would wait on two channels or a channel and a timeout and explain which clause wins when several are ready. select suspends until the first of several clauses becomes ready and runs only that clause: onReceive , onReceiveCatching , onSend , onAwait , onJoin , onTimeout . Others are discarded without side effects. If several are ready, the first listed wins it is biased ; selectUnbiased picks randomly. On a closed channel onReceive throws, so I use onReceiveCatching .

title: Channel vs Flow
text: When do you choose a Channel and when a Flow? Give concrete criteria, not "Flow is the modern way". Flow is cold, declarative, lifecycle-friendly and multi-collector-safe, so it is my default for data streams. A Channel is hot, point-to-point, and has explicit lifecycle send , close , so I use it for work queues, one-shot signals, fan-out workers, and as the internal glue behind callbackFlow / channelFlow / buffer / flowOn . For UI I usually expose a Flow state, or receiveAsFlow of a channel and keep the Channel private.

title: Channel for UI events
text: Why are events lost, how do you prove it, and what is the right design? A shopping app 2.1M DAU, 38% on Android 9 to 11 with aggressive background limits sends a one-off "navigate to order confirmation" from the ViewModel through a Channel. Crashlytics shows no crash, but support reports "paid, nothing happened, spinner stays". It happens in about 0.4% of payments 1,100/day . Code: class CheckoutViewModel : ViewModel { private val events = Channel<Event // RENDEZVOUS val events = events.receiveAsFlow fun onPaid id: String { events.trySend Event.GoToConfirmation id } } // Fragment override fun onViewCreated v: View, s: Bundle? { viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle Lifecycle.State.STARTED { vm.events.collect { navigate it } } } } Breadcrumbs show the payment webhook returns while the user is in the 3-D Secure bank app the app is in the background .

title: receiveAsFlow vs consumeAsFlow
text: What is the difference between receiveAsFlow and consumeAsFlow ? What happens with multiple collectors and when the collector is cancelled? consumeAsFlow consumes the channel: it can be collected only once a second collection throws IllegalStateException , and when that collector finishes or is cancelled, the channel is cancelled too. receiveAsFlow just receives: it can be collected repeatedly and by multiple collectors each element still goes to one , and cancelling a collector leaves the channel alive. For UI event flows that must survive resubscription repeatOnLifecycle , receiveAsFlow is the one.

title: Worker pool failure handling
text: Diagnose the hang, and design the pool so one bad item cannot stall or kill the sync, without leaking resources. A photo-backup service Android foreground service, 4 workers, 3,000 photos on first sync, p95 upload 1.8 s uses a channel-based pool. After a release, support sees "sync stops at about 40%, then the notification says 'running' forever". Logs show one java.io.FileNotFoundException user deleted a photo mid-sync followed by silence. Code: suspend fun sync photos: List<Photo = coroutineScope { val ch = Channel<Photo 8 launch { photos.forEach { ch.send it }; ch.close } repeat 4 { launch Dispatchers.IO { ch.consumeEach { api.upload it } // throws on missing file } } } Red herring: server returns 200 for all uploads in the logs; Wi-Fi is stable.

title: select internals and patterns
text: How does select work internally, and what are its guarantees and costs? Why can it be unsafe to select over onSend / onReceive with side effects in the clause, and how do you build a "priority queue with timeout" correctly? select registers one waiter object with every clause's source. The first source to complete must win an atomic state change on the select instance; losers are then unregistered, and only the winner's clause body runs. That is why a losing onReceive never consumes an element. Clause order is priority, so a priority queue is a select with the high channel first; to avoid starvation I add a fairness policy such as selectUnbiased or a budget. Timeouts via onTimeout experimental or by racing a Job .

title: UNLIMITED channel and memory
text: Explain the growth, estimate it, and fix it without losing the data that matters. A fitness app streams accelerometer data at 100 Hz from a wearable over BLE, writes to Room in batches, and also feeds a live chart. Android vitals shows OOM-kill rate rising from 0.2% to 1.9% of sessions after launching "workout recording" to all users, concentrated on 2-3 GB RAM devices, in sessions longer than 40 minutes. Heap dumps show 14M Sample objects retained by a LinkedQueue inside a channel. Code: private val samples = Channel<Sample Channel.UNLIMITED fun onBleNotification s: Sample { samples.trySend s } // 100 Hz x 3 sensors scope.launch Dispatchers.IO { samples.consumeAsFlow .chunked 500 .collect { db.insertAll it } // 1.2 s per batch under contention } chunked here is a custom Flow operator. Red herrings: the chart collector is cheap; GC logs show no leak after sessions end.

title: Channel as a queue (actor-style)
text: Design it, and defend the choice between one global channel, per-conversation channels, and a persistent queue. You own the "outbox" of a chat app 20M MAU . Users send messages offline; the app must deliver in order per conversation, retry with backoff, and never double-send. Today each send does scope.launch { api.send msg } , causing out-of-order delivery under flaky networks roughly 0.8% of chats see reordering and duplicates on retry. A teammate proposes "one Channel for everything with one consumer coroutine". Another proposes a Channel per conversation.

title: Channel internals and obsolete APIs
text: How is Channel implemented under the hood, and which channel-related APIs are obsolete BroadcastChannel , actor , ConflatedBroadcastChannel , receiveOrNull ? What replaced them? Modern Channel is a lock-free, segment-based structure: an conceptually infinite array of cells split into fixed-size linked segments, with atomic counters for send and receive positions. Senders and receivers each take a cell index, then either hand off, buffer, or park a continuation in the cell. That implementation replaced the older linked-list one around kotlinx.coroutines 1.7. BroadcastChannel and ConflatedBroadcastChannel are deprecated in favor of SharedFlow/StateFlow; receiveOrNull is replaced by receiveCatching ; the actor builder is marked obsolete build it with launch + channel .

title: Fan-out vs broadcast
text: What is the bug, why does it split points, and what would you ship? In a ride-hailing app, a LocationRepository exposes val updates: ReceiveChannel<Location produced from GPS. The map screen and the ETA service both do for loc in repo.updates ... . In QA the map "jitters" and the ETA is often stale. Telemetry shows each consumer receives about half of the points map gets 1 Hz out of 2 Hz . class LocationRepository scope: CoroutineScope { val updates: ReceiveChannel<Location = scope.produce capacity = Channel.CONFLATED { gps.requests .collect { send it } } } Red herring: GPS provider interval is stable at 500 ms.

title: select starvation
text: Run the post-incident review: what happened, why was it invisible, and how do you fix and prevent it? Post-incident review: a notification service in an Android foreground process also running on a small gateway multiplexes three channels in one select loop: critical alerts , normal messages , and bulk marketing/analytics uploads . On a promo day the bulk queue grew to 180k items, the oldest 9 hours, while the CPU stayed at 20%. Critical and normal channels were emitting about 40 items/s combined, always ready. Dashboard: "bulk delivery latency p99 = 9 h, no errors". Code: while isActive { select<Unit { critical.onReceive { send it } normal.onReceive { send it } bulk.onReceive { send it } } } Red herring: the sender coroutine send it takes 5 ms 200 items/s max capacity .

title: Callback to coroutine bridging basics
text: You have an SDK with fun fetch id: String, cb: Callback<User . Walk me through how you expose it to coroutine code, and how you decide between a suspend function and a Flow. "First I ask how many times the callback can fire. Exactly once, success or error, means a suspend function built on suspendCancellableCoroutine : I register the callback, resume the continuation in onSuccess , resumeWithException in onError , and cancel the underlying work in invokeOnCancellation . Many times, like location, sensors or listeners, means a Flow built with callbackFlow : trySend from the callback, close error on failure, and awaitClose { unregister } as the last line. If a library already ships an await or asFlow Task, Rx, Guava , I use that instead of hand-rolling."

title: suspendCoroutine vs suspendCancellableCoroutine
text: What is the difference between suspendCoroutine and suspendCancellableCoroutine , and which one should you use by default? " suspendCoroutine gives you a plain Continuation that knows nothing about the coroutine's Job. If the coroutine is cancelled while suspended, nothing happens until the callback eventually resumes it, so a callback that never comes means a coroutine that never ends and a parent scope that cannot finish. suspendCancellableCoroutine gives a CancellableContinuation : cancellation resumes the suspension immediately with CancellationException and lets me run cleanup via invokeOnCancellation . Default to suspendCancellableCoroutine , always, for anything that touches I/O or can take time."

title: invokeOnCancellation
text: What does invokeOnCancellation do, when exactly does it run, and what rules must the handler follow? "It registers a handler on the CancellableContinuation that runs only if the continuation is cancelled, not when it is resumed normally. I use it to cancel the underlying request or unregister the listener. The handler can run on any thread, possibly concurrently with my callback, so it must be fast, non-blocking, thread-safe and must not throw. It is not a suspend context, and only one handler can be installed per continuation."

title: Resuming twice and resume semantics
text: What happens if you call resume twice on a continuation? What about resuming after the coroutine was cancelled, or after resume but before the dispatcher runs the coroutine? "A second resume on a live continuation throws IllegalStateException: Already resumed . A resume on an already cancelled CancellableContinuation is silently ignored. And since 1.4, if I resume and the Job is cancelled before the dispatcher actually runs the coroutine, the suspension point throws CancellationException and the value I passed is dropped, which is the prompt cancellation guarantee. If that value is a resource like a Cursor or Response, I use resume value { cause, value, ctx - value.close } to release it."

title: callbackFlow vs channelFlow vs flow
text: When do you use callbackFlow , channelFlow , and plain flow {} ? Why can't I call emit from a callback inside flow {} ? " flow {} is sequential and context-preserving: emit must be called from the collector's coroutine, so I can't call it from a callback thread; it would throw or violate the flow invariant. channelFlow backs the flow with a channel, giving me a ProducerScope , so multiple child coroutines can send concurrently. callbackFlow is channelFlow specialised for callbacks: same machinery, but it enforces that the block ends with awaitClose so the listener is unregistered. Callbacks use callbackFlow , concurrent producers use channelFlow , everything sequential uses flow {} ."

title: awaitClose and leaks
text: What exactly does awaitClose do inside callbackFlow , what happens if you omit it, and what does the lambda you pass to it do? " awaitClose suspends the producer coroutine until the channel is closed or cancelled, which happens when the collector goes away or I/the callback call close . Its lambda runs afterwards as cleanup: that's where I unregister the listener. Without it the block returns immediately, callbackFlow sees an open channel and throws IllegalStateException , so I find out in testing. The worse variant is a workaround like awaitCancellation or an empty awaitClose {} : no crash, but the listener is never unregistered and keeps firing, leaking the callback and everything it captures."

title: callbackFlow without awaitClose
text: Find the bug, explain why it surfaces at runtime and not compile time, and fix it. Then tell me what the tempting wrong fixes are. A teammate adds a battery-level stream to a diagnostics screen and says "works on my device". QA reports the app crashes on every open of the diagnostics screen, in debug and release R8 builds alike, and Crashlytics shows IllegalStateException on 100% of opens of this screen 1.8% of sessions, 600k DAU . The code: class BatteryRepo private val ctx: Context { fun levels : Flow<Int = callbackFlow { val receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver { override fun onReceive c: Context, i: Intent { val level = i.getIntExtra BatteryManager.EXTRA LEVEL, -1 trySend level } } ctx.registerReceiver receiver, IntentFilter Intent.ACTION BATTERY CHANGED } } // ViewModel val level = repo.levels .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, 0 Stack: java.lang.IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block. at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.CallbackFlowBuilder.collectTo .

title: Task.await (play-services)
text: How do you consume a Google Play services / Firebase Task<T from a coroutine? What does await do on success, failure and cancellation, and what does it not do? "I add kotlinx-coroutines-play-services and call task.await . It suspends, returns the result on success, throws the task's exception on failure, and throws CancellationException if the Task itself was cancelled. If the calling coroutine is cancelled, await stops waiting and throws, but a plain Task has no cancel API, so the underlying work keeps running unless I passed the SDK a CancellationToken . For SDK calls that accept a CancellationTokenSource , I use the overload that wires coroutine cancellation to it."

title: ListenableFuture and CompletableFuture await
text: How do you bridge ListenableFuture CameraX, Media3, WorkManager and CompletableFuture into coroutines? What happens to the future when the coroutine is cancelled, and in the other direction? "For ListenableFuture I use await from kotlinx-coroutines-guava or from androidx.concurrent:concurrent-futures-ktx . For CompletableFuture / CompletionStage I use kotlinx.coroutines.future.await . Both are cancellable and one-shot. If my coroutine is cancelled, the future is cancelled too, so the producer can stop; if the future is cancelled, await throws CancellationException . Futures are one-shot, so no Flow here. I never call future.get on the main thread because that blocks."

title: Wrapping location updates
text: Review this wrapper. What do you change and why, and what stays the same? A ride-sharing app 1.5M DAU, mix of Android 8-14, many low-end devices streams driver location. A teammate's wrapper: fun FusedLocationProviderClient.updates req: LocationRequest : Flow<Location = callbackFlow { val cb = object : LocationCallback { override fun onLocationResult r: LocationResult { r.lastLocation?.let { trySend it } } } requestLocationUpdates req, cb, Looper.getMainLooper awaitClose { removeLocationUpdates cb } } Crashlytics shows SecurityException crashes on 0.6% of sessions after Android 11 users revoke "precise" permission mid-session, p95 main-thread frame time rises 12% on the tracking screen, and the system status bar GPS indicator sometimes stays on a few seconds after leaving. Product also wants "offline GPS off" to surface as a UI message.

title: Wrapping Firebase listeners and sensors
text: Firebase Realtime/Firestore listeners and SensorManager both use "register, receive many, unregister". How do you wrap them as Flows? What differs between them, and what do you watch out for? "Both use callbackFlow with awaitClose doing the unregister. Firestore's addSnapshotListener returns a ListenerRegistration and delivers an error through the same callback, so I map errors to close e and values to trySend . Sensors deliver at high frequency with no error channel, so the main decisions are sampling rate, which thread pass a Handler , and buffer policy, usually conflate . If the Firebase SDK already ships a snapshots / dataObjects Kotlin extension, I use that instead of my own."

title: Listener registered twice
text: Find why the number of deliveries grows with each background/foreground cycle, prove it, and fix it. Then say what else could cause duplicates even after the fix. An order-tracking screen in a delivery app shows events from a socket-like SDK. After the team added repeatOnLifecycle STARTED collection, support reports "each status update plays the notification sound 2, 3, then 5 times" the longer a session goes on. The analytics team sees order status received events per user growing with the number of times the user backgrounded and returned average 4.1 events per real update, 480k DAU . class TrackingRepo private val sdk: TrackingSdk { // app-scoped singleton private val bus = MutableSharedFlow<OrderEvent extraBufferCapacity = 64 val events: Flow<OrderEvent = bus.asSharedFlow // keeps the SDK subscription alive while collected fun subscribe orderId: String : Flow<Unit = callbackFlow { val l = TrackingListener { e - bus.tryEmit e } sdk.addListener orderId, l awaitClose { sdk.removeListener orderId, TrackingListener { e - bus.tryEmit e } } } } // Fragment viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle Lifecycle.State.STARTED { launch { vm.subscribe orderId .collect } launch { vm.events.collect { sound.play ; render it } } } } Red herrings: the team suspects repeatOnLifecycle "collecting twice", and a recent SDK upgrade.

title: How Retrofit supports suspend
text: How does Retrofit make suspend fun getUser : User work? What happens under the hood when it is called and when the calling coroutine is cancelled? "Since Retrofit 2.6.0 a suspend interface method compiles to a method with a trailing Continuation parameter and an Object return type. Retrofit detects that parameter, creates a Call<T for the real response type, and calls an internal Call<T .await extension that uses suspendCancellableCoroutine with enqueue . onResponse resumes with the body or an HttpException , onFailure resumes with the throwable, and invokeOnCancellation { cancel } cancels the OkHttp call. The request runs on OkHttp's dispatcher threads, which makes Retrofit suspend functions main-safe."

title: RxJava bridges (kotlinx-coroutines-rx3)
text: You are incrementally moving from RxJava 3 to coroutines. What does kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 give you, and what behaviours cancellation, backpressure, nulls, error handling must you reason about at each boundary? "The artifact has two directions. Rx to coroutines: Single/Maybe/Completable.await , Observable.awaitFirst/awaitLast/awaitSingle , and ObservableSource/Publisher.asFlow . Coroutines to Rx: rxSingle {} , rxMaybe {} , rxCompletable {} , rxObservable {} , rxFlowable {} , Flow.asObservable / asFlowable . At every boundary I check: cancellation disposing the Rx subscription when the coroutine is cancelled, and cancelling the coroutine when the Rx subscriber disposes , backpressure hot Observables have none, so the bridge must buffer , nulls Rx3 forbids null , and errors Rx onError becomes thrown exceptions from await /Flow, undeliverable errors go to RxJavaPlugins ."

title: Resuming twice
text: Diagnose and fix this, and tell me what the contract changes should be so it cannot recur. A fintech app 900k DAU wraps a third-party identity-verification SDK for the KYC flow. After release 7.12, Crashlytics shows a new top crash: 0.35% of sessions, 100% on the KYC screen, from the SDK's own callback thread: Fatal Exception: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Already resumed at kotlin.coroutines.SafeContinuation.resumeWith SafeContinuation.kt:... at com.app.kyc.SdkBridgeKt$verify$2$1.onFailure SdkBridge.kt:41 at com.vendor.idv.Session.dispatchResult Session.java:... Thread: vendor-callback-3 The bridge: suspend fun IdvSdk.verify doc: Doc : Verdict = suspendCoroutine { cont - start doc, object : IdvCallback { override fun onSuccess v: Verdict = cont.resume v override fun onFailure e: IdvError = cont.resumeWithException e.toException } } Release notes of 7.12 list: SDK upgrade 4.1 to 4.3, a new 20-second timeout in the ViewModel withTimeout 20 000 , and a retry button. Red herrings: the team suspects a coroutines upgrade and a threading bug in the ViewModel.

title: Callback threading and buffer policy
text: A callback fires on an arbitrary SDK thread, at an unpredictable rate. Inside callbackFlow , how do you choose between send , trySend and trySendBlocking , and how do you choose the buffer? What can you lose, and what can you break? "Callbacks are plain functions on someone else's thread, so I can't use suspending send . trySend never blocks and never throws; it returns a ChannelResult that I may check. With the default BUFFERED capacity 64, suspend on overflow a slow collector makes trySend fail once full, so events are dropped silently unless I look at the result. So the buffer policy is the real decision: conflate when only the latest matters location, battery , buffer UNLIMITED only when every event matters and rate is bounded, DROP OLDEST / DROP LATEST with a size when I want a window. trySendBlocking blocks the SDK's thread until there is room, so I only use it when that thread is mine and a stall is acceptable; never on Main or a sensor thread."

title: Non-cancellable bridge leak
text: The job?.cancel is there, so why is old work still happening? Diagnose, fix, and prove the improvement. A news app 2M DAU has a feed that does Call.await through a custom OkHttp extension for non-Retrofit endpoints. After a redesign with fast swipe-through of categories, data usage per session rose 38%, server QPS from this client is 2.2x higher than product expected, and the p95 of the feed endpoint is 2.4 s on slow networks. Also viewModelScope children survive after leaving the screen, LeakCanary reports FeedFragment retained for up to 30 s the OkHttp read timeout . suspend fun Call.await : Response = suspendCoroutine { cont - enqueue object : Callback { override fun onResponse call: Call, response: Response = cont.resume response override fun onFailure call: Call, e: IOException = cont.resumeWithException e } } fun load category: String { job?.cancel job = viewModelScope.launch { val body = client.newCall req category .await .body!!.string state.value = parse body } } Red herrings: "the server is slow", "swipes cause duplicate triggers from the UI".

title: Error mapping in bridges
text: In a bridge, how should errors flow? Compare close cause , cancel CancellationException ... , resumeWithException , and exceptions thrown from inside callbacks or from the registration call. "For one-shot bridges: resumeWithException for failures; the caller sees the real exception. For callbackFlow : close cause terminates the flow with that exception, which the collector or catch sees as a normal failure. cancel CancellationException ... is cancellation, not failure: it ends the producer and downstream sees a CancellationException , which in many structures just silently stops the collector's coroutine, so I avoid it for real errors even though the official example uses it. I never throw from inside an SDK callback, because the exception lands on the SDK's thread and can kill the process. And if the registration call itself throws, I let it propagate as a flow exception or close e so the collector can handle it."

title: Wrapping a stateful callback SDK
text: Design the coroutine-based wrapper. How do you model each operation, handle cancellation and timeouts so the device is never left in a bad state, and enforce one-operation-at-a-time? A health-device app 350k MAU, BLE glucose meters uses a vendor SDK with this callback API: connect device, ConnectionCb , readHistory range, ResultCb , startLiveStream StreamCb , disconnect . Rules from the vendor docs: only one operation at a time per device, connect can take up to 45 s, disconnect must be called after any aborted operation or the next connect fails with BUSY , and StreamCb.onReading fires up to 10 times per second until stopLiveStream . Today the app uses nested callbacks in the ViewModel; users report "stuck on connecting" and rare BUSY errors after leaving the screen mid-sync about 4% of syncs . Product wants a 20 s cap on connect with a retry, cancel-on-leave, and a live graph.

title: Single-listener API
text: What is wrong with the straightforward approach, what questions do you ask about the unclear requirement, and how do you design it? The team must expose a legacy in-house NetworkMonitor as a Flow. Its API: setListener l: Listener? . Only one listener at a time: setting a new one silently replaces the old, setListener null clears it. Three features want connectivity: the offline banner lives while the app is foreground , the upload queue lives while uploads are pending, may overlap the banner , and analytics lives always . The product spec says only "expose connectivity as a Flow so any feature can observe it". After a first attempt with a callbackFlow per consumer, QA reports "the banner stops updating after an upload starts" and "analytics goes silent after visiting settings" reproducible 100% .

title: What Flow is
text: What is a Kotlin Flow , and how is it different from a suspend fun that returns a List ? A Flow is a cold, asynchronous stream: it can emit many values over time, and each emission can suspend. Nothing runs until someone calls a terminal operator like collect . A suspend fun returning List gives me one value, all at once, after everything has finished. With Flow the consumer can process item 1 while the producer is still working on item 2, and the stream can be unbounded.

title: Builders
text: What are the ways to create a Flow flow {} , flowOf , asFlow , emptyFlow , and when do you use each? flow { emit x } is the general builder for anything that needs suspend calls or loops. flowOf a, b, c is a fixed set of values, good for tests and defaults. asFlow converts an existing collection, range, sequence, or a suspend - T lambda. emptyFlow is a flow with no values. For callback APIs I use callbackFlow , which is a different chunk's topic.

title: Terminal operators
text: What are terminal operators in Flow? Name the common ones and say what each does and what it throws on an empty flow. Terminal operators are suspend functions that start collection and produce a result or just consume. collect runs a lambda per value, toList/toSet gather everything, first takes the first value and cancels the upstream, single requires exactly one, fold/reduce aggregate, count counts, and launchIn scope collects in a new coroutine and returns a Job . first and single throw NoSuchElementException on an empty flow; use firstOrNull / singleOrNull to avoid that.

title: Cold semantics
text: What does "cold" mean for a Flow? If two collectors collect the same flow {} , what happens, and how is this different from a hot stream? Cold means the producer block is a recipe, not a running process. Every call to collect executes the flow {} lambda from the start, independently, in the collector's coroutine. Two collectors means two executions, two network calls, two independent sequences of values. A hot stream like SharedFlow/StateFlow exists independently of collectors, and collectors just observe values emitted by someone else. To share one execution among collectors, I convert with shareIn or stateIn .

title: Flow vs Sequence vs List
text: When would you return Flow<T , Sequence<T , or suspend fun : List<T ? Why can't you use a Sequence for async data? suspend fun : List<T for a one-shot result that is bounded and small enough to hold in memory. Flow<T for values arriving over time or when I want to start consuming before the producer is done, and when I need cancellation and suspension. Sequence<T for synchronous lazy computation on in-memory or blocking data. A sequence block can only call suspend functions via SequenceScope 's restricted suspension @RestrictsSuspension , so I cannot delay or call a network suspend function in it; if I block inside a sequence I block the thread.

title: Terminal operators / launchIn
text: What is the difference between flow.collect { } , flow.onEach { }.launchIn scope , and scope.launch { flow.collect { } } ? What happens to code after collect ? collect is a suspend call that returns only when the flow completes, so the code after it runs only for finite flows. launchIn and scope.launch { collect } are the same thing: they start a new coroutine that does the collection and return a Job immediately, so my current coroutine continues. For an endless flow Room, StateFlow, DataStore I must collect in its own coroutine if I need to do other things in the same scope.

title: Context preservation
text: Explain Flow's context preservation property. Where does the producer code of flow { } run, and how do you change the dispatcher correctly? A flow must emit in the same coroutine context it is collected in; that is "context preservation". So the flow {} lambda runs in whatever context the collector calls collect from. To move upstream work to another dispatcher I use flowOn Dispatchers.IO , which affects only operators upstream of it. Using withContext around emit violates the invariant and throws IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated .

title: Context preservation
text: Find the bug, explain why it only crashes sometimes, and fix it. A teammate's PR adds disk caching to a repository. QA reports that opening the Feed crashes 100% of the time on debug builds and on release for 8% of users those with a stale cache . Stack excerpt: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated: Flow was collected in StandaloneCoroutine{Active}@3c1a, Dispatchers.Main.immediate , but emission happened in DispatchedCoroutine{Active}@7d2, Dispatchers.IO . Please refer to 'flow' documentation or use 'flowOn' instead at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.internal.SafeCollector commonKt.checkContext at com.app.FeedRepo$feed$1.invokeSuspend FeedRepo.kt:31 Code: fun feed : Flow<List<Post = flow { val cached = withContext Dispatchers.IO { cache.read } if cached != null emit cached withContext Dispatchers.IO { val fresh = api.fetchFeed cache.write fresh emit fresh } } Only the second block emits inside withContext . 92% of users have a fresh cache and the API call is skipped by an early return elsewhere, which is why it was not caught. A red herring in the PR: the team also changed Moshi to codegen.

title: Exception transparency
text: What is exception transparency in Flow, and how does it affect where you put try/catch versus the catch operator? Exception transparency says a flow must not hide exceptions thrown by its downstream the collector or later operators . If emit throws, the producer must let it propagate and stop emitting. Practically: the catch operator catches exceptions from upstream only, never from the collect lambda or operators below it. And I must not wrap emit in a try/catch that swallows the exception, since that breaks the rule and the runtime throws IllegalStateException: Flow exception transparency is violated if I then emit again.

title: Flow internals
text: How is Flow implemented internally? Explain Flow , FlowCollector , AbstractFlow and SafeCollector , and why a library should not implement Flow directly. Flow<T is an interface with one method, suspend fun collect collector: FlowCollector<T . FlowCollector<T is a fun interface with suspend fun emit value: T . The flow {} builder creates a SafeFlow , a subclass of AbstractFlow , whose collect wraps my collector in a SafeCollector that enforces the two contracts at runtime: context preservation and exception transparency. Operators like map are just new Flows whose collect calls the upstream's collect with a wrapping collector. Third parties are discouraged from implementing Flow directly because they would have to uphold those invariants by hand; AbstractFlow or the builders do it for you.

title: Room Flow
text: How does a Room DAO method returning Flow<List<T work? When does it emit, on which thread does it query, and what are its gotchas? The DAO method is cold. On collect, Room runs the query on its query executor off Main, no need for flowOn , emits the result, then registers an invalidation observer on the tables in the query. Any write to any of those tables, even to rows that are not in my result, triggers a re-query and a new emission. It never completes, so I collect it in a long-lived scope. Gotchas: it re-emits equal lists after unrelated writes, so I add distinctUntilChanged ; and first is how I get a one-shot read.

title: DataStore Flow
text: How do you read from Jetpack DataStore with Flow? What does the data flow guarantee, and how should you handle errors? DataStore exposes val data: Flow<Preferences or Flow<T for Proto/typed . It is cold, emits the current persisted value upon collection, then emits again after each successful write, and does not terminate. Reads can throw IOException , so I add .catch { if it is IOException emit emptyPreferences else throw it } . For a one-time read I use data.first . Writes go through edit {} or updateData , which are suspend and transactional.

title: Cold semantics
text: Why is the traffic 3.4x, and how do you fix it without regressing the architecture? A news app has 1.2M DAU. After a release, the backend team reports /v2/home traffic is up 3.4x with no DAU increase, and p95 backend latency rose from 180 ms to 640 ms. App-side, the Home screen shows three widgets Hero, Trending, Stats each in its own Composable/ViewModel collecting repo.homeData . The code: class HomeRepo private val api: HomeApi { fun homeData : Flow<HomeData = flow { emit api.getHome // network call } } // Hero VM val hero = repo.homeData .map { it.hero }.stateIn viewModelScope, Eagerly, null // Trending VM val trending = repo.homeData .map { it.trending }.stateIn viewModelScope, Eagerly, null // Stats VM val stats = repo.homeData .map { it.stats }.stateIn viewModelScope, Eagerly, null Charles Proxy shows 3 identical GETs per Home open. Another 0.4x comes from pull-to-refresh, which re-collects. Crash rate and ANR rate are unchanged. A red herring: the CDN cache hit ratio also dropped, which the infra team suspects as the cause.

title: Cancellation in flows
text: How does cancellation work for a Flow? Is a flow {} with a tight loop cancellable? What does cancellable do and when do you need it? Flow cancellation is the normal coroutine cancellation: cancelling the collector's job cancels the producer, since it runs inside collect . The cooperative check happens at suspension points and, for flow {} , in every emit via SafeCollector . A flow {} that emits is cancellable; a loop that does CPU work without suspending or emitting is not. Flows built by asFlow and flowOf historically did not check cancellation on each element; for these and .asFlow on ranges/sequences I add .cancellable or ensureActive if the downstream is not suspending.

title: Sequential execution & back-pressure
text: A Flow producer emits every 100 ms and the collector takes 300 ms per item. How long do 3 items take, and why? How does back-pressure work in a plain cold Flow, and what changes with buffer ? Without a buffer the producer and collector share one coroutine, so emit does not return until the collector finishes that item. Total time is the sum of everything: 3 x 100 + 300 = 1200 ms. Back-pressure is automatic because the producer is suspended inside emit . With buffer the producer runs in a separate coroutine and puts items in a channel, so the stages overlap: about 100 + 3 x 300 = 1000 ms.

title: Emission rules
text: Why can't you call emit from a different coroutine inside flow { } for example launch { emit x } ? What do you use instead for concurrent producers? emit isn't thread-safe and must be called from the same coroutine that runs the collector. Calling it from a child launch , even with the same dispatcher, throws "Flow invariant is violated" because the emitting coroutine's Job differs from the collector's. For concurrent producers I use channelFlow { launch { send x } } , which is built on a channel, or callbackFlow for callbacks, or combine multiple flows with merge .

title: Cold semantics
text: What is wrong and what are the consequences beyond the mismatched number? A ticketing app shows an order-confirmation number generated locally. Customer support reports 0.7% of users see different numbers on the confirmation screen and in the e-mail receipt about 900 tickets/week .
