Code review for a DetailActivity in a shopping app 12M MAU, crash dashboard shows OOM at 3% of sessions, mostly on 3 GB devices . Heap dump shows 11 instances of DetailActivity alive after a user browsed 11 product pages and went back. Each instance retains about 9 MB view tree plus product images . object ImageBus { var current: Activity? = null val listeners = mutableListOf< Bitmap - Unit } class DetailActivity : AppCompatActivity { private lateinit var binding: ActivityDetailBinding private val sensorManager by lazy { getSystemService SensorManager::class.java } private val sensorListener = object : SensorEventListener { override fun onSensorChanged e: SensorEvent { binding.tilt.rotation = e.values 0 } override fun onAccuracyChanged s: Sensor?, a: Int {} } override fun onCreate b: Bundle? { super.onCreate b binding = ActivityDetailBinding.inflate layoutInflater setContentView binding.root ImageBus.current = this ImageBus.listeners.add { bmp - binding.image.setImageBitmap bmp } sensorManager.registerListener sensorListener, sensorManager.getDefaultSensor Sensor.TYPE ACCELEROMETER , SensorManager.SENSOR DELAY UI Handler Looper.getMainLooper .postDelayed { binding.title.text = "Sale ends" }, 10 60 000L } }

title: Hardware bitmaps
text: What is Bitmap.Config.HARDWARE , what does it save, and what breaks when you use it? From API 26, a hardware bitmap keeps its pixels only in graphics memory GPU-accessible , not in the app's CPU-side memory. That saves the second copy the renderer otherwise makes when it uploads a software bitmap into a GPU texture, so it can roughly halve memory per image and removes upload cost at draw time. The price: the bitmap is immutable and its pixels cannot be read on the CPU, so getPixel , copyPixelsToBuffer , software Canvas drawing, and some libraries Palette, blur, certain transformations fail.

title: OOM kinds
text: "OutOfMemoryError" in Crashlytics can mean very different things. List the distinct kinds of memory-related failure on Android, how to tell them apart from the message, and what each one implies about the fix. There are at least six: 1 Java heap exhaustion "Failed to allocate a N byte allocation ... growth limit" , 2 thread creation failure "pthread create 1040KB stack failed" , 3 native allocation failure abort in native code, SIGABRT or SIGSEGV , 4 oversized draw "trying to draw too large bitmap" , 5 resource exhaustion like file descriptors "Too many open files" , and 6 silent LMK kill with no exception at all. Each has a different message, different telemetry, and a different fix.

title: Low-end devices
text: How do you drive the OOM rate in the new market down without degrading the flagship experience? A video-and-photo sharing app is expanding to a new market. DAU goes from 800k to 8M over 3 months. Device mix in the new market: 62% have 2 GB RAM or less, many on Android 9 to 11 Go-edition-like builds, 32-bit userspace common. Existing numbers: crash-free users 99.4% overall, but in the new market 96.8%. Of crashes there, 58% are OutOfMemoryError . A sample message: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 14745616 byte allocation with 2097152 free bytes and 3MB until OOM, target footprint 134217728, growth limit 134217728 at ImageFilters.applyVignette ImageFilters.kt:41 , called from the "edit photo" screen. The product team wants to "just set largeHeap and ship".

title: Native memory
text: A user's app has a flat Java heap but total memory keeps rising and the OS eventually kills it. How do you determine whether native memory is the cause, and what are the common native-side leaks in an Android app? I compare dumpsys meminfo rows over time: if Native Heap or Graphics grows while Java Heap stays flat, it's native or graphics. Common sources are direct ByteBuffers, bitmap pixels, JNI/NDK code that never frees, unclosed Cursors or media codecs/players, and third-party SDK native libraries. To find the allocation sites I use the native memory profiler heapprofd under Perfetto, via Android Studio's Native Memory Profiler on Android 10+ .

title: ART GC internals
text: How is ART's modern garbage collector designed to keep pauses short, and how has the collector changed across Android releases? What would a senior app engineer need to know about it? ART moved from Dalvik's stop-the-world mark-sweep, to concurrent mark-sweep, to the Concurrent Copying CC collector as default in Android 8.0. CC copies live objects out of fragmented regions while the app runs, using read barriers so threads see consistent references, which keeps pauses tiny and compacts the heap. Android 14 introduced a userfaultfd-based Concurrent Mark-Compact collector on supported kernels, and newer releases continue to add generational behavior. Exact release/default status changes, so I verify against current AOSP and release notes. For app code the takeaways are: allocation rate matters more than pauses, and large objects and native pressure are handled differently.

title: Leak diagnosis
text: Walk me through diagnosis and fix. Why did LeakCanary say clean, and why does it only show up late in the shift? A delivery-rider app 400k riders, shifts last 6 to 8 hours, mostly 3 GB devices with memoryClass 256 . After release 8.4: support reports "app freezes and then restarts after about 45 to 90 minutes", and rating drops from 4.4 to 4.0. Crashlytics: OOM rate from 0.3% to 2.1% of sessions, but sessions shorter than 20 minutes are unaffected. Heap used after "Force GC" in a staging soak: 92 MB at 0 min, 147 MB at 30 min, 202 MB at 60 min, i.e., +1.8 MB/min. The release also added: live map markers per delivery, a retry wrapper around location updates, an RxJava stream for order status, and a debug-only logger that was left enabled by mistake. LeakCanary is only in debug builds and reports no Activity leaks.

title: In-memory image cache sizing
text: Design the cache sizing. What is wrong with the current code, and how do you pick numbers? A photo-feed app 6M DAU uses a hand-rolled LruCache<String, Bitmap fixed at 64 MB. Device spread: 35% have memoryClass 128 or less, 45% have 192 to 256, 20% have 384+. Thumbnails are 400x400 ARGB 8888. OOM is 1.4% of sessions on low devices, while on flagships scrolling re-decodes images constantly cache hit rate 38% because 64 MB is too small for their big grids. The code: val cache = object : LruCache<String, Bitmap 64 1024 1024 { override fun sizeOf key: String, v: Bitmap = 1 // bug: counts entries, not bytes } Product wants one setting that works for everyone.

title: Thread and native exhaustion
text: Run the post-incident review: what happened, why heap telemetry didn't warn you, and what changes. Post-incident review for release 5.7. Within 6 hours of 20% rollout, crash-free users fell from 99.3% to 98.1%. The top new issue 0.9% of sessions : java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread create 1040KB stack failed: Try again at java.lang.Thread.nativeCreate Native Method at java.lang.Thread.start Thread.java:1063 at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.addWorker ThreadPoolExecutor.java:957 at com.example.net.Prefetcher.fetch Prefetcher.kt:58 Devices: 78% are 32-bit-process devices with 2 to 3 GB RAM. The Java heap at crash time is 70 to 110 MB with maxMemory 256 MB. The release added an image prefetcher for the feed. Dashboards for heap OOM were green. fun fetch urls: List<String { urls.forEach { u - Executors.newCachedThreadPool .execute { download u } // new pool per URL } }

title: Low-RAM strategy
text: How do you turn this into a plan? The PM writes: "Our new market uses cheap phones, make the app work well on 1 GB devices." No further details. Current numbers on devices with isLowRamDevice == true about 9% of users : cold start p50 3.4 s vs 1.6 s on others, 7-day retention 8 points lower, crash-free 98.2% vs 99.5%, 40% of sessions end with REASON LOW MEMORY in exit info. Engineering team is 6 people, one quarter.

text: Explain the failure with numbers and redesign it. A finance app's "export transactions" fetches up to 80 MB of JSON about 400k records and stores it for offline search. In production, 1.1% of sessions that use it OOM on devices with memoryClass 256; p95 time for the screen is 14 s. Current code: val body = client.newCall req .execute .body!!.string // 80 MB val list: List<Txn = Gson .fromJson body, object : TypeToken<List<Txn {}.type dao.insertAll list Stack: OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 167772176 byte allocation with 18874368 free bytes and 18MB until OOM in okio.Buffer / String creation.

title: Hardware bitmap rollout
text: How do you migrate safely? To cut graphics+native memory, the team plans to enable hardware bitmaps for all image loads Coil/Glide default flipped in an app with 15M DAU. Test results: median PSS down 18% on image-heavy screens. Concerns from QA: "share as image", the color-accent feature Palette , and the profile photo blur may break. Android 8.0 and 8.1 make up 4% of users. You have a 2-week window and a 5%-10%-50%-100% staged rollout.

title: Zygote
text: What is Zygote, and why can an Android app process start so much faster than launching a fresh JVM-style process? Zygote is a process that init starts at boot. It boots ART, preloads thousands of framework classes, resources and shared libraries, and then waits on a socket. When a new app process is needed, system server asks Zygote to fork itself. The child inherits all that preloaded memory copy-on-write, so I don't pay for runtime startup or class loading of the framework. Only the app-specific specialisation uid, SELinux context, then my APK's code is left to do.

title: system_server services
text: What do ActivityManagerService, ActivityTaskManagerService, WindowManagerService and PackageManagerService each do? Where do they live and how does my app talk to them? They are Java services running inside the system server process. My app reaches them through Binder via Context.getSystemService or hidden managers. PackageManagerService knows what is installed and resolves intents and permissions. ActivityTaskManagerService, split out of ActivityManagerService in Android 10, owns activities, tasks and the back stack. ActivityManagerService now owns processes, services, broadcasts, providers, OOM adjustment and ANR handling. WindowManagerService owns windows, surfaces, insets, input focus and transitions.

title: DEX and multidex
text: What is a DEX file, and what is the 64K method limit? When do I need multidex today? Android runs DEX bytecode, not JVM .class files. D8 converts and merges classes into classes.dex . A single DEX can reference at most 65,536 methods because method IDs are indexed with 16 bits. Past that you get multiple DEX files classes2.dex ... . On minSdk 21 and above ART supports multiple DEX files natively, so I just enable it, no library. Below 21, Dalvik only loads the main DEX and I need the androidx.multidex library.

title: APK vs AAB
text: What is the difference between an APK and an Android App Bundle? What actually gets installed on a user's phone from the Play Store? An APK is the installable file. An AAB is a publishing format that Play cannot install directly. Play takes my AAB and generates split APKs per device: a base APK plus config splits for ABI, screen density and language, and any dynamic feature modules. The user installs only what their device needs, signed with the Play app signing key. So the artifact I test locally may not be byte-identical to what ships.

title: App process spawn path
text: Walk me through everything that happens, from the user tapping my app's icon to Activity.onCreate , for a cold start. Which parts run in which process? The launcher calls startActivity , which is a Binder call into ATMS in system server. ATMS sees no process for my package, so AMS asks Zygote over its socket to fork one. The child specialises uid, SELinux , runs ActivityThread.main , creates the main Looper and calls back to AMS with attachApplication . AMS replies with bindApplication , which loads my APK, creates the Application , installs ContentProviders, runs Application.onCreate . Then ATMS schedules the launch transaction and Activity.onCreate runs, followed by first frame.

title: ART execution modes
text: How does ART execute my code? Explain interpreter, JIT, AOT and profile-guided compilation, and how that changed from Dalvik to now. Dalvik pre-5.0 interpreted and later had a JIT. Android 5 switched to ART with full AOT compilation at install, which made installs slow and big. Android 7 moved to a hybrid: start interpreting, JIT hot code while running, record what was hot in a profile, then compile only that profile ahead-of-time while the device is idle and charging. Since then, profiles can also come from outside the device, from Play cloud profiles and from Baseline Profiles I ship, so new installs start with the hot paths already compiled.

title: Install-time dexopt, compile filters and profiles
text: What happens to my APK's DEX at install time? What are compile filters, and where do Baseline Profiles and Play cloud profiles come in? When the package is installed, PackageManager runs dex2oat with a compile filter. Plain installs usually only verify the DEX verify , leaving code to be interpreted and JIT'd. If the install includes a profile, such as my Baseline Profile or a Play cloud profile, the installer can compile the listed methods ahead of time with speed-profile . Later, the idle/charging bg-dexopt job refines it from the device's own usage profile.

title: Classloading
text: How does class loading work on Android? What is PathClassLoader , how does it find a class across multiple DEX files, and what goes wrong with duplicate classes? My app's code is loaded by a PathClassLoader a BaseDexClassLoader whose parent is the boot class loader. It holds a DexPathList with an ordered array of dex elements. A lookup asks the parent first, then walks classes.dex , classes2.dex , ... in order and returns the first match. So if two libraries bundle the same class, whichever dex comes first wins, silently. Classes are loaded lazily on first use, then verified and initialised.

title: Hidden API restrictions
text: What are hidden API restrictions? How do they affect reflection and direct linking, and how do I find out if my app or a library is affected? Since Android 9 API 28 the platform limits access to non-SDK interfaces: methods and fields that exist in the framework but are not in the public SDK. They are sorted into lists: SDK allowed , unsupported conditionally allowed , and blocked. Restrictions apply through reflection, JNI and direct linking, to all apps regardless of targetSdk, though the "unsupported" lists graduate to blocked with each release depending on targetSdk. Violations throw NoSuchMethodException / NoSuchFieldException or print warnings. I check with StrictMode.detectNonSdkApiUsage and the veridex tool.

title: Multidex
text: Diagnose the crash, fix it for the old cohort, and tell me why CI did not catch it. Your app supports minSdk 19 for a regional market 6% of 2.1M DAU, mostly low-end devices . A dependency bump pushes method references from 63,800 to 69,200. CI builds fine, because the debug variant uses minSdk 24 via a dev flavour. Release crash rate for the Android 4.4 cohort jumps from 0.3% to 11% right after rollout. Crashlytics shows: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Failed resolution of: Lcom/foo/di/AppGraph; at com.foo.App.onCreate App.java:41 Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: Didn't find class "com.foo.di.AppGraph" on path: DexPathList zip file "/data/app/com.foo-1.apk" ,nativeLibraryDirectories= /system/lib class App : Application { override fun onCreate { // MultiDex.install is NOT called anywhere super.onCreate AppGraph.init this // lives in classes2.dex after the bump } } multiDexEnabled = true is set in defaultConfig .

The app code uses java.time only inside a third-party analytics SDK AAR your code does not call it . Within hours: crash-free sessions drop from 99.6% to 96.8% on Android 7.x devices, which are 14% of users. The SDK's release notes say "supports API 21+ with library desugaring".

title: ART profiles and first launch
text: Explain what is happening and what you would change. Your e-commerce app 8M installs, 70% Play, 30% sideloaded via enterprise MDM and OEM preload has a cold start p50 of 1.1 s on a mid-range device on day 7, but p50 of 2.3 s and p95 of 4.8 s for users in their first launch after install. Day-1 retention is 8 points lower for the sideloaded group. After you enabled Baseline Profiles through the Gradle plugin last month, Play installs improved but sideloaded numbers did not. adb shell dumpsys package com.foo.app shows status=verify reason=install on a freshly installed sideloaded device. Product wants a plan within a week without raising the APK size.

title: Hidden API reflection
text: Walk me through diagnosis and fix. How do you prevent repeats? After targeting API 34 and the new OS release rolling out, a "smart keyboard-aware chat" feature crashes for 2.4% of sessions all on the latest OS version, which is 9% of your 3M DAU . Crashlytics: java.lang.NoSuchFieldException: No field mShowing in class Landroid/widget/PopupWindow; declaration of 'android.widget.PopupWindow' appears in /system/framework/framework.jar at java.lang.Class.getDeclaredField Native Method at com.foo.ui.KeyboardHelper.<init KeyboardHelper.java:31 The helper was copied from a Stack Overflow answer five years ago. QA tested on Android 12 and 13 only. Logcat on older versions shows Accessing hidden field Landroid/widget/PopupWindow;- mShowing:Z unsupported, reflection, allowed .

title: APK signing and install verification
text: How does Android verify an APK at install and update time? Explain signature schemes v1-v4, key rotation, and where Play App Signing fits. At install PackageManager verifies the APK's signature, checks it against any existing install of the same package updates must be signed by the same certificate or a rotation lineage , and refuses on mismatch. Schemes evolved: v1 signs individual zip entries JAR signing , v2 Android 7.0 signs the whole APK file so tampering is detected quickly, v3 Android 9 adds key rotation, v3.1 Android 13 improves rotation targeting, and v4 Android 11 is a separate Merkle-tree signature enabling incremental install. With Play App Signing, I sign my upload with an upload key and Play re-signs with the app signing key it holds.

title: USAP pool and app zygote
text: Beyond the basic Zygote fork, what are USAPs and app zygotes? What problem does each solve, and what are the trade-offs? The USAP pool Android 10+ keeps a few pre-forked, unspecialised app processes ready, so a launch skips the fork and early setup and only pays for specialisation uid, SELinux, ABI . The app zygote Android 10+ is a per-app child zygote I can opt into for isolated services, preloading my own classes/data once so every isolated process forks from it. USAP trades idle memory for faster starts; app zygote trades complexity for faster, safer isolated processes.

title: system_server watchdog and failure modes
text: What is the system server Watchdog, and what happens to my app when system server hangs or crashes? How would I recognise this from an app developer's seat? system server is one process hosting many services, so a deadlock in one lock can freeze others. The Watchdog thread periodically checks monitor locks and handler threads; if a check does not complete in about a minute, it dumps stacks and kills system server. Because Zygote is tied to it, the Java framework restarts, a "soft reboot", and every app process dies. From the app side I see all my processes disappear, Process: system server watchdog logs, or Binder calls into the system blocking.

title: R8 full mode
text: What changed, how do you stabilise the rollout, and how do you prevent a repeat? Your app 5M DAU upgrades AGP from 7.4 to 8.2 for a security requirement. The release candidate passes all instrumented tests which run on the debug variant . In the 10% staged rollout, crash-free sessions drop from 99.7% to 97.1%. New top crashes: java.lang.NoSuchMethodException: com.foo.model.Profile.<init at java.lang.Class.getConstructor0 Class.java:2332 at com.google.gson.internal.ConstructorConstructor... and, on one screen, Gson-parsed objects have null for non-null Kotlin fields, then NPE. Retrofit calls with suspend functions fail with ClassCastException: Class cannot be cast to ParameterizedType . The proguard-rules.pro was written four years ago and has -keep class com.foo.model. { ; } for only some packages. android.enableR8.fullMode is not set in gradle.properties .

title: ABIs and native libraries
text: Explain the failure, how Android picks a native ABI, and how to fix it. A new "document scanner" feature loads a native library from a vendor AAR. QA's emulator and several devices pass. In production, crash rate for the feature is 0% on most devices but 100% for the feature on about 1.4% of daily users about 70k sessions , all on devices reported as arm64 new mid-range phones . Crash: java.lang.UnsatisfiedLinkError: dlopen failed: library "libscannercore.so" not found at java.lang.Runtime.loadLibrary0 Runtime.java:1087 at com.vendor.scanner.Native.<clinit Native.java:12 The APK contents: lib/arm64-v8a/libfoo image.so our own library lib/armeabi-v7a/libfoo image.so lib/armeabi-v7a/libscannercore.so vendor ndk { abiFilters += listOf "arm64-v8a", "armeabi-v7a" } is set. The vendor says "armeabi-v7a runs on arm64 devices."
