Since JDK 12 a default archive for JDK classes ships and is on by default; AppCDS adds your application classes. JDK 24's AOT cache JEP 483 goes further by caching classes in loaded and linked state. They cut startup, not peak performance.

title: Deoptimization
text: What is deoptimization in HotSpot? Give examples of what triggers it, and how would you detect it hurting a production service? C2 compiles using assumptions from profiles, for example "this branch is never taken" or "this call site only sees one class". When an assumption fails, the code hits an uncommon trap, execution falls back to the interpreter at that point, the compiled method is marked "not entrant", and the method gets recompiled later. A few are normal; repeated cycles mean a deopt storm with latency spikes.

title: TLAB allocation
text: Why is object allocation on the JVM so cheap, and what is a TLAB? When does allocation leave the fast path? Each thread gets a Thread-Local Allocation Buffer, a private chunk of eden. Allocating an object is "bump the pointer, check against the end": a handful of instructions with no locking. When the TLAB is full the thread gets a new one a synchronised, slower step ; very large objects bypass the TLAB and allocate directly in the heap, which is slower and for G1 may mean humongous allocation. The cost that remains is not the allocation but the GC work that high allocation rate causes.

title: Code cache
text: What is the JVM code cache? What happens when it fills up, and how do you monitor and size it? The code cache is the native memory region where the JVM stores generated machine code: interpreter stubs and JIT-compiled methods. With tiered compilation its reserved size is 240 MB by default. If it fills, the JVM logs "CodeCache is full. Compiler has been disabled", stops JIT compiling, and the service degrades to running whatever is already compiled plus the interpreter, with no exception.

title: Class generation and Metaspace
text: What is wrong, how do you prove it, and how do you fix it? A pricing service Java 17, G1, 4 GiB heap, 6 GiB pod evaluates tenant-defined discount rules written in Groovy. Every 3 weeks it OOMs; this time it started restarting daily after a marketing campaign raised traffic from 50 to 400 RPS. jstat -gc shows heap OK old gen 35% but MU Metaspace used climbs about 120 MB/hour; jvm classes loaded classes rises from 40k to 600k over 8 hours. Log at death: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace . Code: public double price Order o, String ruleSource { GroovyShell shell = new GroovyShell ; // new GroovyClassLoader inside Script s = shell.parse ruleSource ; // compiles source into a new class every call Binding b = new Binding ; b.setVariable "order", o ; s.setBinding b ; return Number s.run .doubleValue ; } Nobody sets -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize .

title: JVM in containers
text: Explain the behaviour and propose a better configuration. A platform team cuts cost by moving 120 Java 17 microservice pods from 4 CPU / 8 GiB to limits: cpu 1500m, memory 1536Mi requests equal , JVM flags unchanged: just -XX:+UseContainerSupport defaults, no -Xmx . After rollout, services show p99 from 80 ms to 600 ms, with 300-400 ms stalls every few seconds. container cpu cfs throttled periods total is climbing. GC log first line: Using Serial . Heap is auto-sized to about 384 MiB and the old gen fills quickly. JVM startup log: Runtime.availableProcessors = 2 . A team lead suggests adding -XX:+UseG1GC and moving on.

title: GraalVM native image
text: Would you convert A, B, both or neither, and how do you decide? A company runs two Spring Boot 3 / Java 21 services: A a nightly-triggered report generator on AWS Lambda-style infrastructure with a 700 ms cold-start budget, currently 6.5 s; B a 24/7 pricing API at 3,000 RPS per instance with p99 = 25 ms, 4 vCPU, 4 GiB RSS. Management read that native image gives "10x faster startup and lower memory" and asks to convert both. Build time budget on CI is 10 minutes; reflection-heavy libraries Jackson with dynamic types, Hibernate, a plugin SPI loaded by classpath scanning are used in both.

title: Memory budgeting
text: How would you decide the new memory configuration, and what do you do before changing 200 pods? Platform FinOps wants to halve memory for 200 pods of a Java 21 gateway service from 8 GiB to 4 GiB. Today: -Xmx5g , G1, 8 GiB limit. Steady-state: heap used after GC about 1.1 GB, peak committed heap 3.2 GB; container memory working set bytes about 6.0 GiB; request rate 1,200 RPS; 350 platform threads; Netty direct buffers hover at 600 MB; Metaspace 180 MB; code cache 70 MB. Product wants no p99 regression today 45 ms and no new restarts.

title: Generational hypothesis
text: What is the generational hypothesis, and why do most JVM garbage collectors split the heap into young and old generations? "The weak generational hypothesis says most objects die young and few young objects are referenced by old ones. So I collect the small young region often and cheaply, copying the few survivors out, and touch the big old region rarely. GC cost is proportional to live data, not garbage, so scanning a mostly-dead young region is a huge win."

title: Collector overview
text: Name the HotSpot garbage collectors and when you would pick each. Which one is the default, and does that depend on the Java version or the machine? "Serial is single-threaded for tiny heaps and containers with one CPU. Parallel maximizes throughput with stop-the-world multi-threaded collections. G1 is the default since Java 9 on server-class machines and balances pause and throughput by region. ZGC and Shenandoah are low-pause concurrent collectors for latency-sensitive or large heaps. Java 8 defaulted to Parallel. And if the JVM sees fewer than 2 CPUs or too little memory, it falls back to Serial even on Java 17 or 21."

title: Young collection
text: Walk me through what happens during a young minor GC. What are Eden, survivor spaces and tenuring? "Threads allocate into Eden via TLABs. When Eden is full, the JVM stops the world, finds live objects from roots plus the remembered set of old-to-young pointers, and copies them to a survivor space or promotes them to old if old enough. Eden and the other survivor are then empty. Survivors age by one each cycle until the tenuring threshold."

title: Reading GC logs
text: Read this G1 log and tell me what happened. How do you enable GC logging in modern Java? 12.401s info gc GC 41 Pause Young Normal G1 Evacuation Pause 3584M- 412M 8192M 22.318ms 98.220s info gc GC 97 Pause Young Concurrent Start G1 Humongous Allocation 5100M- 3900M 8192M 31.002ms 98.231s info gc GC 98 Concurrent Mark Cycle 103.870s info gc GC 98 Pause Remark 4300M- 3800M 8192M 18.4ms 104.600s info gc GC 99 Pause Young Mixed G1 Evacuation Pause 4100M- 3000M 8192M 61.7ms "Format is before- after committed then pause. Line 1 is a routine young GC: 3.5 GB to 412 MB in 22 ms. Line 2 is a young GC that also started concurrent marking, triggered by a humongous allocation, with heap at about 62% of capacity. Then Remark ends marking, and the Mixed GC starts reclaiming old regions at 62 ms. Logging is unified -Xlog since Java 9."

title: G1 regions
text: Explain how G1 organizes the heap and what the collection set is. Why is it called "Garbage First"? "G1 splits the heap into equal regions, 1 to 32 MB, each dynamically assigned a role: Eden, Survivor, Old or Humongous. A collection picks a set of regions, the collection set, that it can evacuate within the pause target. 'Garbage first' means that for old regions it prefers the ones with the most reclaimable space, because they give the most free memory per unit of copying work."

title: G1 mixed collections and IHOP
text: How does G1 decide when to start concurrent marking and how does it reclaim old regions? What is IHOP and what goes wrong if marking starts too late? "G1 starts concurrent marking when old-gen occupancy crosses the Initiating Heap Occupancy Percent, which is 45% initially and adaptive by default. After marking and cleanup, it runs several mixed GCs that add the most garbage-heavy old regions to each young collection. If the old gen fills before marking and mixed GCs finish, G1 hits to-space exhaustion or a full GC."

title: Humongous objects
text: What is a humongous object in G1, why is it a problem, and how do you find and fix it? "A humongous object is one at least half a region. G1 allocates it directly into contiguous old-type regions, bypassing Eden. It wastes the unused tail of its last region, can fragment the heap, triggers concurrent cycles early, and historically was only freed by marking or eager reclaim. I find them with GC logs and JFR allocation events, then fix by streaming, chunking, or raising region size."

title: G1 flags
text: Review these flags. What is wrong, what would you change, and what would you keep? A payments API Java 17, 8 CPU / 16 GB container, 4 GB heap wanted was migrated from Java 8 Parallel GC. The team carried over its flags. After rollout, p99 rose from 120 ms to 480 ms, and GC logs show a Young pause every 300 ms and occasional Pause Full . JAVA OPTS="-XX:+UseG1GC -Xms512m -Xmx4g -Xmn3g -XX:SurvivorRatio=6 \ -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=5 -XX:ParallelGCThreads=2 \ -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC -XX:+DisableExplicitGC"

title: Parallel vs G1 trade-off
text: When would you pick Parallel GC over G1 and what exactly are you trading? What does MaxGCPauseMillis actually do? "Parallel does multi-threaded stop-the-world young and full collections with the simplest barriers and no concurrent work, so it gets the best raw throughput and lowest overhead, but pauses scale with heap and live data. G1 pays barrier cost, remembered-set memory and concurrent threads to bound pauses. I pick Parallel for batch/offline jobs where total time matters, G1 when requests wait on pauses. MaxGCPauseMillis is a soft goal that G1 uses to size young and pick the collection set, not a limit."

title: Heap sizing
text: How do you size the heap and the young generation for a service? Why do people set -Xms equal to -Xmx , and what does that cost? "I start from the measured live set after full-cycle GC, then give roughly 2-3x that as heap so the collector has room, and make Xms equal Xmx to avoid resize pauses and surprises. In G1/ZGC I leave young sizing to the collector. The cost is committed memory from the start, which matters in containers, so I also leave non-heap headroom."

title: Evacuation failure
text: What is happening and what do you do? Order service on Java 17, G1, 6 GB heap, 2000 RPS. After a feature launch that caches order history for 24 h, alerts fire: p99 jumped from 90 ms to 2.5 s every 20 minutes. Logs: 6221.4s info gc GC 512 Pause Young Mixed G1 Evacuation Pause 5400M- 5200M 6144M 310.4ms 6221.7s info gc,heap To-space exhausted 6224.9s info gc GC 513 Pause Full G1 Compaction Pause 5900M- 4800M 6144M 2480ms Heap after Full GC stays at 4.8 GB. Prior to launch, post-GC heap was 1.9 GB.

title: GC barriers and remembered sets
text: What is a write barrier and a card table? How do barriers differ between Parallel, G1, and ZGC? "A barrier is a small piece of code the JIT inserts around reference reads or writes so the collector can track what the application changes. Parallel marks a card on reference writes so young GC knows which old regions to scan. G1 adds an SATB pre-write barrier for concurrent marking and a post-write barrier feeding remembered sets. ZGC uses load barriers, checking pointer metadata on every reference load so it can fix pointers lazily during concurrent relocation."

title: ZGC design
text: How does ZGC achieve sub-millisecond-class pauses regardless of heap size? What stays stop-the-world and what is the cost? "ZGC does marking, relocation and reference processing concurrently. Its STW pauses are only brief root-scanning and phase-transition handshakes, whose duration doesn't scale with heap or live set. It relies on load barriers and pointer metadata so threads can see and heal relocated objects while the app runs. The price is barrier overhead, CPU spent by concurrent GC threads, no compressed oops, and the need for headroom or you get allocation stalls."

title: Generational ZGC and versions
text: What did Generational ZGC change, and which Java version do you use which flag on? Should I just enable it? "Non-generational ZGC collected the whole heap every cycle, so it burned CPU re-marking long-lived data and needed lots of headroom. Generational ZGC JEP 439, JDK 21, opt-in with -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational adds young and old generations so most work targets young objects. In JDK 23 it became the default under -XX:+UseZGC JEP 474 and JDK 24 removed the non-generational mode JEP 490 ."

title: Shenandoah
text: How does Shenandoah get low pauses, and how does it differ from ZGC? Where is it available? "Shenandoah is a region-based collector that evacuates concurrently, so pauses don't scale with heap. It uses a load-reference barrier to find the current copy of an object during concurrent copying. It is not in Oracle builds but ships in Red Hat, Corretto, Zulu and others. Default mode is single-generation SATB; a generational mode became a product feature in JDK 25."

title: Choosing a collector
text: Recommend a collector and key flags for each, with reasoning and the measurements you want before committing. You own three JVM workloads on Java 21 in Kubernetes all on 4-8 vCPU nodes : A Public REST API, 4 GB heap, 1500 RPS, SLO p99 < 200 ms, allocation 250 MB/s, live set 1 GB. B Nightly Spark-like batch in plain Java, 24 GB heap, runs 3 hours, SLO is finishing before 6 am. C Real-time bidding service, 16 GB heap, p99 < 15 ms, allocation 1.5 GB/s, live set 5 GB. Each team asks "which GC?"

title: ZGC allocation stalls
text: Diagnose and fix. Pricing service, Java 21, -XX:+UseZGC not generational , 10 GB heap in a 12 GB pod, 6 vCPU. Black Friday traffic doubles to 4000 RPS. p99 jumps from 25 ms to 400 ms though GC pauses in logs are all < 1 ms. Excerpt: 3402.1s info gc GC 881 Garbage Collection Allocation Rate 9100M 89% - 8900M 87% 3402.4s info gc Allocation Stall http-nio-8080-exec-17 87.3ms 3402.4s info gc Allocation Stall http-nio-8080-exec-3 91.0ms CPU is 95%, live set 6.5 GB. A colleague says "ZGC pauses are sub-ms, so GC is not the problem."

title: Allocation rate vs live set
text: Explain the relationship between allocation rate, live set, heap size, GC frequency and GC pause. How would you reason about a change in each? "Frequency of young GC is allocation rate divided by Eden size. Pause duration is driven by live data surviving that cycle plus root and remembered-set work, not by garbage or total heap. For old collections, cost scales with the live set. So more heap lowers frequency, more live data raises per-collection cost and reduces headroom, and a higher allocation rate raises frequency and promotion pressure."

title: G1 Full GC loop
text: Why are Full GCs repeating, and what do you do now and next? Event-processing service, Java 11, G1, 30 GB heap -Xms30g -Xmx30g , 16 vCPU. Each night p99 spikes. GC log excerpt: 1520.1s info gc GC 204 Pause Young Concurrent Start G1 Evacuation Pause 27800M- 26900M 30720M 140ms 1520.2s info gc GC 205 Concurrent Cycle 1535.9s info gc GC 206 Pause Full Allocation Failure 30200M- 25100M 30720M 31400ms 1567.5s info gc GC 207 Pause Full Allocation Failure 30300M- 25000M 30720M 30900ms Live set after Full GC is 25 GB; steady-state used heap before the nightly job was 9 GB. The job loads a 16 GB reference dataset.

title: Collector migration
text: Describe the migration plan and what could go wrong. Checkout service Java 21, G1, 12 GB heap, 24 pods, 3000 RPS total has p99 = 180 ms and p999 = 900 ms, with G1 pauses of 80-250 ms on bursts. Product wants p999 < 150 ms before a sale in 6 weeks. You propose Generational ZGC. Risk owner asks how you would roll it out without breaking checkout.

title: STW phases in concurrent collectors
text: "ZGC and Shenandoah are pauseless." True? What pauses remain, what else can stop your threads, and what affects their duration? "Not pauseless. They have very short STW phases for root scanning and phase handoffs, plus JVM-wide safepoint operations for other reasons deoptimization, class redefinition, biased-lock-era revocations, thread dumps . Pause duration depends on thread count, root set size, and time-to-safepoint, not heap size. And non-pause stalls allocation stalls, pacing, barrier slow paths can hurt latency without appearing as pauses."

title: Container ergonomics
text: Run the review: root cause, contributing factors, and the guardrails you would add. After moving a Java 17 service from VMs 8 vCPU, 16 GB to Kubernetes with resources.limits: cpu: "1", memory: "2Gi" , latency worsened. Pre-migration G1 pauses were 40 ms; now the first deploy shows p99 up from 110 ms to 700 ms and GC pauses of 300-600 ms every few seconds. No flags were set except -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 . Heap is therefore 1.5 GB. The post-incident review asks why, and what the standard should be.

title: G1 at scale
text: Will Xmx48g meet the p99 target? What do you evaluate and recommend? Search-indexing service on Java 21, G1, -Xmx6g , 200 MB/s allocation, young pauses 35 ms, mixed pauses 90 ms. Business plans 10x data: the in-memory index grows from 2 GB to 20 GB live, allocation rate to 800 MB/s, on a 16 vCPU / 64 GB host. Product asks you to just set -Xmx48g and keep p99 under 200 ms. Early test with -Xmx48g , default flags, shows: Pause Young Mixed G1 Evacuation Pause 31000M- 24000M 49152M 410ms Pause Remark 22.4s... remark/cleanup times 150-300 ms; concurrent mark cycles take 40 s .

title: Key flags and defaults
text: Give me the GC flags you would actually reach for on a modern JDK, their defaults, and which you'd refuse to set without evidence. How has this changed across Java 8, 11, 17, 21? "I set the collector, the heap Xms = Xmx or container percentage , GC logging, and maybe MaxGCPauseMillis for G1. I rarely touch everything else; G1 and ZGC are adaptive. I check defaults with -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal per JDK, because they changed: default collector moved from Parallel to G1 in 9, CMS was removed in 14, ZGC went production in 15, and ZGC is generational by default from 23."

title: OOM kinds
text: "OutOfMemoryError" is not one error. List the kinds you have seen in production, what memory area each one points at, and the first thing you check for each. The text after "OutOfMemoryError:" tells me the region. "Java heap space" is heap: leak or undersized heap. "GC overhead limit exceeded" is heap thrashing. "Metaspace" is class metadata, usually a classloader leak or runaway class generation. "Direct buffer memory" is NIO/Netty off-heap hitting MaxDirectMemorySize. "unable to create native thread" is the OS refusing a thread: ulimit, PID cgroup limit, or native memory exhausted. And a container OOM-kill is not a Java exception at all: the kernel killed the process with exit code 137, and the heap may have been fine.

title: Memory leaks
text: Java has garbage collection. How can a Java application still have a memory leak? The GC frees objects that are unreachable from GC roots. A Java leak is an object that is still reachable but will never be used again. Something holds a reference, typically a static map, a cache without eviction, a listener never deregistered, a ThreadLocal on a pooled thread, or a classloader that cannot unload. GC cannot know your intent, so it keeps them forever and the live set grows until OOM or GC thrash.

title: Allocation rate vs live set
text: What are allocation rate and live set, and how does each affect GC pause time and frequency? Allocation rate is how many MB/s the application creates; it determines how often young collections happen. Live set is how much data survives collections; it determines how long each collection takes, since copying/marking cost scales with live data, not garbage. High allocation with a small live set gives frequent, cheap young GCs. A large or growing live set gives longer pauses and eventually full GCs.

title: Heap dumps and MAT
text: You have a 4 GB heap dump from a leaking service. Walk me through analyzing it in Eclipse MAT. What are shallow heap, retained heap, and the dominator tree, and why do they matter? Shallow heap is the object's own size. Retained heap is memory that would be freed if that object were collected: everything only reachable through it. The dominator tree arranges objects by who keeps whom alive, sorted by retained size, so the biggest retainers float to the top. I run the Leak Suspects report, then open the dominator tree, then use "Path to GC Roots exclude weak/soft refs " on a suspicious object to see which static field or thread holds it.

title: ThreadLocal leaks
text: How can a ThreadLocal cause a memory leak, especially on a servlet container or thread pool? How do you prevent it? Each Thread owns a ThreadLocalMap whose entries are weakly keyed by the ThreadLocal but strongly hold the value. Pool threads live as long as the pool, so a value you set on a request and never remove stays reachable from the thread, which is a GC root. If the value, or its class, references a webapp classloader, it also blocks classloader unloading on redeploy. The fix: always remove in a finally , and keep values small and few.

title: Classloader leaks / Metaspace
text: What is a classloader leak? Why does it show up as OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace , and how do you diagnose and cap it? A class can be unloaded only when its ClassLoader is unreachable, which requires that all its classes, their instances and the loader itself are unreachable. If anything long-lived a static in a parent loader, a pooled thread's ThreadLocal, a JDBC driver registration, a shutdown hook references any of them, the whole loader stays and its metadata stays in Metaspace. Repeated redeploys or runtime class generation then grow Metaspace until it hits the cap or the container limit.

title: Heap leak
text: Find the problem, explain how you'd prove it, and fix it. An order service Java 17, G1, -Xmx2g, 8 pods, 300 RPS per pod restarts every 20 hours with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space . Post-GC heap floor rises about 70 MB/hour. A recent feature added this in-memory idempotency guard to avoid duplicate processing: @Service class IdempotencyGuard { private final Map<String, OrderResult seen = new ConcurrentHashMap< ; OrderResult process String requestId, Supplier<OrderResult work { return seen.computeIfAbsent requestId, id - work.get ; } } GC pauses are normal G1 young 25 ms , CPU is 40%, and the DBA says the database is healthy. The team suspects the new JSON library.

title: GC overhead limit
text: What does java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded mean, and why is it often a better signal than plain heap OOM? It is thrown when the JVM spends nearly all its time in GC while recovering almost nothing. For the Parallel collector the documented heuristic is more than 98% of time in GC and less than 2% of heap recovered, repeated over several consecutive collections. It means the live set is at or near the heap limit: the application is already effectively dead, crawling between full GCs. It is the same root problem as heap OOM leak or undersized heap , just caught earlier.

title: Heap dump capture
text: How do you take a heap dump from a running production JVM safely, and what are the risks? Use jcmd <pid GC.heap dump <path or jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=... . It is a stop-the-world operation proportional to the heap size: a 16 GB heap can freeze the process for tens of seconds and needs equal disk. So drain the instance from the load balancer first, write to a volume with enough space, and make sure -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError is already set for the crash case.

title: Humongous allocation
text: What is a humongous object in G1, why does it cause trouble, and how do you detect and fix it? In G1, any object at least half a region size is humongous. It's allocated directly into contiguous old-gen regions, bypassing young generation, and is never copied during evacuation. If there are many of them they fill old gen fast, trigger concurrent cycles early, fragment the heap and, in the worst case, cause Full GCs even with plenty of total free space. I detect it via GC logs and fix it by eliminating the large allocations, or by raising -XX:G1HeapRegionSize .

title: Container OOM-kill
text: What is happening and how do you fix it? A Java 17 service runs in Kubernetes with resources.limits.memory: 2Gi and JAVA TOOL OPTIONS=-Xmx1536m . About every 36 hours, pods restart with Reason: OOMKilled , Exit Code: 137 . Heap graphs show used heap peaking at about 900 MB, no Java exception, no hs err file. The container working-set metric climbs gradually over a day and a half to 2 GiB. The service uses Netty-based HTTP client, 220 threads, and serves 400 RPS. Last month someone raised Xmx from 1g to 1.5g "for headroom".

title: Native memory tracking
text: Explain Native Memory Tracking. How do you use it, and what does it not tell you? NMT is a HotSpot feature that tracks the JVM's own native allocations by category heap, class, thread, code, GC, internal, symbols, etc. . Enable it with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary or detail , take a baseline with jcmd <pid VM.native memory baseline , then summary.diff later to see which category grew. It does not see memory allocated by native libraries through their own malloc, JNI code, or glibc arena fragmentation, so I compare NMT's total against the process RSS to find the gap.

title: Direct buffer OOM
text: What causes OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory , how is direct memory limited, and how do you debug it? ByteBuffer.allocateDirect allocates native memory, limited by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize defaulting to roughly the max heap size . The memory is freed only when the small on-heap DirectByteBuffer object is garbage collected via a Cleaner , so lots of direct allocation with little heap pressure means GC rarely runs and the limit is hit while the heap looks fine. Netty avoids this with pooled buffers and reference counting, and leaks appear when a ByteBuf isn't released.

title: Native thread OOM
text: You see java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread . What are the possible causes, and how do you tell them apart? The JVM asked the OS for a thread and was refused. Three families: too many threads leak or unbounded pool, hitting ulimit -u or cgroup pids.max , not enough native memory for stacks each thread reserves -Xss , default 1 MB on 64-bit Linux, and the container limit or address space is exhausted , or kernel limits kernel.threads-max , vm.max map count . I count threads with a thread dump, then check limits.

title: Long pauses not caused by GC work
text: The GC log says a pause was 40 ms of GC work but the application saw a 1.8 s stall. What non-GC causes of "GC-looking" pauses do you know and how do you find them? I compare wall time to CPU time in the GC log user , sys , real . If real is much bigger than user+sys /threads, the JVM was waiting on something: swapping, CPU throttling by the cgroup, a slow disk writing the GC log, or time-to-safepoint where threads take long to reach a safepoint. I then check safepoint logs -Xlog:safepoint , cgroup throttling counters, swap, THP, and noisy neighbors.

title: Humongous storm
text: Diagnose and fix this. A Java 17 G1 service heap 8 GB, region 4 MB, so humongous threshold 2 MB exposes a CSV export endpoint. After a feature release, p99 goes from 180 ms to 4.5 s every few minutes; throughput normal otherwise RPS 600, CPU 55% . GC logs: gc GC 311 Pause Young G1 Humongous Allocation 5120M- 3980M 8192M 212.4ms gc GC 312 Pause Young Concurrent Start G1 Humongous Allocation 5400M- 4900M 8192M 301.9ms gc GC 313 Pause Full G1 Compaction Pause 7900M- 3100M 8192M 3920.1ms Heap used after concurrent cycle floor 3 GB. The new export builds the whole file in a ByteArrayOutputStream , with typical files 20-40 MB. Someone proposes "switch to ZGC".

title: Evacuation failure
text: What is going on and how do you fix it? A Java 21 service G1, Xmx 12 GB, 4 CPU, 10k RPS aggregate over 20 pods is stable for months. After a Monday deploy that added a 3 GB in-memory reference-data cache per pod loaded at startup , the p99 jumps from 90 ms to 1.2 s during peak. GC logs at peak: gc GC 88 Pause Young Normal G1 Evacuation Pause 9800M- 8900M 12288M 640.3ms gc To-space exhausted gc GC 91 Pause Full G1 Compaction Pause 11800M- 5400M 12288M 5210.5ms Allocation rate 900 MB/s. The old gen after mixed cycles sits around 5.4 GB. -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 is set. The team's idea: "halve the pause target to 50 ms".

title: Slow leak triage
text: Explain the cause and a full fix, including what to do about the existing metrics. A Java 17 payments gateway G1, Xmx 4 GB, 16 pods has no OOMs but every pod needs a restart after 9 days because p99 degrades from 120 ms to 900 ms. At day 8, young GCs take 90 ms from 20 ms , mixed GCs are frequent, and the post-GC floor is 3.1 GB from 1.2 GB on day 1 . A heap dump from a day-8 pod 3.4 GB shows: 1.6 GB retained by io.micrometer.core.instrument.composite.CompositeMeterRegistry via 2.4M Meter objects, tag values like uri=/users/8f4c-... and userId=... . CPU is moderate; threads stable at 140. Team lead says "it's Metaspace-like, maybe a classloader thing".

title: Heap sizing and cost
text: How do you decide new sizes and roll it out safely? A fleet of 60 pods runs a Java 17 G1 service with -Xmx6g and container limit 8Gi cost: 60 x 8 GiB . Dashboards show post-GC heap floor of 1.4 GB, peak used heap 2.8 GB, young GC every 4 s at 30 ms, no Full GCs, p99 = 140 ms, SLO 300 ms. Finance asks you to halve memory cost. A colleague proposes "set -Xmx2g and limit 3Gi".

title: Collector migration
text: Should we migrate? How do you plan and execute it? A trading-adjacent API Java 21, G1, Xmx 24 GB, 8 CPUs, 3,000 RPS/pod, SLO p99.9 < 50 ms shows G1 pauses of 80-300 ms every few minutes live set 11 GB . The team wants to migrate to generational ZGC -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational in Java 21; verify the flag for your release . Constraint: no downtime, and the same service must keep its CPU budget already 65% on average .

title: Visibility, atomicity, ordering
text: Concurrency bugs are usually described as visibility, atomicity or ordering problems. Explain each, and say which Java tools fix which. Visibility is whether one thread's write can be seen by another thread at all. Atomicity is whether a multi-step operation can be observed half-done or interleaved. Ordering is whether the sequence of writes that another thread sees matches program order. volatile fixes visibility and ordering but not atomicity of compound actions. synchronized and locks fix all three. Atomics AtomicInteger give atomic single-variable read-modify-write plus volatile-style visibility.

title: volatile
text: What exactly does volatile guarantee in Java, and what does it not guarantee? A write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that field. So the reader sees that write and everything the writer did before it. All volatile accesses are also in a single total order, and volatile long / double accesses are atomic. It does not make compound actions like i++ or check-then-act atomic, and it gives no mutual exclusion.

title: synchronized and memory barriers
text: Besides mutual exclusion, what does synchronized do for memory visibility? Why does reading a variable inside synchronized matter even if you only read? Unlocking a monitor happens-before every later lock of the same monitor. So everything thread A wrote before releasing the lock is visible to thread B after acquiring the same lock. It only works if both sides use the same lock object. A reader that skips the lock gets no guarantee.

title: Data race vs race condition
text: What is the difference between a data race and a race condition? Can you have one without the other? A data race is a memory-model term: two threads access the same variable, at least one writes, and no happens-before edge orders them. A race condition is a logic bug where correctness depends on timing, for example check-then-act. You can have either without the other: a race on a volatile counter is not a data race but is a race condition; a benign racy read can be a data race with no logic bug.

title: Visibility
text: Why does it hang and how do you fix it? A batch job runs a worker thread and a main thread. In staging with -Xint it terminates. In production on JDK 17 C2 compiled the process hangs forever after "stopping worker" is logged. Thread dump shows the worker RUNNABLE at Worker.run using 100% of one core. class Worker implements Runnable { private boolean stopped = false; long processed; public void run { while !stopped { processed++; } } void stop { stopped = true; } } // main: t.start ; Thread.sleep 5000 ; w.stop ; log "stopping worker" ; t.join ;

title: Happens-before
text: List the happens-before rules in the Java Memory Model and explain what "happens-before" does and does not mean. Happens-before is a partial order: if A happens-before B, A's effects are visible to B and ordered before it. Edges: program order within a thread; monitor unlock to later lock of the same monitor; volatile write to later read of that variable; Thread.start to the first action of the started thread; the last action of a thread to a successful join or isAlive ==false in another; an interrupt call to detection of the interrupt; and transitivity. It does not mean A executes earlier in time, only that if B reads, it must see A's effects.

title: Instruction reordering
text: Who reorders instructions in a Java program, and what rules limit it? Why does it not break single-threaded code? Three layers reorder: the javac/JIT compiler, the CPU out-of-order execution and store buffers , and the cache system. Single-threaded code is protected by as-if-serial semantics: any reordering must give the same result as program order for that thread. Other threads get no such promise unless a happens-before edge exists. Volatile, locks and final-field freeze insert compiler and hardware barriers to restrict reordering.

title: Double-checked locking
text: Explain double-checked locking for lazy singletons. Why was it broken before Java 5, and what makes it correct now? DCL checks a field without a lock, then locks and checks again before creating. Without volatile , instance = new Foo can be reordered so the reference is stored before the constructor's writes are visible, so another thread sees a non-null, half-built object. Since Java 5 JSR-133 , declaring the field volatile makes it correct. The better choices are the initialization-on-demand holder or an enum.

title: final fields
text: What special guarantee do final fields have in the JMM? What are the conditions, and when does it fail? When a constructor finishes, the JVM performs a freeze on its final fields. Any thread that gets a reference to the object, even through a data race, sees the correctly initialized final fields and the objects reachable through them as of the freeze. It fails if this escapes during construction, if the fields are not final, or if someone modifies them with reflection.

title: Safe publication
text: What is safe publication, and what are the idioms to achieve it in Java? Safe publication means the reference and the object's state both become visible to another thread in a correct order. The idioms: initialize in a static initializer, store the reference in a volatile field or AtomicReference , store it in a field guarded by a lock, store it in a final field of a properly constructed object, or hand it through a thread-safe collection or queue or executor. If the object is effectively immutable, publication must still be safe; if it is mutable, it also needs ongoing synchronization.

title: volatile misuse
text: What is wrong, and how do you fix it without adding a global lock? A rate limiter in an API gateway 8 pods, 4 vCPU each, 20k RPS peak enforces 100 requests/second per tenant. After a load test, tenant quotas are exceeded by 15% and the dashboard counter value does not match access logs. class TenantLimiter { private volatile int used; private volatile long windowStart = System.currentTimeMillis ; boolean tryAcquire { long now = System.currentTimeMillis ; if now - windowStart = 1000 { used = 0; windowStart = now; } if used < 100 { used++; return true; } return false; } }

title: Atomicity of long/double, word tearing
text: Is reading and writing a long atomic in Java? What is word tearing and does Java allow it? For non-volatile long and double , the JLS permits a write to be split into two 32-bit writes, so a racing reader can see half of one value and half of another. Volatile long / double accesses are always atomic, and references are always atomic. Word tearing, where a write to one field or array element clobbers a neighbouring one, is forbidden by Java: each field and array element is independent.

title: this escape
text: Find the bug and explain why final does not save you. An internal library publishes pricing events. After upgrading to a 16-core node, about 1 in 200,000 events processed by the listener throws NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length " because "this.region" is null . Stack points to PriceFeed.onTick , called by the dispatcher thread, never from the constructing thread. public class PriceFeed implements TickListener { private final String region; private final Map<String, Double prices = new HashMap< ; public PriceFeed String region, Bus bus { bus.register this ; // dispatcher thread starts delivering ticks this.region = region; // ... more setup } public void onTick Tick t { prices.put t.sym , t.px ; log region.length ; } }

title: Cost of volatile
text: How expensive is a volatile read or write? Does it differ between x86 and ARM? A volatile read on x86 is an ordinary load with compiler restrictions, so it is nearly free except it blocks some optimizations such as keeping the value in a register. A volatile write needs a StoreLoad barrier after it on x86, typically a locked instruction, costing tens of cycles. On ARM, HotSpot uses load-acquire and store-release style instructions verify the exact instruction for your JDK , so both sides have some cost. The bigger costs are contended cache lines and lost optimizations, not the barrier alone.

title: Immutability as a strategy
text: Why is immutability the simplest concurrency strategy on the JVM, and what traps remain when you say "this class is immutable"? An immutable object cannot change after construction, so it needs no locks, can be shared freely, and is safe to cache. For real immutability: all fields final, no this escape, the class cannot be subclassed or is final , mutable inputs and outputs are defensively copied, and the fields themselves reference immutable types. Records give final fields but are shallow: a record holding a List is not deeply immutable. You still need safe publication of the reference unless all fields are final.

title: Immutable snapshot vs locking
text: How would you restructure it, and what are the memory-model implications of each option? A pricing service has a RateTable of 50,000 entries, read on every request 6,000 RPS, 8 cores, each request does 5 lookups and rebuilt from a database every 30 seconds by a scheduler thread. Today the code uses a synchronized method for both read and refresh; p99 is 90 ms and profiling shows RateTable.get blocked threads JFR lock profile: 35% of samples waiting on one monitor, refresh holds the lock for 300 ms while rebuilding .

title: False sharing and @Contended
text: What is false sharing, how does it affect JVM programs, and how do @Contended and padding address it? CPUs move memory in cache lines, typically 64 bytes. If two threads write different variables that happen to share a line, each write invalidates the other core's copy, so throughput collapses even though there is no logical sharing. In Java you fix it by padding or by @Contended , which makes the JVM pad the field or class to separate cache lines. It costs memory, and user code needs -XX:-RestrictContended .

title: False sharing
text: Why does it not scale, and how do you fix it? A request-metrics component keeps per-worker counters in one array so the exporter can sum them cheaply: final class Metrics { private final long perThread = new long 64 ; // index = workerId, each worker writes only its slot void inc int workerId { perThread workerId ++; } // plain, single-writer per slot long total { long s = 0; for long v : perThread s += v; return s; } } At 4 workers it handles 40M increments/s total. Moving to a 32-core host with 32 workers, throughput is 55M/s total, not the 320M/s expected; CPU shows 100% across cores, no lock contention in JFR, GC is idle. The team wants to 10x traffic next quarter.

title: VarHandle access modes
text: What are the VarHandle access modes plain, opaque, acquire/release, volatile , and when would you use release/acquire instead of volatile? Access modes form a hierarchy of increasing guarantees: plain no ordering, any reordering or elimination , opaque per-variable coherence and eventual visibility, but no cross-variable ordering , release/acquire a release write is ordered after earlier accesses and an acquire read before later ones, so message passing works , and volatile all of that plus a single total order, i.e. sequential consistency . Use release/acquire for single-writer publication patterns where you do not need a total order across threads; it is cheaper than volatile on weak hardware and avoids the StoreLoad barrier on x86.

title: SC-DRF and racy programs
text: What does the JMM actually promise for a correctly synchronized program, and what does it promise for a program with data races? If a program has no data races in its sequentially consistent executions, then all its executions appear sequentially consistent SC-DRF . That is the simple model you should program to. For racy programs, Java still gives safety: no out-of-thin-air values, type safety, no memory corruption, and a read sees either the default value or some write that is not ordered after it by happens-before. But the exact value is unpredictable, and non-volatile long/double can tear.

title: Unsafe publication
text: Lead the post-incident review: cause, why now, fix, and prevention. A company migrated a checkout service from x86 c5.2xlarge, 8 vCPU to ARM Graviton, 8 vCPU nodes for 20% cost savings, same JDK 17 build, same traffic 2,500 RPS . Within a day, 1 in 3M requests failed with NullPointerException in ShippingRules.apply or applied rate 0.0 . It had never occurred on x86 in 18 months. Heap is healthy, GC pause p99 is 12 ms, no deploys changed code. The class: class ShippingRules { double baseRate; Map<String,Double zones; // plain fields ShippingRules Loader l { baseRate = l.base ; zones = l.zones ; } } class RuleHolder { static ShippingRules current; // plain static static void refresh { current = new ShippingRules loader ; } }

title: volatile references and arrays
text: What is the bug and what are the correct designs? A feature-flag cache keeps its enabled flags in a volatile array and a background poller flips entries. Request threads occasionally keep serving a disabled feature for minutes after the poller updated it poll log says "flag payments v2 - off at 10:04:11", requests at 10:09 still use it, on a few pods only . class Flags { private volatile boolean enabled = new boolean 256 ; boolean isOn int id { return enabled id ; } void set int id, boolean v { enabled id = v; } // called from poller } Pods: 12, 4 vCPU, JDK 17.

title: Verifying memory-model correctness
text: How do you test or prove that concurrent code is correct under the JMM? Why do ordinary unit and stress tests fail to catch memory-model bugs? Memory-model bugs depend on the JIT, CPU architecture and timing, so ordinary tests pass for years. I reason by happens-before: for each shared variable I name the edge between every write and read. To test, I use jcstress, the OpenJDK harness that runs small actor tests millions of times and tabulates the outcomes, on the real target architectures. I also use static analysis and review checklists, and I prefer designs immutability, confinement, locks that make reasoning easy.

title: Lock removal review
text: Do you approve it? What do you say, and what do you propose? A code review lands on your desk. Author's note: "p99 on /quote is 40 ms and profiling shows synchronized on QuoteCache.get ; I removed the locks since reads are safe and writes are rare, 5 writes/min vs 9,000 reads/s." Diff: class QuoteCache { private final HashMap<String, Quote map = new HashMap< ; private Quote latest; // was guarded by this public Quote get String k { return map.get k ; } // lock removed public void put String k, Quote q { synchronized this { map.put k, q ; latest = q; } } public Quote latest { return latest; } // lock removed } The author also says "p99 improved 12 ms in the benchmark".

title: Thread lifecycle
text: Walk me through the states a Java thread goes through. What is the difference between BLOCKED and WAITING, and does RUNNABLE mean the thread is on a CPU? " Thread.State has six values: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED WAITING, TERMINATED. BLOCKED means the thread is trying to enter a synchronized block or re-enter after wait and another thread owns the monitor. WAITING means it called something like Object.wait , join or LockSupport.park and needs another thread's action to wake it. TIMED WAITING is the same with a timeout sleep , wait ms , parkNanos . RUNNABLE only means 'eligible to run in the JVM's view'. It may be on a CPU, queued for one, or sitting in a native blocking call like a socket read."

title: Daemon threads
text: What is a daemon thread, when does the JVM exit, and why can daemon threads be dangerous for background work that must finish? "The JVM exits when the last non-daemon thread finishes or System.exit is called . Daemon threads do not keep the JVM alive and are killed abruptly: no finally blocks, no cleanup. So a daemon thread is right for housekeeping you can lose, like a metrics flusher, and wrong for anything that must complete, like writing a file or committing an offset. Conversely, a leaked non-daemon pool thread will keep a process from exiting."

title: Interrupt semantics
text: How does thread interruption work in Java? What do interrupt , isInterrupted and Thread.interrupted do, and what should you do when you catch InterruptedException ? " interrupt does not stop a thread. It sets the thread's interrupt flag. Blocking methods like sleep , wait , join , BlockingQueue.take check it, throw InterruptedException and clear the flag. isInterrupted reads the flag without clearing it; static Thread.interrupted reads and clears it. When I catch InterruptedException I either propagate it, or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread .interrupt and exit promptly. I never swallow it."

title: ExecutorService types
text: Describe what Executors.newFixedThreadPool , newCachedThreadPool , newSingleThreadExecutor , newScheduledThreadPool and newWorkStealingPool actually build. Which of them would you avoid in production and why? "They are factory methods over ThreadPoolExecutor or ForkJoinPool . Fixed uses core = max = n with an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue , so a slow consumer means unbounded memory growth. Cached uses core 0, max Integer.MAX VALUE , a SynchronousQueue and 60s keep-alive, so a burst means unbounded thread creation. Single is fixed with n = 1 wrapped so you cannot reconfigure it. Scheduled uses a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor with an unbounded delay queue. Work-stealing is a ForkJoinPool . In production I construct ThreadPoolExecutor directly with a bounded queue, a named thread factory and an explicit rejection policy."

title: ThreadPoolExecutor internals
text: Explain exactly what ThreadPoolExecutor does when you call execute task . What are corePoolSize, maximumPoolSize, the queue and keepAlive, and why does a pool with a large queue never grow past core? "On execute : if fewer than core threads exist, start a new thread for this task even if others are idle. Otherwise try to offer the task to the queue. If the queue accepts it, done. If the queue is full, try to start a non-core thread up to max. If that also fails, call the RejectedExecutionHandler . So threads above core are only created when the queue is full. With an unbounded queue the queue never fills, so max is ignored."

title: Unbounded queue
text: Explain what happened, how you would confirm it, and what you would change. An order-enrichment service runs on a pod with -Xmx1g , 2 vCPU. It calls a partner pricing API through Executors.newFixedThreadPool 20 , submitting one task per incoming Kafka message 800 msg/s . Normally each call takes 20 ms, so 20 threads handle 1000/s. At 14:02 the partner degrades to 250 ms per call capacity now 20 / 0.25 = 80 calls/s . By 14:09 the pod restarts. Log before death: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space ; GC logs show Full GCs every 2 s reclaiming nothing. CPU is 85% during GC. Consumer lag looked fine on the dashboard the whole time. private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool 20 ; void onMessage Order o { pool.submit - enrich o ; }

title: Rejection policies
text: What are the built-in RejectedExecutionHandler policies, when is each one acceptable, and what are the failure modes of CallerRunsPolicy ? "Four built-ins. AbortPolicy default throws RejectedExecutionException , which is the honest one: the caller learns it is overloaded. CallerRunsPolicy runs the task on the submitting thread, which slows the producer and acts as crude backpressure. DiscardPolicy silently drops the new task and DiscardOldestPolicy drops the queue head and retries; both lose work silently, so I use them only for best-effort data like metrics samples. Rejection also happens after shutdown . I choose based on whether the caller can slow down, fail, or lose the task."

title: Pool sizing
text: How do you size a thread pool for CPU-bound versus IO-bound work? Give the formula and its limits. "CPU-bound work: about N cores, maybe N+1, because extra threads just add context switching. IO-bound: more threads, using the Goetz formula threads = cores x target utilization x 1 + wait/compute . With 8 cores, 80% target, and 90 ms waiting per 10 ms of CPU, that is 8 x 0.8 x 10 = 64. It's an estimate: wait/compute varies, downstream capacity caps useful concurrency, and I validate with a load test and watch queue wait."

title: Pool sizing
text: How would you size and structure the fan-out executor s ? Show the numbers. You own a REST gateway endpoint POST /quote that, per request, fans out to 3 internal services in parallel: pricing p50 40 ms, p99 120 ms , inventory p50 30 ms, p99 90 ms , and tax p50 10 ms, p99 30 ms . Peak target: 600 requests/s. Each downstream call burns about 1 ms of CPU for serialization. Pod: 4 vCPU, Tomcat with 200 request threads. A colleague proposes one shared newCachedThreadPool for the fan-out. Another suggests Executors.newFixedThreadPool 8 "because we have 4 cores". Production p99 target: 250 ms.

title: Bounded vs unbounded queues
text: Bounded versus unbounded work queues: how do you choose the queue type and size, and how do SynchronousQueue , ArrayBlockingQueue , LinkedBlockingQueue and PriorityBlockingQueue change pool behavior? "The queue is where overload shows up, so I bound it and size it by the latency I can tolerate: queue depth = tolerated wait x service rate. An unbounded queue hides overload as latency and eventually as an OOM. SynchronousQueue is direct hand-off with zero buffering: tasks either get a thread now or the pool grows needs a large max or rejects. ArrayBlockingQueue is a fixed ring buffer with one lock; LinkedBlockingQueue can be bounded and uses two locks put/take so higher throughput under contention; PriorityBlockingQueue is unbounded, so combine with care. And the true fix for overload is backpressure upstream, not a bigger queue."

title: submit vs execute
text: What is the difference between execute and submit , and what happens to an exception thrown inside a task in each case? " execute Runnable runs the task and any exception propagates to the worker thread: the thread dies, the uncaught exception handler prints it, and the pool starts a replacement. submit wraps the task in a FutureTask ; exceptions are caught and stored, and only surface when you call get wrapped in ExecutionException . If you never call get , the exception disappears without a log line. So with submit , I always keep the Future and handle it, or wrap tasks in try/catch with logging."

title: CallerRunsPolicy cascade
text: What is the mechanism of the outage, and how do you fix it without losing emails? A checkout service 4 vCPU pod, Tomcat maxThreads=200 , 12 pods sends a confirmation email asynchronously via an emailPool : new ThreadPoolExecutor 10,10,0,SECONDS,new ArrayBlockingQueue< 100 , new CallerRunsPolicy . SMTP provider normally replies in 80 ms. At 19:40 the provider starts taking 8 s per call. Checkout traffic is 150 req/s across the fleet 12.5 req/s per pod . By 19:43: checkout p99 goes from 300 ms to 25 s, liveness probes fail, and pods restart in a loop. CPU is 10%, heap is fine. A thread dump from one pod shows 198 of 200 http-nio-8080-exec- threads in SmtpTransport.sendMessage - SocketInputStream.socketRead0 , and the 10 email- threads in the same call.

title: ForkJoinPool & work stealing
text: How does ForkJoinPool differ from a ThreadPoolExecutor , and how does work stealing work? When is it the right tool? " ForkJoinPool gives each worker its own double-ended deque instead of one shared queue. A worker pushes and pops its own forked subtasks from one end LIFO, cache-friendly, depth-first , while idle workers steal from the opposite end of other workers' deques FIFO, taking the biggest, oldest chunks . Fewer contended queue operations means good throughput for many small, CPU-bound, recursively split tasks. A joining worker doesn't sit idle: it runs other tasks while waiting. It is a bad fit for blocking IO because the pool is sized to cores."

title: Parallel streams & common pool
text: What are the pitfalls of parallelStream in a backend service? Which pool does it use and how can one stream hurt the rest of the application? "Parallel streams run on the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool , sized availableProcessors - 1 by default, and the caller thread participates too. That pool is JVM-wide: every parallel stream, and by default every CompletableFuture. Async without an executor, shares it. Blocking IO or a long-running job in one stream starves everything else. Other pitfalls: tiny workloads are slower than sequential due to split/merge overhead, non-thread-safe accumulators, ordered operations that kill parallelism, and thread-locals not propagating to pool threads. In a request path I usually avoid parallel streams and use an explicit executor."

title: Common pool starvation
text: Diagnose and fix. What does the arithmetic tell you about the 90 seconds? A recommendation service pods: 4 vCPU, 4 GB, Java 17 serves GET /home with p99 of 180 ms. After release 2.14 on Tuesday, p99 spikes to 9 s every 10 minutes for about 90 seconds, and returns to normal. CPU stays at 25%; no GC anomalies young pauses < 30 ms . The release added a "fraud-score refresh" job, which every 10 minutes runs: List<Account accts = repo.findFlagged ; // 3,000 rows accts.parallelStream .forEach a - fraudClient.score a ; // HTTP call, 120 ms each Request handlers also call CompletableFuture.supplyAsync - profileService.load id with no executor, and they use .parallelStream for layout assembly. Thread dump during a spike shows 3 ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker- threads in SocketInputStream.socketRead0 inside fraudClient.score and a pile of http-nio-exec threads in CompletableFuture.get .

title: ScheduledExecutorService
text: Explain schedule , scheduleAtFixedRate and scheduleWithFixedDelay . What happens if a run takes longer than the period or throws? " schedule runs once after a delay. scheduleAtFixedRate initial, period tries to start runs at start times initial + n x period ; if a run overruns, later runs start late but never overlap each other. scheduleWithFixedDelay initial, delay waits delay after each run finishes, so there is never a catch-up. If a periodic task throws, the exception is captured in the Future and all subsequent runs are suppressed , silently unless you check the Future or catch inside the task."

title: Scheduled task silently stops
text: Find the bug, explain why there are no logs, and fix it properly. A pricing service refreshes an in-memory exchange-rate map every minute. In staging it works. In production, rates freeze about once every few weeks: ratesAge metric climbs and no errors appear in logs after the last successful refresh. Thread dump shows the scheduler thread rates-1 idle in DelayedWorkQueue.take . The code: class RateRefresher { private final ScheduledExecutorService ses = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor r - new Thread r, "rates" ; private volatile Map<String, BigDecimal rates = Map.of ; void start { ses.scheduleAtFixedRate this::refresh, 0, 1, TimeUnit.MINUTES ; } void refresh { var fresh = client.fetchAll ; // may throw on 5xx / timeout rates = Map.copyOf fresh ; } } The provider returned HTTP 503 for a few seconds last night. Heap, CPU and GC are normal.

title: ThreadLocal in pools
text: What are the pitfalls of ThreadLocal with thread pools? Explain both data leakage between requests and memory leaks, and how InheritableThreadLocal behaves with pools. "A ThreadLocal value lives as long as its thread. Pool threads live for the process, so a value set while handling request A is still there when request B runs on the same thread unless someone calls remove . That gives cross-request data bleed wrong tenant, stale user and memory retention. The map holds weak keys but strong values, so when the ThreadLocal object itself becomes unreachable the entry's key is cleared, but its value stays until the map happens to clean the stale entry. InheritableThreadLocal copies the parent's value only when a thread is created, so pool threads capture a stale snapshot from whichever thread triggered their creation. The rule: set and remove in try/finally at the task boundary."

title: ThreadLocal leak
text: Explain both symptoms with one root cause, and how you would prove and fix it. A WAR-deployed service on Tomcat Java 17, -Xmx2g , -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m is hot-redeployed twice a day by an internal tool. After about 6 redeploys the node logs java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace ; metaspace used climbs 40 MB per redeploy and never drops. Tomcat's catalina.out also shows on undeploy: The web application orders created a ThreadLocal with key of type com.acme.RequestCtx$1 ... but failed to remove it when the web application was stopped. Threads are going to be renewed over time to try and avoid a probable memory leak. Separately, users occasionally report seeing another user's locale in emails. Heap is stable at 900 MB. public final class RequestCtx { private static final ThreadLocal<Ctx CURRENT = new ThreadLocal< { @Override protected Ctx initialValue { return new Ctx ; } }; public static Ctx get { return CURRENT.get ; } } // Filter: no remove anywhere. Also an app-owned executor: static final ExecutorService MAIL = Executors.newFixedThreadPool 8 ;

title: Graceful shutdown
text: How do you shut down an ExecutorService gracefully? Explain shutdown , shutdownNow , awaitTermination and what changed with close in Java 19+. "Two-phase: shutdown stops accepting new tasks and lets queued and running ones finish; awaitTermination timeout waits; if it times out, shutdownNow interrupts workers, drains the queue and returns the tasks that never started; then wait again. Restore the interrupt flag if I am interrupted while waiting. In Java 19+ ExecutorService is AutoCloseable : close does shutdown plus an untimed wait, and if the caller is interrupted it does shutdownNow, so try-with-resources works for scoped pools."

title: Shutdown during rolling deploy
text: Explain the losses and propose a shutdown and delivery design that makes deploys lossless. A payment-reconciliation service Kubernetes, 10 pods, terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 processes events from a queue via a ThreadPoolExecutor 16,16, ArrayBlockingQueue 2000 . Each task takes 200 ms to 6 s p99 10 s . Each deploy replaces pods one at a time. Since moving to Java 21 and Spring Boot with default settings, after every deploy reconciliation finds 20-60 events marked processed in the queue but with no ledger entry. Shutdown code today: @PreDestroy void stop { pool.shutdownNow ; } Logs at SIGTERM: Stopping service , then several java.lang.InterruptedException stack traces in LedgerClient.post , then silence. The consumer acks the message when it is handed to the pool.

title: Naming & uncaught handlers
text: Why should every thread pool have a custom ThreadFactory , and what should it set? Mention naming, daemon status and uncaught exception handling. "The default factory names threads pool-N-thread-M , which tells you nothing in a dump. A custom ThreadFactory gives a meaningful prefix like orders-http-%d , sets daemon status deliberately, sets an UncaughtExceptionHandler so failures are logged, and optionally sets priority and a thread group. With names I can match a CPU-hot thread from top -H to its pool in seconds, and filter logs and metrics per pool."

title: Monitoring pools
text: What would you monitor on every thread pool in production, which signals indicate saturation before users notice, and how do you instrument it? "Per pool I track active threads versus max, pool size, queue depth and remaining capacity, completed tasks, rejections, and most importantly queue wait time and task run time as timers. Saturation shows up as active/max near 1 and a growing queue; depth alone is ambiguous without service rate, so I alert on queue wait p99 and on sustained active ratio. Micrometer's ExecutorServiceMetrics exposes the basics for a ThreadPoolExecutor ; I add a custom rejection counter and a wrapper timing enqueue-to-start."

title: Bulkheads & cost
text: Using numbers, how would you restructure the executors and what is the minimum scale-out you can justify? A B2B platform backend Java 21, 12 pods x 4 vCPU/8 GB, roughly $280 per pod per month, so about $3,400/month in total uses one shared ThreadPoolExecutor 64, 64, queue 5000 named appPool for: customer-facing quote requests p99 target 300 ms, avg task 40 ms of mostly DB wait , nightly-style CSV exports triggered by users avg 20 s CPU+IO , and webhook deliveries to customers avg 600 ms, p99 30 s because some endpoints are slow . Sales announces a 10x customer ramp over the quarter: 30 quotes/s per pod now - 300/s; export requests from 0.2/s to 2/s per pod; webhooks 15/s to 150/s per pod. The CFO wants infra cost growth under 3x.

title: Composition operators
text: What is the difference between thenApply and thenCompose on a CompletableFuture ? When do you use each? " thenApply takes a function from a value to a plain value, like map . thenCompose takes a function from a value to another CompletionStage , like flatMap , and flattens it so I get one future instead of a nested one. If my next step is itself asynchronous, I use thenCompose ; if it is a cheap in-memory transformation, thenApply ."

title: Default executor
text: If I call CompletableFuture.supplyAsync - callService with no executor, where does it run, and why is that a problem in a backend service? "It runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool , a JVM-wide shared pool whose parallelism is roughly cores minus one. It is sized for CPU-bound work, so if I put blocking IO on it, a few slow calls can starve everything else on the JVM that uses the common pool, including parallel streams. For IO I pass my own bounded executor."

title: Async variants and threads
text: What is the difference between thenApply and thenApplyAsync ? Which thread runs each? " thenApply runs the function on whichever thread completes the source future, or on the caller's thread if the source is already complete when I attach the stage. thenApplyAsync always submits the function to an executor, the common pool by default or one I pass. So plain thenApply gives no guarantee about the thread; Async gives a hop to a pool."

title: Manual completion and Future vs CompletableFuture
text: How is CompletableFuture different from the plain Future , and how do you complete one manually for example from a callback-based client ? " Future can only be polled or blocked on with get . CompletableFuture supports non-blocking callbacks, composition and manual completion. I can create an empty one with new CompletableFuture< and call complete value or completeExceptionally t from a callback to bridge any callback API into the future world."

title: Combining futures (thenCombine, allOf, anyOf)
text: How do you run several independent calls in parallel and combine the results with CompletableFuture ? What are the gotchas of allOf and anyOf ? "I start all the calls first, then combine them. For two I use thenCombine . For N, allOf returns CompletableFuture<Void , so I collect each future's result with join after allOf completes. anyOf returns CompletableFuture<Object and completes with the first to finish, which can be an exception, not necessarily a success. Neither cancels the other futures."

title: Exception handling
text: Explain exceptionally , handle and whenComplete . What does CompletionException wrapping do to your exception handling? " exceptionally runs only on failure and replaces the result with a fallback. handle runs always with value, exception and returns a new value. whenComplete runs always but cannot change the result; it is for side effects like logging, and the original outcome flows through. In dependent stages the exception is wrapped in a CompletionException , so I unwrap with getCause before checking the type."

title: Fan-out parallelism
text: Why is it slow, and how do you fix it? What else would you check before shipping? A product-page endpoint fetches prices for up to 20 SKUs from a pricing service each call about 100 ms . The team "parallelized" it with CompletableFuture. At 200 RPS, the endpoint p50 is 2.1 s for 20 SKUs, and the pricing service shows concurrency of 1 per request. The code: List<Price prices = skus.stream .map sku - CompletableFuture.supplyAsync - pricing.get sku , io .map CompletableFuture::join .collect Collectors.toList ; The io pool has 32 threads. CPU is 15%. The load balancer shows no errors.

title: Timeouts
text: How do you put a timeout on a CompletableFuture ? What does orTimeout actually do to the underlying work? "Since Java 9, orTimeout t, unit completes the future exceptionally with TimeoutException if it is not done in time, and completeOnTimeout value, t, unit completes it normally with a default. Both only change the future. The task already running on a pool thread keeps going, so I also need a real timeout on the underlying client call. On Java 8 there is no built-in, so I use a scheduler."

title: Blocking inside async stages
text: Why is calling join or get inside a CompletableFuture stage dangerous? Show how it deadlocks a bounded pool. "A stage that blocks on another future occupies a pool thread while waiting. If the future it waits for needs a thread from the same bounded pool, and all threads are already waiting, nothing can run: pool-starvation deadlock. The fix is to compose with thenCompose instead of blocking, or run dependent work on a different pool."

title: Executor sizing and rejection
text: How do you size and configure the executor you pass to CompletableFuture stages, and what happens when it is saturated? "I use a dedicated bounded ThreadPoolExecutor per dependency class. For IO-bound calls, threads ≈ target throughput x average latency Little's law , with a small bounded queue and a rejection policy I chose deliberately. When saturated, a rejected submission throws RejectedExecutionException at the supplyAsync call site, which I must turn into a failed future or fast 503, not an uncaught exception."

title: Context propagation
text: You log with MDC request ID, user ID and use Spring Security's context. After moving work to a CompletableFuture on another pool the IDs vanish from the logs. Why, and how do you fix it? "MDC, SecurityContextHolder and tracing context live in thread-locals. A pool thread has its own, so values set on the request thread are not there. I capture the context on the submitting thread, restore it around the task on the worker thread and clear it afterwards. I do this once in a wrapping executor, or use a library such as Micrometer's context-propagation or Spring's DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor ."

title: Context propagation
text: Diagnose all three symptoms and propose the fix and prevention plan. A checkout service 6 pods, 8 vCPU each, 400 RPS total added a CompletableFuture step that calls a fraud API. Since release, three things are reported: 1 logs from the fraud step have no traceId , 2 audit logs show userId=u-7731 on a request belonging to another user, roughly 0.3% of requests, 3 SecurityContextHolder.getContext .getAuthentication is null in the fraud step, causing 401s from an internal API that needs the caller identity. The wrapper they added: Executor ctxExec = r - { MDC.setContextMap captured ; pool.execute r ; }; // captured = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap at construction captured is a static field assigned in the first request after boot.

title: Partial results and deadlines
text: How do you design the aggregation to meet the 300 ms goal, and what clarifications do you need from the product team? Product asks: "The home page should show recommendations, promotions and loyalty points. It must load in under 300 ms. Show whatever we have." Current backends: recommendations p50 90 ms / p99 700 ms, promotions p50 40 ms / p99 150 ms, loyalty points p50 60 ms / p99 400 ms. Traffic 1,200 RPS. The first implementation uses allOf with no timeouts and the page p99 is 780 ms. Loyalty points must be accurate if shown money-related ; recommendations are optional.

title: Stage execution and ordering
text: For a long chain of CompletableFuture stages, precisely how does the runtime decide which thread runs each stage, and what surprises does that produce ordering, stack depth, running on the wrong thread ? "Each future keeps a lock-free stack of dependent completions. When a future completes, the completing thread pops and runs them inline, which is why non-async stages run on whichever thread finished the source. If I attach a stage to an already-completed future, it runs immediately on my thread. Multiple dependents of one future run in LIFO order, so I must not depend on ordering, and a stage that completes another future can run that future's dependents inline too."

title: Cancellation
text: What does cancel on a CompletableFuture really do? How do you build cancellation that actually stops work, including through a chain? " cancel just completes that future with CancellationException ; the mayInterruptIfRunning flag is ignored by the documented contract because the future does not control the thread running the computation. The upstream task keeps running, and cancelling a downstream stage does not cancel its source. To really stop work I hold the underlying handle a Future from the executor, an HTTP call object , make the task interruptible or check a flag, and wire cancellation myself."

title: Async models compared
text: Compare thread-per-request with blocking calls, CompletableFuture composition, reactive streams and virtual threads for a service that fans out to several downstream services. How do you choose? "Thread-per-request with blocking calls is simplest but limited by platform thread count. CompletableFuture gives parallel fan-out inside a request but still blocks threads on IO unless the client is truly non-blocking. Reactive gives end-to-end non-blocking with backpressure and few threads, at a big cost in code complexity and debuggability. Virtual threads, final in Java 21, bring back simple blocking code with cheap threads. For a new Java 21+ service I default to virtual threads for IO-bound request handling and use CompletableFuture or structured concurrency only for explicit parallel fan-out."

title: Common pool starvation
text: Diagnose the incident, stop the bleeding and prevent recurrence. An order-enrichment service 4 vCPU pods, 12 pods, 900 RPS calls inventory, pricing and shipping via CompletableFuture.supplyAsync - httpClient.get ... with no executor. At 14:05 pricing began taking 8 to 12 s per call normally 60 ms . Within 90 seconds, /enrich p99 went from 250 ms to 30 s, health checks to /health still return in 5 ms, and CPU is at 6%. A nightly report job in the same JVM using parallelStream also hangs. A thread dump shows: "ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1" 31 daemon WAITING/RUNNABLE at java.net.SocketInputStream.socketRead0 Native Method at ... pricing client "ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-2" ... same "ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-3" ... same "http-nio-8080-exec-17" WAITING at CompletableFuture$Signaller.block Only 3 commonPool-worker threads exist.

title: Timeouts, retries, and load
text: Why does a 6x load increase produce a collapse rather than a degradation, and what do you change before the campaign? A recommendation gateway handles 500 RPS, calling a ranking service with orTimeout 200ms and one retry on timeout. Ranking's p50 is 40 ms and p99 150 ms; it runs at 55% CPU on 8 pods. The gateway's executor is 64 threads with a queue of 1,000, client read timeout is the library default 30 s . Marketing plans a campaign that will take traffic to 5,000 RPS 10x . In a load test at 3,000 RPS, ranking's p99 hits 900 ms, the gateway reports 60% timeouts, ranking CPU is 100%, and the gateway executor shows 64 active, queue 1,000, rejections climbing.

title: Swallowed failures
text: Lead the review: how did this go unnoticed, what are the contributing factors, and what changes do you recommend? Postmortem draft: "Between 02:10 and 09:40 about 11,000 orders were charged but never got a confirmation email or an inventory decrement. No alerts fired, error rate stayed at 0.02%, and the order API returned 200." The relevant code: public OrderResponse place Order o { Payment p = payments.charge o ; CompletableFuture.runAsync - inventory.decrement o .thenRun - emailService.sendConfirmation o ; // returned future dropped return OrderResponse.ok p.id ; } A dependency upgrade at 02:05 changed inventory.decrement to throw IllegalStateException "schema v3 required" . The app runs runAsync on the common pool.

title: Migration to virtual threads
text: How do you plan the migration and explain the canary spikes? A pricing API Java 17, Spring Boot, Tomcat, 16 vCPU / 8 GB pods, 24 pods, 6,000 RPS uses CompletableFuture chains over a 200-thread io executor for 5 downstream calls per request, p99 180 ms. The team wants to move to Java 21 virtual threads to simplify code and cut the pod count. Known facts: some libraries use synchronized around JDBC/HTTP calls a legacy rate limiter and a vendor SDK , the DB pool HikariCP is 50 connections per pod, and the code relies on ThreadLocal for MDC. A canary on Java 21 with virtual threads shows p99 spikes to 2 s every few minutes while CPU stays low.

title: synchronized / monitor
text: What exactly does synchronized lock on, and what is the difference between a synchronized instance method, a static synchronized method, and a synchronized block? Every Java object has an intrinsic lock, called its monitor. A synchronized instance method locks on this , a static synchronized method locks on the Class object, and a synchronized block locks on whatever object I name. Two threads exclude each other only if they lock the same object. The lock is reentrant, and entering and leaving also gives me happens-before visibility.

title: wait/notify
text: How do wait , notify and notifyAll work? Why must wait be called in a loop, and when is notify not enough? wait must be called while holding the object's monitor. It releases that monitor, parks the thread in the object's wait set, and re-acquires the monitor before returning. notify wakes one waiter, notifyAll wakes all. I always wait inside a while !condition loop because of spurious wakeups and because another thread may have consumed the condition first. I default to notifyAll unless all waiters wait on the same single condition and any one can proceed.

title: Lock states / biased locking
text: How does HotSpot implement synchronized under the hood? What are the lock states, and what happened to biased locking? The lock state lives in the object's header mark word . Uncontended locking is cheap and CAS-based "thin"/lightweight . When threads actually contend, the JVM inflates to a heavyweight monitor an ObjectMonitor where losers spin briefly and then park. Biased locking, which optimised single-thread reuse, was disabled by default in JDK 15 JEP 374 and deprecated for removal; I believe it was fully removed in a later release, so I'd verify the exact version. Today synchronized and ReentrantLock perform similarly in most workloads, so I choose on features, not on speed myths.

title: ReentrantLock
text: When would you use ReentrantLock instead of synchronized ? What do you give up? ReentrantLock gives me things synchronized can't: tryLock optionally with a timeout , interruptible acquisition, optional fairness, multiple Condition s, and introspection like isLocked and getQueueLength . What I give up is automatic release: I must unlock in a finally . If I need none of those features, I use synchronized because it can't leak a lock and is simpler.

title: ReentrantLock misuse
text: Find the bugs, explain the production symptoms, and fix it. A pricing service caches rates and refreshes them with this code. After a deploy, once an upstream DB timeout began, the service logged IllegalMonitorStateException and then stopped serving rates: p99 went from 40 ms to timeouts, and a thread dump showed 150 threads WAITING on ReentrantLock$NonfairSync . class RateCache { private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock ; private Map<String, BigDecimal rates = Map.of ; void refresh { try { lock.lock ; rates = loadFromDb ; // may throw on timeout } finally { lock.unlock ; } } BigDecimal get String k { lock.lock ; BigDecimal r = rates.get k ; if r == null return BigDecimal.ZERO; // early return lock.unlock ; return r; } }

title: Fairness
text: What does a fair ReentrantLock do, and why isn't it the default? When would you pay for fairness? A fair lock grants the lock to the longest-waiting thread; a non-fair one lets an arriving thread "barge" in if the lock happens to be free. Barging is faster because it avoids waking a parked thread and a context switch, so non-fair gives higher throughput. I use fair only when starvation is a real, observed problem or ordering is part of the requirement.

title: Condition
text: What is a Condition , and how does it improve on wait/notify ? Show a bounded buffer. A Condition is created from a Lock and gives that lock multiple independent wait sets. I use one condition for "not full" and another for "not empty", so a producer signals only consumers and vice versa, avoiding the wasted wakeups and lost-signal traps of a single wait set.
