If I know the number of entries, I presize to n / 0.75 + 1 , or use HashMap.newHashMap n since Java 19. Iteration order is unspecified and can change after a resize; if I need order, I use LinkedHashMap or TreeMap."

title: TreeMap, PriorityQueue, ArrayDeque
text: Compare TreeMap , PriorityQueue and ArrayDeque : data structure, complexity, ordering guarantees, and when you would pick each. "TreeMap is a red-black tree: sorted by key, O log n get/put/remove, plus range operations like floorKey , subMap . PriorityQueue is a binary min-heap in an array: O 1 peek, O log n offer/poll, O n remove Object , and iteration order is not sorted. ArrayDeque is a resizable circular array: O 1 amortized at both ends, the right default for stacks and queues, no nulls. The first thing I ask is whether I need sorted lookup TreeMap , repeated min/max extraction PriorityQueue or plain FIFO/LIFO ArrayDeque ."

title: LinkedHashMap LRU
text: How do you build an LRU cache with LinkedHashMap , and what are the limits of that approach in a real service? "LinkedHashMap is a HashMap whose entries are also in a doubly-linked list. With the constructor new LinkedHashMap< cap, 0.75f, true the list is in access order: every get/put moves the entry to the tail. I override removeEldestEntry to return size max , which evicts the head, the least recently used. It is O 1 but not thread-safe, even reads mutate the structure in access-order mode, and it has no TTL or weight-based eviction, so in production I use Caffeine."

title: Immutable collections
text: What is the difference between Collections.unmodifiableList , List.of , List.copyOf , Guava ImmutableList and a Kotlin List ? Which are truly immutable? " Collections.unmodifiableList is a read-only view : if someone holds the original list and changes it, the view changes. List.of Java 9+ and List.copyOf and Guava ImmutableList are genuinely immutable and don't depend on the source; List.of rejects nulls. Arrays.asList is fixed-size but writable-through to the array. A Kotlin List is only a read-only interface; the object behind it may still be a mutable ArrayList . And all of these are shallow: the elements can still be mutable."

title: Stream pitfalls
text: List every defect, explain each failure mechanically, and fix them. A pricing service processes order lines. A reviewer approved this change; after release, intermittent wrong totals and occasional ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException appear under load about 300 RPS, orders of 5-2000 lines . Another report: some orders produce duplicate-key errors. List<Line lines = order.lines ; List<Double prices = new ArrayList< ; lines.parallelStream .filter l - l.qty 0 .forEach l - prices.add l.price l.qty ; // 1 Map<String, Line bySku = lines.stream .collect Collectors.toMap Line::sku, l - l ; // 2 Stream<Line s = lines.stream .filter Line::taxable ; long taxable = s.count ; double sum = s.mapToDouble Line::price .sum ; // 3 Red herring: the team suspects a JDK bug in ArrayList.

title: String immutability and interning
text: Why are Java Strings immutable, what is the string pool, and when does intern help or hurt? "String is immutable so it can be shared safely across threads, its hash can be cached, it is safe as a map key and for security-sensitive values like class names or file paths. Literals and compile-time constants are interned in the string pool, which lives in the heap since Java 7. new String "a" == "a" is false, .intern returns the pool instance. I'd rarely call intern manually: it costs a native table lookup and can pin memory; for many duplicate strings I'd use G1 string deduplication or fix the source instead."

title: Integer cache and boxing
text: Why does Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b print true but 128 prints false? And what does autoboxing cost? "Autoboxing compiles to Integer.valueOf , which returns cached instances for -128..127 guaranteed by the Javadoc , so == on identical small values compares the same object. Outside the range it may allocate a new object, so == compares different references. Always use equals for boxed types. Boxing also costs an allocation 16 bytes for an Integer with compressed oops , extra pointer chasing, and a null can NPE on unboxing."

title: Hash collisions
text: Diagnose and fix it, and explain why Java 8+ treeification did not save you. An internal pricing API on 4 vCPU pods heap 2 GB, G1 normally serves 1,200 RPS at p99 40 ms. After a deploy that introduced an in-memory index Map<RouteKey, Quote with about 300k entries, p99 climbs to 6 s within an hour of warmup; CPU sits at 100%. GC logs are normal young pauses 15 ms, no Full GC . Thread dumps show 30+ threads RUNNABLE in: at java.base/java.util.HashMap$TreeNode.find HashMap.java:... at java.base/java.util.HashMap$TreeNode.getTreeNode HashMap.java:... at java.base/java.util.HashMap.get HashMap.java:... at com.acme.pricing.RouteIndex.lookup RouteIndex.java:41 Key class: record -like final class RouteKey String origin, String dest, int serviceLevel with hashCode { return serviceLevel; } author reasoned "equals compares all three, hash needs only be consistent" . serviceLevel takes 5 values. Red herring: the team wants to increase heap and switch to ZGC.

title: Stream cost and parallel streams
text: When do streams cost more than loops, and when is parallelStream actually a good idea in a server application? "A stream pipeline allocates lambda/stage objects and, for object streams, boxes primitives. The JIT usually inlines it well for monomorphic hot code, but in cold or megamorphic paths a loop wins, and the overhead matters only at tight inner loops or tiny workloads. Parallel streams split work across the single JVM-wide common ForkJoinPool, so in a server they let one request's CPU-heavy or blocking work starve others. I use them rarely: large CPU-bound data, good splittability arrays, ArrayList, ranges , no blocking, no shared state, and only after a JMH benchmark."

title: Boxing memory cost
text: Where does the memory go, what would you change, and what are the risks? A fraud-feature service keeps Map<Long, Long accountId - lastEventEpochMs in memory. It holds 10 million entries on a 4 GB heap pods limited to 6 GB RAM, G1 . Live set after GC is about 2.6 GB, and old-gen collections are frequent: young GC every 4 s, mixed collections up to 120 ms, p99 request latency 90 ms vs a target of 30 ms. The map is built once at startup then updated at about 20k writes/s, read at 60k reads/s. The team wants to cut the heap rather than add pods. Red herring: someone proposes -XX:+UseCompressedOops already enabled at 4 GB and G1 tuning flags.

title: StringBuilder and concatenation
text: When do you need StringBuilder , and what does + on Strings compile to? Is StringBuffer ever the right choice? "Since String is immutable, each concatenation produces a new String. A single expression like a + b + c is fine. Before Java 9, javac compiled it into a StringBuilder chain; from Java 9 it emits an invokedynamic call to StringConcatFactory JEP 280 , which can size the result exactly. Concatenation inside a loop is the problem: each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, giving O n^2 . Use one StringBuilder preferably presized outside the loop. StringBuffer is the synchronized legacy variant; I almost never use it."

title: Exception cost
text: How expensive are exceptions in Java, where does the cost come from, and when is it acceptable to throw them in a hot path? "Creating a Throwable is the expensive part, because the constructor calls fillInStackTrace , a native stack walk whose cost grows with stack depth. Unwinding to a handler costs less, and a try block that does not throw is essentially free. So deep stacks in frameworks make throwing costly; a stackless exception override fillInStackTrace or use the four-argument constructor with writableStackTrace=false is cheap, and when the JIT inlines throw and catch into the same compiled method it can turn the throw into a jump. Control-flow exceptions in hot paths are still a smell."

title: Exception design
text: Lead the post-incident review: what is wrong in the exception handling, what do you change, and what standards do you set? Post-incident review for a payment-capture outage. A nightly settlement job 30k payments, 4 worker threads reported "SUCCESS" while 1,100 payments were never captured. Findings in the code: public void settle List<Payment batch { for Payment p : batch { try { gateway.capture p ; // throws GatewayException checked or TimeoutException } catch Exception e { log.error "capture failed" ; // no id, no cause, no stack } } } public Payment load long id { try { return repo.find id ; } catch SQLException e { throw new RuntimeException e.getMessage ; } // cause dropped } Also: a finally { return status; } block in the outer run swallowed an OutOfMemoryError from a worker, and the on-call saw only "capture failed" 1,100 times with no ids. Red herring: management blames the payment gateway.

title: Records and sealed types
text: What do records and sealed types give you, what are their limits, and how do they change domain modelling compared with POJOs/Lombok and Kotlin data/sealed classes ? "A record final in Java 16 is a transparent, shallowly immutable data carrier: its components define the canonical constructor, accessors, and equals / hashCode / toString . A sealed type final in Java 17 lists its permitted subtypes, so the compiler knows the hierarchy is closed. Together with pattern-matching switch final in 21 I get algebraic data types with exhaustiveness checks: add a subtype and every switch that misses it fails to compile. Limits: records are shallow, so a List or array component is still mutable; they can't extend classes; and most ORMs want mutable entities, so records suit DTOs and value objects, not JPA entities."

title: Collection exposure and API migration
text: How do you diagnose it and migrate the API to safe collection exposure under live traffic? A Kotlin/Java monolith exposes OrderService.getItems : List<Item backed by a mutable ArrayList inside an Order object cached in a Caffeine cache 200k orders, 30 min TTL . Symptoms in production at 2,500 RPS: occasionally an order shows items from another request's mutation; ConcurrentModificationException in the pricing module about 3x/hour; a stack trace shows ArrayList$Itr.checkForComodification . A recent module added discount logic that calls items.removeIf ... on the returned list. You want to make Order safe without a flag day: 14 downstream callers some Java, some Kotlin and two other teams.

title: Choosing data structures
text: Critique the proposed structures and propose better ones, with complexity, memory and concurrency considerations. You are building a rate limiter and a leaderboard inside one API gateway process 8 vCPU, 4 GB heap, 20k RPS . Requirements: 1 sliding-window rate limit: at most 100 requests per client per 60 s, with 500k active clients; 2 "top 100 users by score" refreshed continuously from a stream of 50k score updates/s; 3 expire idle clients' state after 2 minutes. A candidate proposes: Map<String, List<Long with LinkedList for timestamps and a TreeMap<Integer, String for the leaderboard keyed by score .

title: Comparable consistency and sorted collections
text: What does it mean for compareTo to be "consistent with equals", and what goes wrong in TreeSet / TreeMap and HashSet when it isn't? " compareTo is consistent with equals if a.compareTo b == 0 exactly when a.equals b . Sorted collections TreeSet , TreeMap , PriorityQueue ordering define equality by the comparator, not by equals . So a comparator that compares only lastName makes TreeSet treat two different people with the same last name as duplicates and silently drop one, while a HashSet of the same objects keeps both. Comparators must also be transitive and antisymmetric, or sorting can throw Comparison method violates its general contract! ."

title: Container memory accounting
text: A Java pod has a 2 GiB memory limit and -Xmx1536m . Heap usage never exceeds 1 GiB, yet Kubernetes keeps OOMKilling it. How can that happen, and what does the container limit actually count? "The cgroup limit applies to the whole process RSS, not the heap. Metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, direct buffers, GC structures and malloc arenas all sit outside -Xmx. If the heap can grow to 1.5 GiB and the rest needs 600 MB, we cross 2 GiB and the kernel OOM killer sends SIGKILL, so there is no Java exception and no heap dump. I size the heap to about 50-75% of the limit and verify the rest with NMT."

title: JIT warmup
text: Why only after deploy, and what do you change? A payment-quote service Java 17, 4 pods, 4 vCPU each, 1,200 RPS total is rolled out with a normal rolling update. Steady-state p99 is 90 ms. For about 3 minutes after each new pod becomes Ready, that pod shows p99 of 1.8-2.5 s and CPU at 380%; then it settles. Error rate is 0 but the upstream gateway times out at 1 s, so 4-6% of requests fail during every deploy. GC logs show young pauses of 15-20 ms, nothing unusual. The readiness probe is a TCP check on the port.

title: Direct memory / OOMKilled
text: Find the cause and fix it without a guess-and-restart loop. A Netty-based gateway Java 17, G1 runs in a 3 GiB pod with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 heap about 2.1 GiB . Every 6-9 hours a pod restarts with OOMKilled , exit code 137. Heap in Grafana peaks at 1.1 GiB, GC pauses under 30 ms, no OutOfMemoryError in the logs. Pod RSS climbs steadily from 1.9 GiB to 3.0 GiB over a few hours. The service proxies request bodies of 1-50 MB. It was upgraded last week from a library that used heap buffers to one using pooled direct buffers.

title: Thread pool starvation
text: Explain what is happening and fix it. An order service Java 17, Spring MVC, Tomcat 200 threads has a shared Executors.newFixedThreadPool 16 named appPool used for parallel enrichment. At 9:05 traffic rises from 400 to 900 RPS. Latency climbs to 30 s, then every request times out. CPU is 4%. jstack shows 200 Tomcat threads in WAITING at CompletableFuture.get , and all 16 appPool threads also WAITING in Future.get , none doing work. Queue size of appPool a LinkedBlockingQueue : 3,400. DB and downstream metrics are healthy.

title: Connection pool exhaustion
text: What is happening, what do you do right now, and how do you prevent it? A Spring Boot service Java 17, HikariCP maximumPoolSize=20 , 8 pods, Postgres max connections=300 starts logging HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms total=20, active=20, idle=0, waiting=146 . It began 10 minutes after a deploy that added a call to a partner API inside a @Transactional method. Partner p99 went from 200 ms to 6 s during the incident. DB CPU is 12%, query times are normal. Tomcat threads: 200 each, 190 busy.

title: Data races on HashMap
text: What are the bugs, why are the symptoms so different, and how do you fix it? A metrics aggregator, deployed in production on Java 11 behind a 32-thread request pool, counts events per customer: class Stats { private final Map<String, Long counts = new HashMap< ; void record String customer { counts.merge customer, 1L, Long::sum ; } long total { return counts.values .stream .mapToLong Long::longValue .sum ; } } Symptoms: totals are 3-8% below the number of requests under load; once a week one pod pegs a core at 100% with a thread stuck in HashMap.putVal / TreeNode frames and never recovers; a rare ConcurrentModificationException in total .

title: Virtual thread pinning
text: Why did it collapse, and how do you recover and migrate safely? A team migrates a Spring Boot 3.2 service Java 21, Tomcat to virtual threads spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true to remove a 400-thread pool. Load test looked good. In production at 1,500 RPS, after 20 minutes throughput collapses to 40 RPS, p99 goes to 20 s, CPU is 8%, and Tomcat accepts requests but they hang. Carrier threads: 4 4 vCPUs . A vendor SDK, called on every request, does synchronized this { return httpClient.send ... ; } taking 300-800 ms. DB pool: 30 connections, fine. A JFR recording shows many jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events with durations over 20 ms.

title: ThreadLocal / classloader leak
text: Explain the mechanism and the fix. A legacy WAR Java 11, Tomcat 9, 6 GiB heap, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m is hot-redeployed twice a day by the release script instead of restarting Tomcat. After 4-5 redeploys the node fails with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace . catalina.out contains The web application shop created a ThreadLocal with key of type com.shop.RequestCtx$1 and a value of type com.shop.RequestCtx ... but failed to remove it when the web application was stopped. ... likely to create a memory leak. Metaspace after each redeploy rises by 90 MB and never drops. Heap looks normal.

title: CPU 100% hot loop
text: Walk me through finding the loop with the pod still running. One of 12 pods of a pricing service Java 17, 8 vCPU sits at 780% CPU while the others are at 60%. Latency on that pod is 12 s, the load balancer keeps sending it traffic because the health check is a static /ping . GC log shows 5 ms young pauses every 20 s; heap is at 40%. No errors in the log. The pod was fine until a 11:40 config push that changed a promotion rule table.

title: Deadlock in production
text: Explain, fix permanently, and discuss how you would make it hard to reintroduce. A wallet service Java 17, Tomcat transfers money between accounts. Once or twice a week, a handful of requests hang forever; then the number of stuck threads grows by about 10 per minute until all 200 are stuck and the pod fails health checks. jcmd <pid Thread.print ends with: Found one Java-level deadlock: "http-nio-exec-41": waiting to lock monitor 0x... object 0x...a Account , which is held by "http-nio-exec-87" "http-nio-exec-87": waiting to lock monitor 0x... object 0x...a Account , which is held by "http-nio-exec-41" The code was reviewed, and the lock is synchronized from { synchronized to { ... } } .

title: Autoscale warmup / startup
text: Make the system survive the ramp. A flash-sale API Java 17, Spring Boot, 4 vCPU pods autoscales on CPU at 70% from 6 to 60 pods during a 5-minute traffic ramp. New pods take 75 s to be Ready Spring context 40 s, 12 s waiting on first DB connections, rest class loading and then run slowly for 2 more minutes. The existing pods hit CPU 95% and p99 latency exceeds 4 s before capacity arrives; HPA launches pods in reaction, too late. Cost constraint: no always-on 60 pods.

title: GC tuning under cost pressure
text: What do you do and what do you check before approving? A recommendations service Java 17, G1 runs 40 pods of 8 GiB 6 GiB heap, 4 vCPU . Finance asks for a 40% cost cut. Current numbers: CPU 35% average, p99 120 ms SLO 250 ms , heap after full mark is 1.4 GiB live set , allocation rate 600 MB/s, young pauses 25 ms every 4 s, G1 concurrent cycles rare. Proposal from the team: halve the heap to 3 GiB and halve pod count.

title: G1 humongous allocations
text: Diagnose and fix. An export service Java 17, G1, 8 GiB heap, default region size = 4 MiB for this heap shows GC pauses of 600-1100 ms every few minutes, while young pauses are 30 ms. Log excerpt: gc GC 412 Pause Young G1 Humongous Allocation 5100M- 4900M 8192M 780.234ms gc,heap ... Humongous regions: 410- 408 Traffic is steady at 300 RPS. A new endpoint builds a byte of the full CSV response average 6 MB, some 80 MB before writing.

title: Incident methodology
text: An alert says "checkout p99 latency is 5x". You have 10 minutes before the incident call. Walk me through the first steps you take on a JVM service, and in what order. "I check what changed deploy, config, traffic , then use RED to see if errors, rate or duration moved and USE on the resources: CPU, memory, threads and pools, network, disk. If CPU is low and latency high, it's waiting: threads, locks, connection pools or a downstream. If CPU is high, profile; if memory, check GC. I mitigate first rollback, shed load, scale and take evidence thread dump, JFR before restarting."

title: Retry storm / timeouts
text: Write the post-incident review: causes, contributing factors, and the changes. A catalog service calls an inventory service p99 80 ms, normally 800 RPS . Inventory gets a bad deploy and slows to 4 s. The catalog's HTTP client has read timeout 10 s, 3 retries no backoff , Tomcat 200 threads, and the gateway in front has a 5 s timeout and also retries once. Within 90 seconds catalog threads are all blocked, its own p99 is 5 s gateway timeouts , and inventory, which was recovering after a rollback, is flooded with 4x its normal request rate and stays down for 25 more minutes. Outcome: a 35-minute outage for a feature that was meant to degrade gracefully.

title: Parallel streams / common pool
text: What is wrong and what are the fixes? A recommendation endpoint on a 4-vCPU pod Java 17 runs this on every request 200 RPS : List<Product enrich List<String ids { return ids.parallelStream .map id - inventoryClient.fetch id // blocking HTTP call, 120 ms .collect Collectors.toList ; } Under load: p50 is fine, but p99 is 9 s, and other endpoints that use parallelStream or CompletableFuture.supplyAsync ... without an executor also slow down at the same time. CPU is 20%. jstack shows ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1..3 blocked in socket reads.

title: Unbounded executor queue
text: Explain the failure, the fix, and the correct overload behavior. A notification service Java 17, G1, 4 GiB heap, 4 vCPU uses Executors.newFixedThreadPool 8 to send emails through a provider whose throughput dropped from 300/s to 40/s. Producers a Kafka listener and an API enqueue 250 tasks/s. After 20 minutes, GC time goes to 60%, the heap is at 3.9 GiB, request latency rises to 30 s, and finally OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError . MAT shows 4.6 million FutureTask objects in a LinkedBlockingQueue , each referencing a 600-byte payload.

title: Async context propagation
text: Why, and how do you fix it correctly? A Spring MVC service Java 17 logs with a traceId stored in SLF4J MDC by a servlet filter, and authorizes using SecurityContextHolder thread-local strategy . A refactor makes a controller do: @GetMapping "/orders/{id}" public CompletableFuture<Order get @PathVariable long id { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync - { log.info "loading order {}", id ; // traceId missing in logs auditService.record currentUser , id ; // currentUser reads SecurityContextHolder - null, sometimes someone else's! return repo.load id ; }, ioPool ; } After release: logs for those requests have no traceId , auditing sometimes shows anonymous , and once a security review finds user A's audit entry written under user B.

title: Heap leak diagnosis
text: How do you get proof and fix it without risking prod? A pricing API Java 17, G1, 4 GiB heap restarts every 30 hours because of OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space . GC logs show the live set after each mixed/full collection rising linearly by 60 MiB/hour; young pauses stay 20-40 ms until the last 2 hours, when full GCs of 3-6 s appear. A deploy 3 days ago added a "price lookup cache" using a static Map<RequestKey, Price and a dependency upgrade. Sizing the cache was never discussed. There is no heap dump yet because the OOM kill came from the liveness probe before the dump finished writing to a 2 GiB ephemeral volume.

title: CPU throttling in containers
text: Why does a 55%-CPU service stall, and what do you change? A service in Kubernetes Java 17, G1 has CPU request 2, limit 2 on a 16-core node. JVM sees 2 CPUs. Latency p99 is 70 ms normally, but exhibits sharp 150-400 ms spikes every few seconds, correlated with traffic bursts, while average CPU shows 55%. GC pauses are 20 ms. Prometheus shows container cpu cfs throttled periods total / container cpu cfs periods total at 38%. The JVM runs 18 GC and compiler threads in addition to 40 request threads.

title: Little's law and capacity
text: Latency is rising during peak. Someone proposes doubling the thread pool and the connection pool. How do you decide if it will help, and how do you size pools from first principles? "Little's law: concurrency L = arrival rate lambda x time in system W. A pool is just the allowed concurrency. If the bottleneck is CPU or the database, more threads only increase queueing and context switching; if threads mostly wait on I/O, I need threads = rate x wait time. I measure service time per resource, find the bottleneck by utilization and saturation, and size each pool to what the next stage can handle, with bounded queues."

title: ScheduledExecutorService
text: What happened and how do you make it robust? A service refreshes a pricing cache every 30 s: ScheduledExecutorService ses = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool 1 ; ses.scheduleAtFixedRate - { cache.putAll pricingClient.fetchAll ; // throws SocketTimeoutException once in a while }, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS ; After a pricing blip at 03:12 the cache is never refreshed again. Prices served are 9 hours stale by morning. No error in logs, no alerts, the thread pool looks healthy, the app is up.

title: Metaspace growth
text: Diagnose, fix, and explain why GC did not clean it. A Spring service Java 17, no hot redeploy, container 3 GiB, heap 1.5 GiB, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize unset grows RSS from 1.8 GiB to the limit over 3 days and is OOMKilled. jcmd <pid VM.native memory summary shows Class committed growing from 90 MB to 900 MB; jstat -class shows loaded classes going from 14,000 to 410,000 with unloaded stuck at 120. The only change last sprint: a feature that builds a Groovy-like rules script per tenant request with GroovyShell.evaluate script , and a custom Proxy.newProxyInstance per request with a fresh ClassLoader .

title: Native thread exhaustion
text: Why does this error say "memory," and what is the fix? A fan-out service Java 17, 2 GiB pod, -Xmx1g logs java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread: possibly out of memory or process/resource limits reached . Heap and GC are healthy. jcmd <pid Thread.print grep -c '^"' returns 14,200. A code path does new Thread - callPartner x .start per downstream call 3 per request, partner latency recently 30 s instead of 300 ms , at 150 RPS. Pod pids.max is 4,096 via a cgroup limit.

title: Virtual thread migration
text: How do you plan and execute the migration? Your team plans to move a Spring Boot 3.3 order service Java 21, Tomcat, 400-thread pool, 12 pods, HikariCP 30 connections per pod, 3,000 RPS total, p99 180 ms to virtual threads to handle a projected 3x load without buying pods. Dependencies: Postgres max 500 connections , a partner REST API with a rate limit of 2,000 RPS, Redis, and a legacy SDK using synchronized . Management wants "flip the flag next Friday".

title: GC death spiral
text: Write the review: what failed, what you change in the JVM, the code and the platform. During a TV-ad spike traffic goes from 600 to 6,000 RPS 10x . A search service Java 17, G1, 6 GiB heap, 4 vCPU pods, autoscaling reached 20 pods in 7 minutes experienced a 22-minute degradation. Timeline from logs: 12:01 Pause Young Normal 28ms every 3.2 s 12:04 Pause Young Concurrent Start ... to-space exhausted 210ms 12:05 Pause Full G1 Compaction Pause 5800M- 4100M 6144M 6120ms 12:06 Pause Full ... 5900M- 4800M 7900ms Full GCs back-to-back 12:06 health check timeouts, pods removed from the LB, traffic shifts to survivors Live set normally 1.8 GiB; during the spike each request builds up to 3 MB of intermediate results, and a result cache grows maximumSize 200k entries x 10 KB .

title: Safe production diagnostics
text: Which JVM diagnostic tools are safe to use on a live production pod serving traffic, which are risky, and how do you gather evidence without making the incident worse? "Cheap and generally safe: GC logs, JFR default/profile settings , jcmd Thread.print , jstat , jcmd GC.class histogram short pause , async-profiler at moderate frequency. Risky: heap dumps STW and large I/O, memory spike , jmap -histo:live forces a full GC , attaching debuggers, -Xcomp , heavy allocation profiling. I take the risky ones from one pod removed from rotation, with enough disk, and keep dumps secured."

title: Triage under ambiguity
text: How do you proceed from this vague request to a defensible outcome in 3 days? A product manager pings you: "The API feels slow sometimes, customers are complaining, fix it before the board demo on Thursday." Facts available: p50 is 45 ms, p99 is 600 ms, p99.9 is 4 s; the service is a Java 17 Spring Boot app, 10 pods, G1 with 4 GiB heap, Postgres, one partner API. No SLO document. Complaints cluster around "weekday mornings" but no endpoint, customer or timestamp is given. There is a JFR-less setup, metrics only in Prometheus RED + JVM + Hikari , no tracing.

title: What an embedding is
text: What is an embedding, how does a text embedding model produce one, and what does "similar" mean in that space? An embedding is a fixed-size vector of floats that a neural network maps an input to, trained so inputs that should be treated as similar land close together. For text, an encoder transformer produces per-token vectors, which are pooled mean or CLS into one vector. "Similar" is defined by the training objective, usually a contrastive loss on query/relevant-passage pairs, so closeness means "would be judged relevant or paraphrastic", not "true" or "same topic" in an absolute sense.

title: Cosine vs dot product vs L2
text: Cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance: how do they differ, and when do they give identical rankings? Dot product mixes angle and magnitude; cosine is dot product divided by both norms, so it is angle only; L2 measures straight-line distance. If vectors are unit-normalized, a-b ² = 2 - 2·cos a,b and cos = dot, so all three give the same ranking. If they are not normalized, they can disagree, and I must use the metric the model was trained with.

title: Embedding dimensions
text: What does embedding dimensionality control, and what are the trade-offs of 384 vs 1024 vs 3072 dimensions? Dimension is the capacity of the vector to separate items. More dims generally buy a little retrieval quality but cost linearly in memory, index build time, and distance compute. I measure recall on my own data at a few sizes and pick the knee of the curve; for large corpora the storage and RAM bill usually decides.

title: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder
text: Explain bi-encoders versus cross-encoders. Why do we not just use a cross-encoder for search? A bi-encoder embeds query and document independently, so documents are pre-computed and searched by vector math; it is fast but compresses each text into one vector. A cross-encoder feeds query and document together through the transformer, so tokens attend across both and it is more accurate, but it needs one forward pass per pair, which is infeasible over millions of docs. So I retrieve top-100 with a bi-encoder and rerank with a cross-encoder.

title: Matryoshka / truncation
text: What is Matryoshka representation learning, and what can go wrong when you truncate embeddings? Matryoshka training makes the first k dimensions of the vector a usable embedding on their own, by applying the loss at several prefix sizes e.g. 64, 128, 256, ... full . So I can store a shorter prefix and trade a little quality for large memory savings. The trap: after truncating I must re-normalize, and I must only truncate models trained that way.

title: Asymmetric query/doc embeddings and prefixes
text: Why do some embedding models require "query:" and "passage:" prefixes or instructions, and what happens if you skip them? Queries and documents are different text types: a query is short and expresses an information need, a passage is long and contains answers. Many models were trained asymmetrically with a prefix or instruction telling the encoder which role the text plays. If I skip or mix the prefixes, the model sees inputs off its training distribution and retrieval quality drops, usually without any error.

title: Choosing an embedding model
text: How do you choose an embedding model for a production search feature? I list hard constraints first: language coverage, max input tokens, dimension/storage budget, latency, license, and hosted vs self-hosted. Then I build a small labeled eval set from real queries 100-300 with relevant docs , shortlist 3-4 models, and compare recall@k and MRR on my corpus. MTEB gets me the shortlist; my own data picks the winner.

title: ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF)
text: Explain at a conceptual level how HNSW and IVF work and what trade-offs they make versus exact search. Exact search compares the query to every vector, O N·d . ANN trades a bit of recall for sublinear time. HNSW builds a layered proximity graph and greedily walks from sparse top layers down to dense bottom ones. IVF clusters vectors with k-means and searches only the nearest few clusters. HNSW gives high recall and low latency but uses lots of RAM; IVF often with product quantization is leaner but needs training and tuning nprobe.

title: Cosine vs dot product
text: Find the bug, explain why only live metrics suffer, and fix it without downtime. A semantic search service uses a self-hosted embedding model whose card says "trained with cosine similarity; outputs not normalized." Index code: import faiss, numpy as np d = 1024 vecs = model.encode chunks float32, shape 2 000 000, 1024 , NOT normalized index = faiss.IndexFlatIP d inner product index.add vecs q = model.encode user query scores, ids = index.search q, 10 After launch, users complain that long boilerplate-heavy chunks legal footers, tables of contents keep outranking the right answer. Offline eval in a notebook which used sklearn.metrics.pairwise.cosine similarity shows recall@10 = 0.82; the live system measures 0.64 on the same queries. Mean vector norm in the index is 11.8 with std 4.1. QPS is 150; p95 is fine.

title: Similarity thresholds and calibration
text: Can you set a cosine similarity threshold of 0.8 to decide "relevant"? How do you pick and maintain thresholds? No, cosine values are not probabilities and their distribution depends on the model, the metric, text length, and the domain. 0.8 might be near-duplicate in one model and "barely related" in another. I pick thresholds empirically: label pairs, plot score distributions of relevant vs irrelevant, choose a cutoff for the precision/recall trade-off the product needs, and re-check whenever the model changes.

title: Embedding drift and re-indexing
text: What is embedding drift, and how do you handle changing or upgrading an embedding model with a live index? There is no mapping between two models' spaces, so a new model means re-embedding the entire corpus and re-indexing, then switching queries to the new model atomically. I run it blue/green: build the new index alongside, shadow-evaluate on a golden set, switch an alias, keep the old index for rollback. "Drift" also covers silent changes: provider updates behind the same name, preprocessing changes, and data distribution shift.

title: Max tokens and truncation
text: Diagnose and fix. Include the trade-offs between possible fixes. A contract-search team indexes 1,800-token clauses with intfloat/multilingual-e5-large using this code: m = SentenceTransformer "intfloat/multilingual-e5-large" vecs = m.encode f"passage: {c}" for c in clauses , batch size=64, normalize embeddings=True Users report: searching a phrase that appears only in the second half of a clause never finds it, while searching the first sentence works perfectly. Recall on "first-half" test queries is 0.91, on "second-half" queries 0.18. No errors or warnings in logs. The model card says inputs longer than 512 tokens are truncated. Corpus: 400k clauses, token length median 1,100.

title: Anisotropy and hubness
text: What are anisotropy and hubness in embedding spaces, and how do they affect retrieval quality? Anisotropy means embeddings occupy a narrow cone instead of spreading across the sphere, so even unrelated texts have high cosine a high baseline . Hubness means some vectors appear in the nearest-neighbor lists of a disproportionate number of queries, crowding out better answers. Both distort rankings and make absolute thresholds unreliable; mitigations are mean-centering/whitening, better-trained models, hybrid retrieval, and reranking.

title: Multilingual and multimodal embeddings
text: How do multilingual and multimodal embedding models work, and what pitfalls should you plan for? Multilingual models train one encoder on many languages, often with parallel or translation-pair data, so equivalent sentences in different languages land near each other and cross-lingual retrieval works. Multimodal models like CLIP train two encoders image and text contrastively on image-caption pairs into a shared space. Pitfalls: uneven quality across languages, language bias in rankings, modality gap, and tokenization/length differences.

title: Matryoshka truncation
text: What went wrong, and how would you get the savings without the quality loss? A product search service has 60M product-description chunks embedded with an MRL-capable 1024-dim model float32 , served from pgvector-like infrastructure with HNSW. RAM bill: 60M × 1024 × 4 B = 245.8 GB of raw vectors; with graph overhead and 2 replicas the team provisions 900 GB. Finance asks for a 60% reduction. An engineer ships "truncate to 256 dims" by slicing vec :256 in the indexer and the query service, storing without renormalization, and keeping the index on inner product. Next day: recall@10 on the golden set goes from 0.88 to 0.79, and the long-description products dominate results. Latency improved 35%.

title: Embedding drift / re-indexing
text: Plan the migration end to end, with numbers. Your vendor announces that embed-v2 is deprecated in 90 days. You have 120M chunks avg 280 tokens , a 1,536-dim index serving 400 QPS peak, p95 SLA of 120 ms, and uptime commitments. The new model embed-v3 has a rate limit of 4M tokens/minute illustrative and costs $0.10 per 1M tokens illustrative; check actual . Total tokens: 120M × 280 = 33.6B. Product wants the new model's better quality ASAP, and also wants "zero downtime". The index team says double the cluster for the migration is too expensive. Some documents change daily 0.5M/day .

title: Similarity thresholds
text: Write the post-incident review: causes, detection gaps, and corrective actions. A support assistant uses a semantic cache: if cosine new query, cached query ≥ 0.88, return the cached answer. It has run for 6 months with a 31% hit rate and "no complaints". Last Tuesday the team upgraded the embedding model new vendor version, same dimension, vectors normalized and re-embedded the cache keys. Hit rate jumped to 58%, p95 latency dropped, and cost fell, so the dashboard looked great. Three days later: a customer received instructions for "downgrading a plan" when asking about "upgrading a plan"; 11 similar tickets follow. Sample logged pairs: "how to upgrade my plan", "how to downgrade my plan" scored 0.91.

title: Cosine similarity caveats
text: Is cosine similarity of learned embeddings always meaningful? What are its limits, and is cosine distance a metric? Cosine is a sensible default when the model was trained for it, but it is not guaranteed meaningful for arbitrary learned embeddings. Steck et al. 2024 show that for matrix-factorization-style models trained with regularization, cosine can be made arbitrary by rescaling latent dimensions while the dot products stay fixed. Practically: use the metric the model was trained with and validate with retrieval evals. Also, 1 - cosine violates the triangle inequality, so it is not a true metric; angular distance is.

title: ANN at scale
text: How do you scale this, and what do you measure before committing? An internal doc-search tool runs brute-force cosine in NumPy on a single 32 GB box: 2M chunks × 768d float32 = 6.1 GB, p95 = 85 ms at 20 QPS. Acquisition of a second company will take the corpus to 25M chunks and traffic to 200 QPS. A quick extrapolation says brute force will be roughly 12x slower per query about 1 s , and memory will be 76.8 GB. The team proposes "just add GPUs" or "move to a managed vector DB, whichever is cheapest".

title: Choosing a model
text: How do you turn this into a decision and a plan? A stakeholder says: "We need semantic search over our contracts in English, German, and Japanese. Make it accurate. Use the best embedding model." Corpus: 300k contracts, average 12 pages, sensitive client data; deadline in 6 weeks; two ML engineers; no labeled queries; legal team available 2 hours/week. Budget is "reasonable".

title: ANN filtering and recall
text: Diagnose, mitigate, and fix. A multi-tenant RAG product with 80M chunks in one HNSW index M=16, efSearch=64 supports a tenant id filter applied after ANN retrieval "post-filter" . Median tenant owns 0.01% of vectors 8k chunks ; the largest owns 12%. Support tickets: "search returns nothing" for small tenants; for some it returns 1-2 results while the tenant has hundreds of relevant docs. Logs: ann.candidates=64 filtered out=63 returned=1 . Overall recall@10 on the global golden set is 0.93 and p95 latency is a healthy 22 ms. A recent change: the team deleted 15M stale vectors via tombstones last week.

title: Evaluating embeddings and retrieval
text: How do you evaluate an embedding model or an index change, and what are the limits of public benchmarks like MTEB? I evaluate the retrieval task end to end on a labeled set drawn from real queries: recall@k, MRR, and nDCG, sliced by language, query type, and document length, and compare against brute-force ground truth to separate model error from ANN error. Public benchmarks like MTEB help shortlist but average across tasks, can be contaminated or tuned for, and rarely match my domain, so they never replace my own eval.

title: Why subword tokenization
text: Why do LLMs use subword tokens instead of words or characters? Word-level vocabularies are huge and can't represent unseen words, so you get an unknown token. Character-level has a tiny vocab but sequences get very long, and attention cost grows with length squared. Subwords sit in the middle: common words are one token, rare words split into reusable pieces, so nothing is out-of-vocabulary and sequences stay short.

title: BPE algorithm
text: Walk me through how Byte Pair Encoding is trained and how it then tokenizes new text. I start with a base vocabulary of characters or bytes , count adjacent symbol pairs across the corpus, merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol, and repeat until I hit the target vocab size. The ordered merge list is the model. At inference I split text into base symbols and replay the merges in learned order, so tokenization is deterministic.

title: Token counting and cost
text: How do you estimate token count and cost for a request before sending it, and how accurate are rules of thumb? For a rough estimate, English is about 4 characters or 0.75 words per token, but I never rely on that for budgets. I count with the model's actual tokenizer tiktoken for OpenAI, the provider's count endpoint or the HF tokenizer for others , count input and output separately because they're priced differently, and add per-message template overhead.

title: Special tokens and chat templates
text: What are special tokens, and what is a chat template? Why can't I just concatenate "User: ... Assistant: ..." myself? Special tokens are reserved vocabulary entries like BOS, EOS, and role/turn markers that carry structure rather than text. A chat template is the exact recipe that turns a list of role/content messages into the token sequence the model was fine-tuned on. If you format it differently from training, the model sees a distribution it never learned and quality drops.

title: BPE vs WordPiece vs Unigram
text: Compare BPE, WordPiece and Unigram. How do they differ in training and in inference? BPE and WordPiece are bottom-up: start from characters and merge. BPE merges the most frequent pair; WordPiece merges the pair that most increases training-data likelihood, roughly freq ab / freq a x freq b . Unigram is top-down: start with a big candidate vocab and prune tokens whose removal hurts likelihood least. BPE encodes with deterministic merge order; Unigram picks the max-probability segmentation and can also sample segmentations.

title: Byte-level BPE and SentencePiece
text: What is byte-level BPE, and how does SentencePiece differ in how it handles whitespace and unknown characters? Byte-level BPE uses the 256 byte values as the base alphabet, so any string in any language or emoji is representable and there is no <unk . SentencePiece treats input as a raw stream including the space written ▁ , needs no language-specific pre-tokenizer, and is reversible; it can use BPE or Unigram, and some models add byte fallback for rare characters.

title: Vocabulary size trade-offs
text: How does vocabulary size affect model quality, cost and speed? Why have vocabularies grown from 32k to 128k-256k? A bigger vocab means fewer tokens per text, so shorter sequences, cheaper attention and faster generation, and better multilingual efficiency. The price is a larger embedding table and output softmax layer, and rarer tokens that get few training updates. Doubling V past a point yields diminishing returns, so labs pick a sweet spot, and recent models moved up mainly for multilingual and code efficiency.

title: Multilingual and code token inflation
text: Why do some languages and code cost more tokens for the same content, and what can you do about it? Tokenizers learn merges from their training corpus, which is English-heavy, so English words become single tokens while Hindi, Thai, Arabic or rare scripts fragment into many tokens, down to individual bytes. The same meaning can cost 2-5x more tokens, which raises cost, latency and context usage. Mitigations: pick a model with a larger multilingual vocabulary, measure per language, and budget by language.

title: Tokenization artifacts
text: Explain why LLMs struggle with spelling, counting letters, arithmetic and odd whitespace, and what "glitch tokens" are. How do you work around each? The model never sees characters; it sees opaque token IDs, so "strawberry" may be 2-3 chunks and letter-level questions require memorized facts about chunks. Numbers split into inconsistent chunks, which hurts digit alignment in arithmetic. Whitespace is part of tokens, so trailing spaces or indentation change the input. Glitch tokens are vocabulary entries that were in the tokenizer's corpus but barely seen in model training, so their embeddings are undertrained and behave erratically. Workarounds: tools or code for exact operations, spaced-out/char-split inputs, normalization, and tokenizer-aware tests.

title: Chat template internals and injection
text: What goes wrong if user text contains special-token strings like < im end , and how should a serving stack handle special tokens at tokenization time? If the tokenizer parses special-token strings inside user content into real control tokens, a user can forge turn boundaries, such as closing their own turn and fabricating a system or assistant turn. So I tokenize untrusted content as plain text special-token parsing disabled , apply the template's control tokens only around it, and test that forged markers become ordinary multi-token text.

title: Token boundaries and prompt endings
text: Why can the exact end of a prompt a trailing space, partial word, or a prefilled string change the model's output, and how do you handle it in completion and constrained-generation code? The model scores whole tokens. If my prompt ends mid-token boundary, for example "http:" where training almost always had "http://" as one token, or a trailing space where the next token would have carried that space, the model is conditioned on a split it rarely saw and gives skewed output. Fixes: don't end prompts with a space, end at natural token boundaries, or use token healing: back up one token and constrain the first generated token to start with the removed text.

title: Self-attention step by step
text: Walk me through self-attention for one layer, with tensor shapes. What are Q, K and V, and where do they come from? "The input is a tensor x of shape B, T, d . I project it three times with learned matrices into queries, keys and values. Scores are Q times K-transpose, giving a T, T matrix per head. I scale, apply a causal mask, softmax each row, and use those weights to take a weighted sum of V. Each token's output is a mixture of value vectors from the tokens it is allowed to see, then an output projection W o mixes it back to d."

title: Scaled dot-product, sqrt(d_k)
text: Why do we divide attention scores by sqrt d k ? What happens if you do not? "If query and key entries have unit variance, their dot product has variance d k, so its standard deviation grows like sqrt d k . Large scores push softmax into a near one-hot regime where gradients vanish. Dividing by sqrt d k restores unit variance so softmax stays in a trainable range."

title: Transformers vs RNNs
text: Why did transformers replace RNNs/LSTMs for language modelling? What did we give up? "Training. An RNN has to process tokens sequentially, so you cannot parallelize across time and GPUs sit idle. A transformer processes all positions in parallel with matmuls, so it scales on modern hardware. Also any two tokens are one attention hop apart, versus up to n hops through an RNN state. The price is O n^2 attention compute and a KV cache that grows with context, whereas an RNN has a constant-size state."

title: Causal masking
text: What is causal masking, how is it implemented, and why can a decoder train on all positions in parallel but must generate one token at a time? "A causal mask sets scores for future positions to minus infinity before softmax so token i only attends to tokens up to i. In training we feed the whole sequence and predict the next token at every position at once, which is valid because the mask prevents leakage. At inference the next token does not exist yet, so we generate one at a time and reuse the KV cache of earlier tokens."

title: Multi-head attention
text: Why multi-head attention rather than one big attention? Does it cost more parameters or compute? "I split the d-dimensional model into h heads of size d k = d/h, run attention independently in each subspace, concatenate, then project with W o. Parameters and FLOPs are essentially the same as one big head. The benefit is that a single softmax can only produce one weighting per query; with several heads a token can attend to different positions for different reasons, such as syntax, copying or position, in parallel."

title: Residual stream
text: What is the residual stream, and what does each transformer block do to it? "Each token has a d-dimensional vector that flows through the whole network. Every attention and FFN sub-layer reads from it, computes an update, and adds the update back. Because of the skip connection the stream is a running sum of all earlier contributions, and gradients flow straight through the identity path, which is what makes deep stacks trainable."

title: Sinusoidal vs learned positional encodings
text: Why does a transformer need positional information, and how do sinusoidal and learned absolute position embeddings differ? "Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: shuffle the tokens and the outputs shuffle identically, so it has no notion of order. We inject position either by adding a vector per position to the embeddings or by modifying the attention scores. Sinusoidal encodings are a fixed function of position; learned embeddings are a trainable table. Both are absolute and neither extrapolates reliably past the trained length, which is why modern LLMs moved to relative schemes like RoPE."

title: LayerNorm vs RMSNorm
text: What is the difference between LayerNorm and RMSNorm, and why do most modern LLMs use RMSNorm? "LayerNorm subtracts the mean, divides by the standard deviation, then applies a learned scale and bias. RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction and the bias and divides only by the root mean square, keeping a learned scale. It is cheaper and simpler, and in practice quality is the same, because the re-centering turned out not to matter much while the re-scaling does."

title: Pre-norm vs post-norm
text: What is the difference between pre-norm and post-norm transformer blocks, and why did LLMs standardize on pre-norm? "Post-norm, as in the original paper, applies the norm after adding the residual: x = Norm x + Sublayer x . Pre-norm applies it to the sub-layer input: x = x + Sublayer Norm x . Pre-norm leaves an unobstructed identity path from input to output, so gradients flow well and deep models train stably without careful warmup. Post-norm can reach slightly better quality when it trains, but it is fragile at depth, so nearly all LLMs use pre-norm."

title: FFN and SwiGLU
text: What does the feed-forward block do in a transformer, and what is SwiGLU? Why is d ff not 4x d model in Llama-style models? "The FFN is a per-token two-layer MLP that expands to a wider hidden size and projects back; it is where most parameters and a lot of factual storage live. SwiGLU replaces the single activation with a gated product: SiLU x W1 times x W3 , then W2. Because it has three matrices instead of two, models shrink the hidden size to roughly 8/3 of d instead of 4 to keep the parameter count equal."

title: Self-attention implementation
text: Find all the bugs, say which one explains the too-good loss, and how you would have caught it before a day of GPU time was wasted. A teammate wrote a from-scratch causal attention layer for a small 125M-parameter GPT trained on 2B tokens. Training loss drops to 0.15 within 2,000 steps a healthy run on this data should plateau near 3.0 . Sampling from the checkpoint produces repetitive nonsense. Validation loss on a held-out split computed by the same code is also 0.2. The code: def attn x, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, n heads : B, T, D = x.shape D = 768, n heads = 12 dk = D // n heads 64 q = x @ Wq .view B, n heads, T, dk k = x @ Wk .view B, n heads, T, dk v = x @ Wv .view B, n heads, T, dk s = q @ k.transpose -2, -1 / D 0.5 mask = torch.tril torch.ones T, T, device=x.device s = s mask a = torch.softmax s, dim=-2 o = a @ v .view B, T, D return o @ Wo Colleagues suggest it is "just a learning-rate issue" and that the tokenizer might be leaking labels.

title: RoPE
text: How does Rotary Position Embedding RoPE work, and why did it become the default in open LLMs? "RoPE doesn't add a position vector to the embeddings. It rotates the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their position, in 2-D pairs of dimensions with different frequencies. The dot product between a rotated query at position m and a rotated key at position n depends only on m minus n, so attention sees relative position directly, with no learned table and no extra parameters."

title: ALiBi vs RoPE
text: Compare ALiBi and RoPE. When would you pick one, and what are their length-extrapolation behaviors? "ALiBi adds a linear penalty proportional to token distance directly to the attention scores, with a fixed head-specific slope; no position vectors at all. RoPE rotates Q and K. ALiBi extrapolates to longer inputs more gracefully out of the box but biases heavily toward recent tokens and has seen less adoption; RoPE gives better quality at trained lengths in most open models and can be extended with scaling methods, so it won."

title: MHA vs MQA vs GQA
text: Explain MHA, MQA and GQA. What do they change, and why does it matter for serving? "In MHA every query head has its own key and value head. MQA shares a single K/V head across all query heads. GQA is the middle: query heads are split into groups and each group shares one K/V head. The KV cache stores keys and values, so cache size per token scales with the number of K/V heads. GQA cuts the cache by h/g, for example 4x with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, with quality close to MHA."

title: KV-cache size math
text: How many concurrent 4k sequences does each model fit? Which do you pick and what would change your mind? You must self-host a chat model on a single 24 GB GPU 22.4 GiB usable total; budget 90% = 20.1 GiB for an internal tool. Typical request: 3,500 prompt + 500 output tokens, so plan for 4,096 tokens per sequence. Two bf16 candidates: - Model A: Llama-2-7B-style, 6.74B params, 32 layers, 32 KV heads MHA , head dim 128. - Model B: Llama-3-8B-style, 8.03B params, 32 layers, 8 KV heads GQA , head dim 128. A colleague says "A is smaller, so it will serve more users." Ignore activations and fragmentation for the first pass. Quality is comparable for this task.

title: Prefill vs decode
text: Explain the symptom mechanically and propose the fix. An internal assistant serves Llama-3-8B-class bf16 on one H100 80 GB . Usual prompts are 1,000 tokens; inter-token latency ITL p99 is 25 ms. After a rollout letting users paste whole documents, support reports "the chat freezes for a second". Dashboard: when a 30,000-token request arrives, every other active stream shows an ITL spike to 1.3 s, then recovers. GPU memory use is 62%, error rate 0%. Someone suggests the KV cache is full. Someone else suggests network problems.

title: O(n^2) attention and FlashAttention
text: Why is attention O n^2 , and how does FlashAttention make long sequences feasible without approximating attention? "Each of the n queries is scored against n keys, so both compute and the score matrix are O n^2 . Standard attention writes that n by n matrix to GPU high-bandwidth memory and reads it back for softmax and for the V multiply. FlashAttention tiles Q, K and V into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM, computes softmax incrementally with a running max and sum, and never materializes the full matrix. The result is exact attention with O n extra memory and far fewer HBM reads and writes, which gives the speedup."

title: KV-cache capacity at scale
text: Estimate GPUs required and say which levers reduce it. Your service runs a 70B-class model 80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, bf16 weights = 140 GB, bf16 KV cache . title: Parameter count
text: Derive the parameter count of a decoder-only transformer from its config. How do you check "8B" for a Llama-3-8B-style model? "Per layer: attention projections plus FFN plus norms, times layers, plus embeddings and the LM head if untied . For d = 4096, 32 layers, 8 KV heads of dim 128, SwiGLU with d ff = 14336 and a 128,256-token vocabulary: about 218M per layer, 6.98B for layers, plus 525M for embeddings and 525M for the untied head, which sums to about 8.03B."

title: FLOPs estimates
text: Estimate the FLOPs to train and to run inference on a transformer. Where do 6ND and 2N come from, and where does the formula break? "Every parameter participates in one multiply and one add per token in the forward pass, so inference costs about 2N FLOPs per token. Backward costs about twice the forward, so training is about 6N per token, or 6ND for D tokens. This ignores the attention score terms, which add roughly 4 x L x d x T per token and matter at long context, and it ignores the real-world efficiency gap, usually 30-50% of peak."

title: What attention heads do (induction, sinks)
text: What have we learned about what attention heads actually do? Explain induction heads and attention sinks, and why they matter in practice. "Induction heads are a two-head circuit that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies what came next, which is a main mechanism behind in-context pattern completion. Attention sinks are tokens, usually the first, that soak up a large share of attention mass because softmax must sum to one; keeping them in the cache is what makes sliding-window streaming work. Both are empirical findings, not guarantees."

title: Sparse/windowed attention and MLA
text: Beyond GQA, what techniques cut attention's cost or KV memory at long context sliding-window, local/global layers, MLA , and what do they trade away? "Sliding-window attention limits each token to a fixed recent window so cache and compute become O window ; information still propagates across layers, but exact long-range recall is limited. Interleaving local and global layers keeps a few full-context layers. Multi-head latent attention compresses K and V into a low-rank latent per token so the cache is much smaller while keeping near-MHA quality. Each trades exactness or complexity for memory."

title: Numerical stability in attention

A 3B-parameter model is being continued-pretrained in fp16 mixed precision loss scaling on on 64 GPUs after a data-mix change. At step 41,200 the loss jumps from 2.31 to 9.8 and the log shows grad norm: inf for 12 consecutive steps, then training reports nan loss. The same config was stable in bf16 on a previous run. Logs show attention logits in layer 24 with max score 7.3e4 pre-softmax shortly before the failure. Data team notes the new mix contains many long repetitive log files. For 8,192-token prompts the process OOMs during prefill even though the KV cache for one sequence is only 1 GiB 128 KiB/token and weights are 15 GiB the logs show CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 3.91 GiB . Memory profile shows a single large allocation right at the end of the forward pass. A teammate proposes upgrading to a 48 GB GPU. Another proposes lowering max context to 4k.

title: Decoder-only vs encoder-only vs encoder-decoder
text: Explain the three transformer architecture families encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder . What is the real difference, and give one production use for each. "The blocks are the same; what changes is the attention mask and the objective. Encoder-only, like BERT, uses bidirectional attention and masked-token prediction, so it makes great representations for classification, NER and embeddings but cannot generate. Decoder-only, like GPT or Llama, uses a causal mask and next-token prediction, so it generates and is what chat LLMs use. Encoder-decoder, like T5 or the original Transformer, encodes the input bidirectionally and a decoder cross-attends to it, which suits translation and summarization. For a classifier at 5k QPS I would reach for an encoder; for open-ended generation, a decoder."

title: Why decoder-only dominates
text: Why did decoder-only models win for general-purpose LLMs, when encoder-decoder looks like a more natural fit for "input to output" tasks? "Three reasons. Every training token is a supervised signal in next-token prediction, so data efficiency per token is high and the objective scales cleanly. One stack handles every task as 'continue this text', so prompting, in-context learning and instruction tuning all fit with no task-specific heads. And inference infrastructure is simpler: one KV cache, one decode loop. Encoder-decoder isn't worse in principle at small scale; decoder-only just got the most scaling investment and tooling."

title: MoE active vs total parameters
text: A model card says "47B total parameters, 13B active". What does that mean, and what does it imply for compute, memory and quality? "In a Mixture-of-Experts model, each FFN layer is replaced by many expert FFNs plus a router, and each token is sent to only a few of them. Total parameters are everything that must exist in memory; active parameters are what a single token actually touches. So per-token FLOPs look like a 13B dense model, but I still need memory for all 47B weights. MoE saves compute, not memory. Quality tends to land between a 13B dense model and a 47B dense model, usually closer to the latter on knowledge-heavy tasks."

title: MoE routing and load balancing
text: How does routing work in a Mixture-of-Experts layer, and how do training recipes stop the router from collapsing onto a few experts? "A small linear router scores each token against every expert, we keep the top-k scores, softmax them into weights, and the layer output is the weighted sum of those experts' outputs. Left alone, the router self-reinforces: experts that get more tokens train faster, get chosen more, and the rest starve. So training adds an auxiliary load-balancing loss that penalizes uneven token distribution, plus an expert capacity limit that drops or reroutes overflow tokens. Some newer recipes, like DeepSeek-V3's, balance with per-expert bias terms instead of a loss, to avoid hurting the main objective."

title: Reasoning models and test-time compute
text: What is a "reasoning model" and what is test-time inference-time compute? How does it differ from just prompting a normal model with "think step by step"? "A reasoning model is trained, usually with reinforcement learning on verifiable outcomes like math answers and unit tests, to produce a long chain of thought before the final answer, and to use that scratchpad to explore, check and backtrack. Test-time compute means I spend more tokens at inference to get better answers, so quality scales with thinking length, not only model size. 'Think step by step' on a normal model is a prompt that elicits a short chain; a reasoning model has learned the behavior, so it is more reliable on hard problems, but it is slower and costs more because the thinking tokens are generated and typically billed."

title: Choosing an architecture
text: Which architecture and model family do you pick, and how do you justify it? A fintech must classify incoming customer emails into 40 intents. Volume is 3M emails/day peak 120 QPS , average 250 tokens, p95 latency budget 150 ms, one 16 GB GPU class per node. They have 60k labeled examples; current macro-F1 is 0.84 with a TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline. A teammate proposes calling a hosted frontier chat model with a 12-example few-shot prompt "it will be 0.9 out of the box" . Estimated prompt: 1,800 tokens in, 10 out. Illustrative price: $2.50 per 1M input tokens.

title: Multimodal architectures
text: How does a vision-language model like LLaVA let a text LLM "see" an image? Walk through the architecture and what is trained when. "A vision encoder, typically a CLIP ViT, turns the image into a grid of patch embeddings. A small projector, a linear layer or MLP, maps those into the LLM's embedding space so they look like token embeddings. They get concatenated with the text tokens and the decoder processes everything as one sequence. Training is usually staged: first train only the projector to align vision and language, then fine-tune the projector and LLM on visual instruction data. Image tokens consume context and compute like text tokens do."

title: State-space and hybrid models
text: What are state-space models like Mamba, how do they differ from attention, and why do production teams build hybrids? "A state-space layer compresses the history into a fixed-size state that it updates per token, like a learned recurrence, so compute grows linearly with sequence length and decode memory is constant, with no growing KV cache. Mamba makes the state update input-dependent, 'selective', so it can choose what to remember. The weakness is that a fixed state is lossy, so exact recall of arbitrary earlier tokens, like in-context retrieval, is weaker than attention. Hybrids such as Jamba interleave a few attention layers with many Mamba layers to get most of the memory savings and keep the recall."

title: Small vs large models
text: When would you choose a small model 1-8B over a large one 70B+ or a frontier API ? What do you give up? "I pick the smallest model that passes my eval at the required reliability. Small models win on cost, latency, on-device or private deployment, and fine-tuning ease. They lose on broad knowledge, multi-step reasoning, instruction-following on messy prompts, and robustness to out-of-distribution inputs. Narrow, well-defined tasks like extraction, classification and routing are where a tuned small model often matches a big one; open-ended reasoning and long, ambiguous tasks still favor large models."

title: MoE memory sizing
text: Why did it fail, what do you propose, and what do you tell the PM about "same speed"? You serve a dense 13B model bf16 on single 40 GB GPUs at 6 QPS with p95 of 1.2 s. Product wants better quality, and a vendor suggests a 47B-total / 13B-active MoE "same speed as what you have now" . Traffic will grow 10x to 60 QPS next quarter. GPUs available: 80 GB class, 8 per node. Average request: 1,500 prompt tokens, 300 output tokens. KV per token for this MoE is 128 KiB GQA, bf16; assume the same as the dense model for simplicity . Staging test on one 80 GB GPU: model fails to load.

title: MoE serving implications
text: You are asked to serve a large MoE model in production. What is different from serving a dense model of the same active size? Cover parallelism, batching, latency and failure modes. "Three differences. Memory: all experts must be resident, so the model needs multi-GPU sharding even though the compute is small. Communication: with expert parallelism each GPU holds a subset of experts, so tokens must be sent to the GPUs hosting their chosen experts and back, an all-to-all per MoE layer, which becomes the bottleneck on slow interconnects. Load imbalance: routing is data-dependent, so a hot expert makes one GPU the straggler and sets the step latency. Batching helps utilization because more tokens means every expert has work, but small batches waste bandwidth by reading experts that few tokens use."

title: MoE routing implementation
text: Find the bug and explain how you would prove it. You port a top-2 MoE layer from a reference implementation. Offline tests pass on shapes, but compared with reference outputs on 1,000 prompts the ported model has mean logit difference of 0.8 and perplexity rises from 6.1 to 7.4. Training-time load-balancing loss is not involved inference only . Code: def route x, router, k=2 : probs = torch.softmax router x , dim=-1 T, E topv, topi = probs.topk k, dim=-1 return topv, topi used directly as combine weights def forward x, router, experts : w, idx = route x, router out = torch.zeros like x for s in range 2 : for e in range len experts : m = idx :, s == e out m += w m, s, None experts e x m return out Distractors: the team suspects bf16 precision, a tokenizer difference, or FlashAttention versions.

title: Distillation
text: Explain knowledge distillation for LLMs. What are the variants, what does a student actually learn, and when is distillation the right architecture decision? "Distillation trains a small student to imitate a large teacher. Classic logit distillation minimizes KL divergence between the student's and teacher's token distributions, which carries more signal than one-hot labels because the teacher's soft probabilities encode which wrong answers are nearly right. For LLMs the common practical version is sequence-level: generate outputs, including reasoning traces, from the teacher and SFT the student on them. DeepSeek did this at scale, distilling R1 reasoning traces into 1.5B to 70B models. It is right when I have a narrow, high-volume task and a strong teacher; it is wrong when the student lacks the capacity or when the teacher's license forbids it."

title: Reasoning models cost and latency
text: How do you diagnose and what do you do? A coding assistant moved from a standard chat model to a reasoning model after a quality push. Traffic: 400k requests/day. Before: average 900 input tokens and 350 output tokens, p95 latency 4 s. After: average 900 input, 350 visible output plus 3,800 reasoning tokens, p95 latency 38 s. Illustrative prices: $3 per 1M input, $15 per 1M output tokens for both verify real pricing; reasoning tokens bill as output on most providers . Pass@1 on the internal eval rose from 61% to 74% overall, but on the 55% of traffic classified as "simple edits and explanations" it rose only from 93% to 94%. Support tickets about "slow responses" tripled; the CFO asks for a 40% cost cut.

title: Multimodal token cost
text: Explain the spike and what you would do. A claims app lets users upload photos of damage and asks a hosted vision-language model to describe them. Last week the median upload was a 1024x768 phone photo costing about 800 image tokens. After a mobile release that sends original 12 MP photos 4032x3024 , logs show: prompt tokens=6,412 per request up from 1,000 , p95 latency 3 s to 9 s, and the daily bill up 5x. Quality on a spot check is unchanged. The model tiling behavior is vendor-defined illustrative: images are split into 512px tiles at 170 tokens each plus a base of 85, with large images downscaled so the short side is at most 768px before tiling; verify the actual provider's documentation .

title: Distillation migration
text: How do you plan the migration? A document-extraction product calls a large model illustrative: $5 per 1M input, $15 per 1M output for 2M invoices/month: 3,000 input and 400 output tokens each, about $42k/month. Field-level accuracy is 96.5% with p95 of 6 s. The team distilled a 8B student from 150k teacher-labeled invoices teacher outputs, not human-verified . Offline on a held-out set the student scores 95.8%. Shadow traffic for a week shows 95.9% agreement-adjusted accuracy, but customer C about 4% of volume, many scanned multi-language invoices shows 88%. Product wants to cut over this month.

title: Test-time compute strategies
text: Besides a model that thinks in a long chain of thought, what other ways can you spend extra inference compute to improve answer quality? What are the trade-offs? "The main families are parallel and sequential. Parallel: sample N answers and pick one, by majority vote self-consistency , by a reward model or verifier best-of-N , or by running tests for code. Sequential: let the model revise, critique and retry using feedback, or use a longer thinking budget. Parallel methods need a way to choose; they work best when a cheap, reliable verifier exists, like unit tests or exact-match math answers. Cost scales roughly linearly with N, while quality gains flatten, so I tune N against the verifier's accuracy and the latency budget."

title: Multimodal vs text pipeline
text: What do you recommend, and how do you handle the ambiguity? A procurement team asks: "Use the new multimodal model so we can just send PDFs and get structured line items." Volume: 50k PDFs/month, 5 to 40 pages each median 12 , mix of digital-native and scanned, 15% with dense tables; they need totals reconciled to the cent and an audit trail. A vision call for a page costs roughly 1,200 image tokens illustrative ; the same page extracted as text is about 600 text tokens. The vendor pitches the multimodal path as "no OCR pipeline needed." There is no labeled dataset yet.

title: Pretraining objective
text: What is an LLM actually trained to do during pretraining, and how does that one objective produce models that can write code, translate and answer questions? "Pretraining minimizes cross-entropy on next-token prediction over trillions of tokens: given tokens 1..t, maximize the log-probability of token t+1. Nothing else is supervised. To predict text well across the web, the model has to compress grammar, facts, code semantics and reasoning patterns into its weights, so those skills emerge as a side effect. The result is a base model that continues text, not one that follows instructions."

title: Base vs chat models
text: What exactly changes between a base model and the chat/instruct model you call through an API? When would you deliberately choose the base model? "A base model is the raw pretrained next-token predictor. The chat model is that same network after supervised fine-tuning on instruction/response pairs, then preference optimization RLHF, DPO or similar , often plus safety and tool-use training. Weights are changed modestly, but behavior changes a lot: it follows a chat template, answers instead of continuing, refuses some requests, and is more verbose and agreeable. I pick a base model for few-shot pattern completion, calibrated probabilities, creative diversity, or as the starting point for my own fine-tune."

title: Pretraining data pipeline
text: Walk me through how a pretraining corpus is built from raw web crawl. Why do deduplication, quality filtering and data mixing matter so much? "Raw crawl goes through extraction HTML to text , language ID, heuristic filters, model-based quality filters, PII and toxicity handling, deduplication at exact and fuzzy levels, decontamination against benchmarks, then mixing across sources web, code, books, math, multilingual with chosen proportions and often an annealing phase of high-quality data at the end. Dedup reduces memorization and wasted compute; filtering raises the average quality per token; mixing sets the capability profile."

title: SFT and instruction data
text: What is supervised fine-tuning instruction tuning for an LLM, what does the data look like, and what does the loss actually apply to? "SFT continues training the base model with the same next-token loss, but on curated prompt/response pairs formatted with the chat template. Loss is usually computed only on the assistant tokens, not the prompt. It teaches format, style and instruction-following, not new knowledge. A few thousand to tens of thousands of very high-quality examples can work; quality beats quantity."

title: SFT pipeline
text: What is wrong, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it without retraining blindly? You SFT a 7B open-weight base model on 18,000 customer-support conversations, 2 epochs, LR 2e-5. Eval loss looks great 0.31, train 0.29 but in a live canary the model answers correctly and then keeps going, inventing a fake "User:" turn and answering itself, in about 35% of requests, averaging 480 output tokens instead of 90. Your data prep: def to text ex : text = "" for m in ex "messages" : text += f"{m 'role' .upper }: {m 'content' }\n" return {"text": text} trainer: standard causal LM loss on "text", max len 1024, no special tokens added inference: tokenizer.apply chat template msgs, add generation prompt=True , stop on eos Red herrings: GPU is fine, the LR is typical, and eval loss is low.

title: Knowledge cutoff
text: What is a model's knowledge cutoff, why is it fuzzy, and how do you design applications around it? "The cutoff is the date after which the pretraining data contains little or nothing. The model's weights know nothing newer, and it is fuzzy because data about recent months is sparse the web has not finished writing about them , so the model's effective knowledge is weaker near the cutoff than the stated date suggests. Models also often misreport their own cutoff. In applications I inject the current date, and use retrieval or tools for anything time-sensitive."

title: RLHF pipeline
text: Explain the classic RLHF pipeline: what are the stages, how is the reward model trained, and what does PPO optimize? "Three stages: SFT on demonstrations; train a reward model on human pairwise preferences using a Bradley-Terry loss; then optimize the SFT policy with PPO to maximize reward minus a KL penalty to the SFT reference, so it does not drift into gibberish that fools the reward model. InstructGPT showed labelers preferred a 1.3B RLHF model over the 175B GPT-3 base."

title: DPO vs RLHF
text: How does Direct Preference Optimization work, and when would you choose it over PPO-based RLHF? "DPO rewrites the RLHF objective so the optimal policy is a closed-form function of the reward. That lets you express the reward as beta times the log-ratio of policy to reference, and train directly on preference pairs with a simple logistic loss.
